And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'"<sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel.<sup>4</sup>David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.<sup>5</sup>At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.<sup>6</sup>And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off"—thinking, "David cannot come in here."<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David.<sup>8</sup>And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house."<sup>9</sup>And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward.<sup>10</sup>And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him.<sup>11</sup>And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house.<sup>12</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.<sup>13</sup>And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.<sup>14</sup>And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,<sup>15</sup>Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>16</sup>Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.<sup>17</sup>When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.<sup>18</sup>Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>19</sup>And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand."<sup>20</sup>And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.<sup>22</sup>And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>23</sup>And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees.<sup>24</sup>And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."<sup>25</sup>And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
5.overview:
After seven and a half years, the whole thing is settled by a delegation walking into Hebron with a three-part argument: kinship, David's record, and the word of God — and all three are true. The last one is the tell. They could quote God's promise about David, Abner had reminded them of it two chapters earlier, and they fought a war anyway until the politics caught up with the theology. He makes a covenant with them before the LORD and only then is anointed: a constitutional act, not an absolute one.

He is thirty. Samuel poured oil on him as a boy, so roughly fifteen years lie between the promise and the throne, and we know exactly what was in them — a giant, four spears, a window and a rope, two caves, a burnt village, sixteen months in a Philistine town. God said it and then took fifteen years, and explained the delay to nobody.

Then Jerusalem, which is the shrewdest decision in the book: a Jebusite city Israel had never taken (Judg. 1:21), belonging to no tribe — not Judah, which would look like the south annexing the country, and not Benjamin, which would be unbearable. He takes it through the water shaft. And verse 12 is the chapter's theological sentence, with all the weight in the last four words: God established him king for the sake of his people Israel. The kingdom was not a reward for patience. It was given to Israel, and David is the arrangement by which they get it.

The next verse is that he took more wives, and the narrator says nothing at all. Then two Philistine battles in the same valley — and the point of having both is that he inquires the second time too, and gets a different answer. A word God gave last time is not a standing order for this time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Your Bone and Your Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All the tribes come to Hebron with a three-part argument: behold, we are your bone and your flesh; you were the one who led Israel out and in even when Saul was king; and the LORD said to you, "You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel" (vv. 1-2). The elders make a covenant with him before the LORD at Hebron and anoint him king over Israel (v. 3). He is thirty years old, and reigns forty years — seven and a half at Hebron over Judah, thirty-three in Jerusalem over all of it (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Kinship, record, and the word of God, in that order — and every one of the three is true. They have known the third one for years; Abner told them so to their faces (3:17-18).
verseByVerse.examples: This is the third anointing, and the arithmetic behind it is the point. Samuel poured oil on a boy in Bethlehem; David is thirty now. Somewhere near fifteen years have passed between the promise and the throne, and he spent most of them in caves and in a Philistine town.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'" So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel. David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and your flesh."'

They come to him. After seven and a half years, the whole thing is settled by a delegation walking into Hebron and making a speech.

The speech has three arguments, and they are the three things people ever appeal to.

The first is kinship. We are your bone and your flesh. It is the oldest belonging formula in Scripture — Adam said it when he first saw the woman, bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Gen. 2:23) — and here it is applied to a nation and a king. We are not two peoples. Whatever the last seven years looked like, you are one of us.

'"In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'"'

The second argument is his record, and they are honest about the awkward part of it. When Saul was king over us — they name the man they served — it was you who led out and brought in Israel. Everybody remembers who actually fought the wars.

The third is the word of God, and it is the one that decides the matter. The LORD said to you.

They knew. That is the thing to notice. The elders of Israel could quote God's promise about David, and Abner had reminded them of it two chapters ago — for some time past you have been seeking David as king over you (3:17). This was not news to anyone in the room, and it had not been news for years, and they fought a war anyway until the politics caught up with the theology.

Note the word they use: shepherd. It is what he was when Samuel sent for him, and it is what God calls the office. A king in Israel is a man who looks after sheep that are not his.

'So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel.'

He does not simply accept the crown. He makes a covenant with them, before the LORD, and then they anoint him.

That is a constitutional act, and it is not what an absolute monarch does. There are terms, and they are sworn in God's presence, and the king is bound by them as much as the people are. Israel's kingship was always meant to sit under a law rather than over it — the king was required to write out a copy of the law for himself and read it every day of his life (Deut. 17:18-19).

'David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.'

Thirty, and now do the arithmetic, because it is the whole story of the last twenty chapters.

Samuel poured oil on the head of the eighth son of Jesse in his father's house at Bethlehem, and he was a boy then — young enough that nobody had thought to call him in from the sheep. Say fifteen or sixteen. He is thirty here.

So roughly fifteen years passed between the anointing and the throne, and we know exactly what was in them: a giant, a harp, four spears, a window with a rope, a priest's massacre, two caves, three thousand chosen men twice, sixteen months in a Philistine town, a burnt village, and seven and a half years as king of one tribe out of twelve.

God said it and then took fifteen years to do it, and did not explain the delay to anybody.

'At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.'

Forty years in total, and the writer splits it for us so that the shape of the reign is clear before it starts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David goes to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, who taunt him: you will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off (v. 6). He takes the stronghold anyway, by way of the water shaft, and it becomes the city of David (vv. 7-9). And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him (v. 10). Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen and builds him a house (v. 11). And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem belongs to nobody. It is not in Benjamin, which is Saul's tribe, and not in Judah, which is David's; it is a Jebusite town Israel had never managed to take (Judg. 1:21). For twelve tribes that have just spent seven years fighting each other, a capital that belongs to none of them is worth more than any fortress.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 12 is the sentence the chapter is built on, with the weight in its last clause: for the sake of his people Israel. He knows two things — that God did this, and that God did not do it for him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off"—thinking, "David cannot come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house." And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him. And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house. And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off" — thinking, "David cannot come in here."'

Jerusalem at this point is not an Israelite city and never has been.

Judges records the failure plainly: the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day (Judg. 1:21). It has been sitting there, unconquered, for the whole period of the judges and the whole reign of Saul, and everybody has learned to live around it.

The Jebusites are confident enough to be funny about it. Even the blind and the lame could hold this place against you.

They have grounds. The city sits on a spur with steep ravines on three sides and a spring below it, and it had held out against Israel for three centuries.

A word about that taunt, because commentators disagree and it is better to say so than to invent certainty. It may be simple mockery — our weakest men could stop you. It may be a reference to defenders posted on the walls as an insult. Some have suggested a ritual meaning, disabled figures set up as a kind of oath against attackers. The Hebrew of verses 6 and 8 is genuinely difficult and the ancient versions differ. What is certain is the tone: contempt.

'Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David.'

One sentence, and no account of how it was done.

'And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house."'

He goes in through the plumbing.

The city's water came from the Gihon spring, outside the walls at the bottom of the slope, and there was a shaft cut through the rock so the defenders could reach it without going outside. A tunnel system of exactly this kind has been excavated on that hill. David sends men up the one route the walls do not cover.

The rest of the verse is harsh, and the writer records the saying without endorsing it. There is also something a reader should hold on to for four chapters' time. The taunt of the blind and the lame becomes a proverb about who does not come into the house — and in chapter 9 the man David goes looking for, and seats at his own table for the rest of his life, is crippled in both his feet.

'And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward.'

Now consider what he has chosen, because it is one of the shrewdest decisions in the Old Testament.

Jerusalem belongs to no tribe.

It is not in Judah, which is his own tribe and would have looked like the south annexing the country. It is not in Benjamin, which is Saul's tribe and would have been unbearable. It is a foreign city that Israel never took, sitting on the border between north and south, and the moment David captures it, it belongs to him personally rather than to any tribal inheritance — which is why it is called the city of David and not the city of Judah.

He has just spent seven and a half years watching a nation tear itself in half along exactly those lines. A capital that belongs to nobody is the one thing that can hold twelve tribes who have been killing each other, and he takes it in the first campaign of his reign.

'And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him.'

The writer will not let the credit settle in the wrong place. He became greater, for the LORD was with him.

'And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house.'

A foreign king sends materials and craftsmen, unasked.

Tyre is the great Phoenician port up the coast, and cedar is its export — the timber everyone in the region wanted and only Lebanon had. Hiram is making an investment in a neighbour who has suddenly become worth having as a friend.

Keep that cedar in mind. Two chapters from now the first thing David says to Nathan is that he is living in a house of cedar while the ark of God sits in a tent, and this is the cedar he means. The gift becomes the occasion of the greatest promise in the Old Testament.

'And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.'

Here is the theological sentence of the chapter, and everything is in the last four words.

He knows two things. The first is that God did this — not the elders, not the covenant at Hebron, not the water shaft, not Hiram's cedar. God established him.

The second is harder and rarer. For the sake of his people Israel.

The kingdom is not a reward for fifteen patient years. It is not compensation for the caves. It was not given to David for David; it was given to Israel, and David is the arrangement by which they get it. He is the shepherd the elders called him in verse 2, and the sheep are the point of the job.

That is the principle underneath every position of authority in Scripture, and it is the exact thing that will fail in chapter 11, when a king who is supposed to be at war stays home and uses the kingdom for himself. Everything good in this reign is downstream of verse 12, and everything catastrophic is downstream of forgetting it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — And David Took More Concubines and Wives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David (v. 13). Eleven more names follow, among them Solomon (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Read where this verse sits. He has just understood that the kingdom was given for the people's sake and not his own — and the very next sentence is about acquiring women. The narrator puts them side by side and does not say a word.
verseByVerse.examples: The law had spoken to Israel's king about exactly this, in advance: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). Six sons at Hebron became Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. This list adds eleven more, and one of them is Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David. And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.'

Read that immediately after verse 12, because the writer intends you to.

The previous sentence was the finest thing said about David in the book: he understood that God had exalted his kingdom for the sake of the people. The next sentence is that he took more women.

There is no transition, no comment, no rebuke. The narrator sets the two down in order and walks away, and that is how this writer does his most serious work. He did it with Gideon's ephod. He did it with the Amalekite's nationality. He does it here.

He took. It is the same verb the law used when it warned about this.

Israel's king had been given three prohibitions in advance, all in the same short passage. He must not multiply horses, or send people back to Egypt to get them. He must not multiply silver and gold. And in the middle: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17).

The reason is stated in the law itself, and it is not about appetite. Lest his heart turn away.

Two things follow from a household like this, and both of them arrive in this book.

The first is faction. Six sons by six mothers were born at Hebron, and eleven more names are about to be listed here. Those boys grow up as rivals with rival mothers and rival claims, and a palace of half-brothers is a civil war waiting for a trigger. Amnon rapes Tamar because she is only his half-sister. Absalom kills Amnon. Adonijah makes his move while the old king is dying. Every one of those crimes is possible because of the arrangement recorded in this verse.

The second is the habit itself. A man who has spent twenty years taking women when he wants them, lawfully, as kings do, is a man who has practised something. And one spring evening he will look down from a roof at a woman washing, and send to find out who she is, and send messengers, and take her (11:2-4). The same verb again.

'And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon,'

'Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.'

Eleven names, and two of them matter enormously.

Solomon — who will build the temple David wants to build, and inherit the throne and the covenant.

And Nathan, who is not the prophet but another son, and who is almost never mentioned again. He appears in one other place of consequence: Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus back through David not by way of Solomon but by way of this Nathan (Luke 3:31).

So a list dropped into a chapter as an aside, in a paragraph the narrator declines to comment on, contains the name the Messiah's line runs through.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines come up in force when they hear David has been made king over all Israel, and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim (vv. 17-18). And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" The answer is yes, and he breaks through them and names the place Baal-perazim — the LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a bursting flood (vv. 19-20). They leave their idols behind and David's men carry them away (v. 21). The Philistines come back and spread out in the same valley (v. 22). And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear... And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you" (vv. 23-24). He does exactly that, and strikes them from Geba to Gezer (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Same enemy. Same valley. Same king. And a different order from God — which is the entire reason the second episode is in the book. A word God gave last time is not a standing instruction for this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Note what the sign is. He is not told to attack when he judges the moment right; he is told to wait for a sound in the treetops and then move, for then the LORD has gone out before you. The victory is God's operation and David's men are following it in.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold. Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand." And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim. And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away. And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees. And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines." And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.'

The moment Israel is united, the Philistines move.

They had been perfectly happy with a divided country and a client king in Ziklag. A single kingdom under the man who killed Goliath is an existential problem, and they come up to end it before it starts.

'Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand."'

He asks.

By now this is the established rhythm of the man, and the writer records it every time because it is the difference between David's good years and everything else. He asked before going to Hebron. He asked four times at Keilah. He asked at Ziklag with his town in ashes. He asks here, and he asks the two questions he always asks: shall I go, and will you give them.

The answer is emphatic. I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand.

'And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.'

He names the ground after what God did, and the image is water.

Like a bursting flood — the picture is of a wadi in a storm, or a dam giving way: a wall of water that goes through whatever is in front of it because nothing built by people can stand against that much weight moving at once. That is what happened to the Philistine line, and David says so, and puts it on the map.

The name means the master of breakings-through, and Israel kept it.

'And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.'

They ran and left their gods on the field.

The reversal here is exact and any Israelite would have caught it. Twenty-odd years earlier the Philistines beat Israel at Aphek and carried the ark of God back to the temple of Dagon at Ashdod — and Dagon was found face down before it, and the next morning with his head and hands broken off on the threshold (1 Sam. 5:1-5). Now it is the other way round: the Philistines flee and their carried gods are picked up off the ground by the men who beat them.

The Chronicler adds what David did with them: he had them burned (1 Chron. 14:12), which is what the law required (Deut. 7:5, 25).

'And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.'

Same enemy. Same valley. Probably the same season.

Now watch what David does, because this is why the chapter contains two battles instead of one.

'And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees."'

He asks again. And God gives him a different answer.

Consider how easy it would have been not to ask. He has a word from God about this exact enemy, in this exact valley, from a matter of weeks ago, and it could not have been clearer: go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand. He obeyed it and it worked and he named a place after it.

Any reasonable man would treat that as covering the rematch.

He would have been wrong, because this time the answer is you shall not go up. Go round behind them instead. Different approach, different direction, different plan.

Why God changes the instruction is not stated and does not need to be. Perhaps the Philistines were expecting the frontal attack that had beaten them before. What the passage establishes is the principle, and the principle is that a word God gave last time is not a standing order for this time.

That is a thing believers get wrong constantly and in good faith. God blessed a thing once, so it becomes the method. A decision that was right in one season hardens into a policy for every season. And it can be sincere, and grateful, and a way of not asking anything ever again — because the answer is already on file.

David had every excuse to run on the previous instruction. He asked.

'"And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."'

The sign is a sound in the trees.

Not a scouting report, not a signal from a lookout, not David's own judgment of the moment. He is to wait in the dark behind an enemy army until he hears something moving in the tops of the balsam trees, and then go.

For then the LORD has gone out before you.

That is the theology of the whole chapter in one clause. The sound is not the wind giving David his cue to win a battle; it is the noise of God going out ahead of him. The LORD strikes the Philistine army and David's men follow him into it.

Picture what that waiting was like. Behind the enemy, at night, with the army in position and every soldier's instinct saying go — and the order is to stand still until you hear leaves move.

'And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.'

He does exactly what he was told, and the Philistine power in the hill country is broken from one end to the other.

This is the man at his best. Hold the picture clearly, because six chapters from now there is a spring evening when he does not ask anybody anything.

5.theology:
They knew, and fought anyway (v. 2). The elders quote God's own word about David as their third argument, and Abner had already reminded them they had wanted him for some time past (3:17). None of this was news, and it had not been news for years. And the word they use for the office is shepherd: a king in Israel is a man looking after sheep that are not his.

A covenant before the anointing (v. 3). He does not simply accept a crown. There are terms, sworn in God's presence, binding on him as much as on them — which is what Israel's kingship was always meant to be, a throne under the law rather than over it (Deut. 17:18-19).

Fifteen years (v. 4). A boy too young to be called in from the sheep, and a man of thirty. The gap is the whole of 1 Samuel 16-31 and 2 Samuel 1-4, and God never once explained it.

A capital belonging to nobody (vv. 6-9). Twelve tribes have just spent seven and a half years killing each other along tribal lines. Jerusalem is in neither rival tribe's territory, has never been Israelite at all, and becomes David's personally by conquest — which is why it is the city of David and not the city of Judah. Note also, for four chapters' time, that the Jebusite taunt turns the blind and the lame into a proverb about who does not come into the house — and the man David seeks out and seats at his own table in chapter 9 is crippled in both feet. (The exact sense of the taunt is genuinely disputed and the Hebrew is difficult; the tone is not in doubt.)

For the sake of his people Israel (v. 12). Two things known at once: that God did it, and that God did not do it for David. The kingdom is not a reward for fifteen patient years or compensation for the caves. It was given to Israel, and the king is the arrangement by which they receive it. That is the principle under every authority in Scripture, and it is the exact thing that fails in chapter 11, when a king who should be at war stays home and uses the kingdom for himself. Everything good in this reign is downstream of verse 12; everything catastrophic is downstream of forgetting it.

Verse 13, and the silence around it. The finest sentence in the book about David is immediately followed by David took more concubines and wives, with no transition and no rebuke. The law had warned Israel's king in advance and given the reason: lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). Two things follow, and both arrive in this book. Faction — a palace of half-brothers with rival mothers is a civil war waiting for a trigger, and Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah are all possible because of this arrangement. And habit: a man who has spent twenty years lawfully taking women when he wants them has practised something, and one spring evening he will look down from a roof and take again (11:4).

The gods left on the field (v. 21). The Philistines carried the ark into the house of Dagon and found their god face down and then broken on the threshold (1 Sam. 5:1-5). Now they run and leave their own idols to be picked up by the men who beat them. The Chronicler says David burned them (1 Chron. 14:12), as the law required.

The second inquiry is why the chapter has two battles (v. 23). Same enemy, same valley, a recent and emphatic word from God about exactly this — and the new answer is you shall not go up. Believers get this wrong constantly and in good faith: God blessed a thing once, so it becomes the method; a decision right for one season hardens into policy for every season. It can be sincere and grateful and still be a way of never asking again, because the answer is already on file. David had every excuse to run on the previous instruction. He asked.

The sound in the balsam trees (v. 24). Not a scout, not a signal, not his own read of the moment — stand still behind an enemy army until you hear leaves move. And the reason given is the theology of the chapter in one clause: for then the LORD has gone out before you. The sound is not a cue for David to win a battle; it is the noise of God going out ahead, and David's men follow him into it.
5.examples:
Then: A king who had just been handed a clear and emphatic word from God about how to beat a particular army in a particular valley met the same army in the same valley a few weeks later — and asked again, and was told to do something completely different, and to wait in the dark behind them until he heard a noise in the treetops.

Now: Verse 23 is the practical one and it is uncomfortable, because the mistake it guards against is made by grateful people. A prayer answered, a decision vindicated, a method God plainly blessed — and it quietly becomes the standing policy, so that the asking stops. What made David's second inquiry remarkable is that nobody would have blamed him for skipping it. And verse 12 is the other: he knew the kingdom had been given for the people's sake and not his own. Every position anybody holds — at work, at church, at home — is held on those terms or held wrongly, and chapter 11 is what forgetting it costs.

6.title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
6.text: <sup>1</sup>David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.<sup>2</sup>And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim.<sup>3</sup>And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart,<sup>4</sup>with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark.<sup>5</sup>And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.<sup>6</sup>And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled.<sup>7</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God.<sup>8</sup>And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day.<sup>9</sup>And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?"<sup>10</sup>So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.<sup>11</sup>And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.<sup>12</sup>And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing.<sup>13</sup>And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.<sup>14</sup>And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod.<sup>15</sup>So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn.<sup>16</sup>As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.<sup>17</sup>And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.<sup>18</sup>And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts<sup>19</sup>and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins to each one. Then all the people departed, each to his house.<sup>20</sup>And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!"<sup>21</sup>And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD—and I will celebrate before the LORD.<sup>22</sup>I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor."<sup>23</sup>And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
6.overview:
Thirty thousand men and a full orchestra, for the purpose of moving a box — which tells you how much David means it. The ark had sat in a private house for about twenty years while Saul reigned and lost a kingdom and never once sent for it, and this is the first genuinely good idea anybody has had about it in a generation. The intention is entirely right.

The method is Philistine. A new cart is exactly what the lords of the Philistines built to send the ark home, and they did it because they had no revelation, no law and no idea (1 Sam. 6:7). Israel had the book: the poles are never removed, the sons of Kohath were given no wagons because they carry it on the shoulder, and they must not touch the holy things, lest they die. Every one of those sentences was available, and thirty thousand men walked past all of them.

So the oxen stumble and Uzzah does what anyone would do in half a second, and dies for it. The sin was the cart; his hand is only where it surfaced. David says so himself later — we did not seek him according to the rule — and the we is the point. Then David is angry with God, and afraid, and both are recorded without apology; the ark goes aside to a foreigner's house and blesses it for three months. The same ark, the same country, the same season, and the difference is not in the ark.

The second attempt is carried on shoulders, with a sacrifice after six paces, and the king dances in a linen ephod — a priest's garment, not a royal one — and hands out bread and meat to every person in the crowd. And one woman watches from a window and despises him, and she is wrong, and she has been wronged more than anyone in the book so far.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — They Carried It on a New Cart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David gathers thirty thousand chosen men to bring up the ark which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim (vv. 1-2). And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill, with Uzzah and Ahio driving it (vv. 3-4). And the whole house of Israel celebrates before the LORD with songs, lyres, harps, tambourines, castanets and cymbals (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The impulse is entirely right. The ark had sat in a private house at Kiriath-jearim for about twenty years (1 Sam. 7:2) while nobody did anything about it, and David wants the presence of God at the centre of the nation's life. Thirty thousand men and a full orchestra say how much he wants it.
verseByVerse.examples: The method is Philistine. A new cart is exactly what the lords of the Philistines built when they sent the ark back, and they did it because they did not know any better (1 Sam. 6:7-8). Israel had the law: the poles are never to be removed, the sons of Kohath carry it on their shoulders, and they must not touch the holy things, lest they die (Ex. 25:14-15; Num. 7:9; 4:15).

verseByVerse.quote: David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim. And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart, with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark. And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.'

Thirty thousand men for a religious procession.

That figure tells you how seriously he means it. This is not a delegation; it is a national mobilisation for the purpose of moving a box.

'And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim.'

The full title is given because we are meant to remember what this object is.

It is not a relic and it is not a symbol. God had said where he would meet Israel and it was precise: there I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you (Ex. 25:22). The lid is a throne with the invisible King seated on it, and the chest under it holds the tablets of the covenant.

Now remember where it has been.

The Philistines captured it at Aphek, and it destroyed their god and gave them tumours for seven months until they sent it back on a cart of their own making. It reached Beth-shemesh, where men looked into it and seventy of them died. And the people of Kiriath-jearim came and took it to the house of Abinadab on the hill, and there it stayed. From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years (1 Sam. 7:2).

Twenty years, in a private house, on a hill, while Saul reigned and fought and lost a kingdom and never once sent for it. Saul asked for it exactly once, in a panic during a battle, and changed his mind before it arrived (1 Sam. 14:18-19).

So David's impulse here is the first genuinely good idea anybody has had about the ark in a generation. He is not building a shrine to himself; he wants the presence of God at the centre of the new capital, and he wants the nation to see it come.

Everything about the intention is right.

'And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart,'

There is the sentence the chapter turns on, and almost nobody notices it on a first reading because it sounds like transport arrangements.

A new cart.

The word new is doing work. It signals care: not any old farm wagon, but one built for the purpose, unused, clean. Somebody thought about this. Somebody wanted to do it properly.

And a cart is precisely, exactly, in detail, how the Philistines had done it.

Go back to 1 Samuel 6. The lords of the Philistines want the ark out of their country and ask their priests how to send it. The instruction is: now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke (1 Sam. 6:7). They built the cart, put the ark on it, and let the cows walk. It worked, in the sense that the thing arrived.

They were pagans. They had no revelation, no law, no priesthood and no idea; they were improvising a way to get rid of something dangerous, and God accommodated their ignorance.

Israel had the book.

The instructions about this object are not obscure and they are not buried. There are rings cast onto the four feet of the ark and poles put through the rings, and about those poles the law says: the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it (Ex. 25:14-15). They are never removed, so the ark is always ready to be lifted and never handled.

Who lifts it is also specified. When the wagons were distributed to the Levitical clans at Sinai, the sons of Kohath got none: but to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder (Num. 7:9).

On the shoulder. The one clan whose job was the ark is the one clan that was given no carts.

And there is a warning attached, in the same passage, in as many words: the Kohathites are to come only after Aaron and his sons have covered the holy things, but they must not touch the holy things, lest they die (Num. 4:15).

Every one of those sentences was available. There were priests in the procession. There were thirty thousand men present and not one of them said anything.

'with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark.'

'And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.'

The joy is real, and the writer lists six instruments to make sure we feel it.

This is a nation that has just been reunited after seven years of civil war, walking behind the throne of God toward a new capital, singing. There is nothing cynical in it anywhere.

Which is what makes the next verse so hard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — God Struck Him Down There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the threshing floor of Nacon the oxen stumble, and Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it (v. 6). And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God (v. 7). David is angry, and names the place Perez-uzzah (v. 8). Then he is afraid: how can the ark of the LORD come to me? (v. 9). So it goes aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The sin was the cart, and Uzzah's hand is only where it surfaced. Thirty thousand men were already in violation before the oxen stumbled, and the one who reached out had grown up with the ark in his father's house — twenty years of familiarity with the throne of God standing in the hall. David says as much himself, later, when he does it properly: we did not seek him according to the rule (1 Chron. 15:13).
verseByVerse.examples: David's anger is recorded without softening, and so is the fear that follows it. And the household God then blesses for three months belongs to a man from Gath.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God. And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day. And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?" So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled.'

Threshing floors are flat ground, but they are reached by tracks, and an ox on rough ground stumbles.

The cart lurches. The ark tips. And a man standing beside the wheel does the thing any person would do, in the half second available, without thinking about it at all: he puts his hand out to steady it.

'And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God.'

Anybody reading this for the first time stops here, and should.

The reaction almost everyone has is that this is not fair. He was helping. He was trying to protect the ark. He did not steal anything or mock anything; he reacted, and he died for reacting.

That reaction deserves an answer rather than a lecture, and there are several parts to it.

The first is that the sin was the cart, not the hand.

Uzzah's hand is not the offence; it is the place where an offence already thirty thousand men deep came to the surface. The entire procession was in violation of an explicit law from the moment it left the hill. The poles existed so that no one would ever have to touch it. Take the poles away and put it on a wagon, and sooner or later an ox stumbles and somebody has to.

The cart made Uzzah's death inevitable. He is the man standing nearest when the bill arrives.

And this is not a modern reading imposed on the text. It is David's own reading, and he says it out loud when he does it properly three months later. Assembling the Levites, he tells them: because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule (1 Chron. 15:13).

We. Not Uzzah. The king says the fault was the nation's and his own.

The second is who Uzzah was.

He is a son of Abinadab, and the ark had been in Abinadab's house on that hill for twenty years. Uzzah has quite possibly lived his whole life with the throne of God standing in the family property. He grew up walking past it. It was furniture.

That is not stated as an accusation and it should not be read as one. It is simply the most likely explanation of the reflex, and it is the most ordinary danger in the world: the thing you live closest to is the thing you stop seeing. Nobody handles a familiar object carefully.

The third is the shape of the instinct itself, and it deserves precision, because it is the most human moment in the chapter.

Uzzah put out his hand to keep the ark from falling in the dirt.

Think about what is assumed in that. That the ark needed him. That God's throne was in danger from a pothole and a man's hand was the remedy. That holy things are fragile and human hands are safe.

It is exactly backwards, and it is the reflex of every religious person who has ever tried to protect God's reputation by means God did not authorise. The ark had already destroyed a temple in Ashdod and flattened a god face down on his own threshold. It did not need steadying.

And the fourth is the one that will not be argued away, and should not be.

This is a hard verse. It is meant to be. Israel had recently watched seventy men die at Beth-shemesh for looking into this same box (1 Sam. 6:19), and had learned nothing from it in twenty years.

The sense of unfairness most readers feel should be examined rather than suppressed, because of what it measures. It does not tell us that God is harsh. It tells us how small a thing we take holiness to be — that we assume, without ever having decided it, that God's presence is basically safe, and that sincerity covers everything, and that a good motive is a sufficient answer to a plain command.

Uzzah was almost certainly sincere. Sincerity was not the question. He was standing next to the place where the God who made the world had said he would sit, on a cart borrowed from the Philistines, in a country that had his instructions in writing.

None of that makes it comfortable, and this commentary is not going to pretend it does. The narrator does not comfort anybody either. He says the man died there beside the ark of God, and moves on to the king's reaction.

'And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day.'

David is angry with God, and Scripture records it without a syllable of apology.

The word is strong — it is the same verb used of Saul's rages. He has just organised the greatest day of his reign, with thirty thousand men and a full orchestra, out of what he was sure was pure devotion, and God has killed a man in the middle of it.

And he names the ground after it. Perez-uzzah, the breaking-out against Uzzah. He puts his grievance on the map, which is what he did with his joy at Baal-perazim one chapter ago, using the same word.

Note that God does not strike him for the anger. He is not rebuked for it here or anywhere. Scripture is not squeamish about people being furious with God — Job is, Jeremiah is, Habakkuk is, the psalms are full of it, and several of those psalms are David's. Anger brought into God's presence is a form of dealing with him. It is not the same as walking away.

'And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?"'

The anger turns into fear, and the fear asks the right question.

How can the ark of the LORD come to me? It is the same question the men of Beth-shemesh asked when the seventy died: who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? (1 Sam. 6:20). And it is the question the whole business exists to raise.

The difference is what each of them does next. Beth-shemesh sent the ark away and asked somebody else to take it. David also sends it away — but he spends three months finding out how it is supposed to be done, and then comes back.

'So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.'

The Gittite. A man of Gath.

That is a Philistine city, Goliath's city, the city David hid in twice. Whether Obed-edom was an ethnic Philistine settled in Israel or an Israelite from a place of that name, the writer chooses to give him that label, and it sits there.

Somebody has to take the ark, and the man who takes it is the foreigner.

'And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.'

This is the other half of the chapter, and without it the first half would be a lie.

The same ark, in the same country, in the same season. It killed an Israelite at a threshing floor and it blessed a Gittite's household for three months, and the difference is not in the ark.

The presence of God is not a hazard to be managed and it is not a convenience to be used. It is God, and God is not tame, and the same nearness that destroyed a careless man filled a house with blessing until people started talking about it.

That is what gets David moving again. He hears that the thing he is frightened of has been making a family prosper for three months, and he goes back for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Dancing Before the LORD with All His Might
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hearing that Obed-edom's house is blessed, David goes and brings the ark up with rejoicing (v. 12). This time it is carried, and when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal (v. 13). And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod (v. 14), with shouting and the sound of the horn (v. 15). Michal watches from a window and despised him in her heart (v. 16). The ark is set in its tent, offerings are made, and David blesses the people in the name of the LORD of hosts and gives every one of them, both men and women, bread and meat and a cake of raisins (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Chronicles supplies what changed: this time the Levites carried it, on poles, on their shoulders, exactly as Moses commanded (1 Chron. 15:2, 13-15). Six steps and a sacrifice — the whole procession punctuated by blood, because the first attempt taught them what it costs to come near.
verseByVerse.examples: And the king dances in a linen ephod, which is a priest's garment, not a royal one. He has taken off the clothes that say he is the king and put on the clothes that say he is a worshipper, and he gives food to every person in the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing. And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal. And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn. As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins to each one. Then all the people departed, each to his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing.'

Three months of fear ends with a report about somebody else's harvest.

What the news tells him is that the problem was never the ark. God had not withdrawn the offer of his presence; the offer had been mishandled. So he goes back, and this time he does it right.

'And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.'

Two words have changed and they are the whole difference: those who bore.

Nobody is driving anything. There is no cart in this procession, and there are no oxen pulling. Men are carrying it, which is what the law said.

Chronicles fills in what David did during the three months. He assembled the Levites and told them plainly: no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD chose them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever — and then the confession, because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule. And so: the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD (1 Chron. 15:2, 13-15).

He went and read the instructions.

That is what repentance looks like when it is real and not merely felt. He was angry, then afraid, and then he found out what God had actually said and did that instead.

And then the sacrifices. When those who bore the ark had gone six steps — six paces from where it stood — an ox and a fattened animal are killed.

Six steps. They have barely started.

Whatever the arrangement was for the rest of the route, the point of that first sacrifice is unmistakable. The last time this ark moved, a man died. Before it goes any further than six paces, blood is shed. They have learned what it costs to come near, and they are not going to take another step on the assumption that it is safe.

'And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod.'

Now the king dances in the street.

With all his might — the same phrase used of the whole nation's celebration in verse 5, now used of one man. This is not dignified swaying. It is whirling, leaping, spending himself.

And look at what he is wearing. A linen ephod is a priest's garment — the simple one, not the high priest's. It is what the boy Samuel wore ministering at Shiloh (1 Sam. 2:18). It is not a royal robe.

He has taken off the clothes that say king and put on the clothes that say worshipper, and he is dancing in front of his entire capital dressed as a servant of the sanctuary.

That is the deliberate act his wife is about to call an indecency, and it is the deliberate act he is about to defend.

'So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn.'

'As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.'

One person in Jerusalem is not in the street.

Everything about the sentence is set up as a contrast. All Israel is outside with the horn and the shouting; she is inside, behind a window, alone, looking down.

And note what the writer calls her: Michal the daughter of Saul. Not the wife of David. He will use that formula four more times before the chapter ends. She is being identified, in every line, by the house that lost.

We will come to her.

'And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.'

A tent. Not a temple — that is the whole subject of the next chapter, and it starts with David noticing this.

'And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts'

'and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, to each a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins. Then all the people departed, each to his house.'

He feeds everybody, and the writer specifies both men and women.

Peace offerings were the sacrifice that was eaten, and the meat here is the meat of the offering: the whole nation sits down to a meal in the presence of God. Every person gets bread, meat and a raisin cake — not the officials, not the fighting men, not the heads of houses. Everyone.

The last thing the king does on the greatest day of his reign is hand out food to the crowd, in a linen ephod, having danced in front of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — I Will Make Myself Yet More Contemptible
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Michal comes out to meet him: how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself! (v. 20). David answers: it was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel — and I will celebrate before the LORD. I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your own eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor (vv. 21-22). And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: She is wrong about what the dancing was, and she has also been wronged more than anyone in this book so far. Given by her father to another man, taken back years later as a clause in a treaty, separated from a husband who followed her weeping for twelve miles — and nobody at any point asked her anything.
verseByVerse.examples: David's answer is true and it is not kind. Above your father is aimed at the wound, and he knows it. And the last verse states a fact and gives no reason for it: the text does not say whether this was God's judgment, David's withdrawal, or simple childlessness, and it is not honest to decide.

verseByVerse.quote: And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!" And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD—and I will celebrate before the LORD. I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor." And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!"'

He comes home to bless his family and is met at the door.

The sarcasm is expert. How the king of Israel honored himself today — every word of it a knife. The title is used to point out how far he fell short of it. And her complaint is specific: he exposed himself in front of the servant girls, and he behaved like a common man without shame.

She is not entirely wrong about the facts. Dancing in a linen ephod is not dignified, and a king who spins and leaps in a short garment in a crowd is not maintaining the distance kings maintain. She is right that he looked like anybody, and wrong about everything that matters, because that was the point.

Now, before David answers, she is owed something the chapter does not give her and a reader should.

Michal loved David. The narrator states it outright, and it is the only place in the Old Testament where a woman is said to love a man (1 Sam. 18:20). She married him. When her father sent men to kill him in the night, she let him down through a window on a rope, put an idol in the bed with goats' hair at its head to buy him hours, and lied to Saul's face about it — and Saul said to her, why have you deceived me thus? (1 Sam. 19:11-17).

She saved his life, and he ran, and he did not come back for her.

Her father then gave her to Paltiel the son of Laish, and she lived as that man's wife for years — long enough for him to love her, since he followed the escort weeping as far as Bahurim when she was taken away, and turned round only when Abner told him to (3:15-16).

And why was she taken away? Because David made her return a condition of a political agreement with Abner, at the exact moment when being married to Saul's daughter would help him with the northern tribes. Not before. Not in the seven years he was king in Hebron with two other wives. When it was useful.

Nobody in that entire transaction asked her a single question.

So she stands at a window in a city she did not choose, watching a man she once risked her life for dance in front of a crowd, in a religion that took her father's kingdom and gave it to him. Her contempt is genuinely wrong, and she has genuinely been wronged, and both of those are true at the same moment.

'And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD — and I will celebrate before the LORD."'

The first clause is the answer and it is unanswerable. It was before the LORD.

Everything she said assumed an audience of servant girls. He says the audience was God, and that what she watched from a window was not a performance for anybody in the street.

And then he says something else, and it should not be smoothed over.

Above your father and above all his house.

That is aimed. He knows exactly where the wound is, and he puts his hand on it. He could have defended the dancing without mentioning Saul at all, and he mentions Saul twice.

This is not the David of chapter 1, who wrote a lament for that same father with nothing in it for himself. It is a man in his own doorway being sneered at by his wife, hitting back with the one fact that hurts.

'"I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your own eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor."'

Here is the great sentence of the chapter, and everything true in his reply is here.

I will make myself yet more contemptible than this.

He does not deny that he looked ridiculous. He agrees, and offers to go further. He is saying that self-abasement before God is not a cost he is reluctantly paying but a direction he intends to keep travelling in, and that her estimate of him is a price he is content to keep paying.

There is a Son of David who took this further than anybody, who emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself to a criminal's execution (Phil. 2:7-8). The instinct is the same and the distance is not comparable. But the man in the linen ephod is pointing in that direction, and he knows what he is doing.

And the last line of his answer is sharp and shrewd and possibly not gracious: the servant girls she is so worried about will think more of him for it, not less. He is telling her that ordinary people understand this and she does not.

'And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.'

The chapter ends on that, and it is stated as a fact with no explanation attached.

Readers reach for one immediately, and there are two on offer. Either God closed her womb in judgment for despising the ark's homecoming, or David never went near her again. The text says neither. It says she had no child, and stops.

What the sentence certainly does is close a door on a dynasty. A child of David by Saul's daughter would have united the two houses in one person and been the obvious heir. There is no such child. The house of Saul ends here, in a childless woman at a window, and the throne passes entirely to David's line and eventually to a son of Bathsheba.

She is called the daughter of Saul one last time in the last verse of the chapter, and the writer has now done it five times in twenty-three verses. That is his verdict and his epitaph in one phrase: whatever she was at the window with the rope in her hands, she died as her father's daughter.

It is a bleak ending to the happiest day of David's reign, and the writer puts it there on purpose. The ark is in Jerusalem, the nation has eaten in God's presence, the king has danced himself hoarse — and inside the house there is a marriage that is finished, and a woman nobody ever asked.

6.theology:
Everything right except the method (v. 3). The word new signals care — somebody built that cart for the purpose. And a cart is precisely how pagans with no instructions had improvised. The law is not obscure: rings and poles, and the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it (Ex. 25:14-15), so that it is always ready to lift and never handled. The one Levitical clan charged with the ark is the one clan given no wagons, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder (Num. 7:9). Sincerity is not a substitute for reading what God said.

Uzzah: the sin was the cart (vv. 6-7). The whole procession was in violation from the moment it left the hill; take the poles away and put it on a wagon, and sooner or later an ox stumbles and somebody has to touch it. Uzzah is the man standing nearest when the bill arrives. This is not a modern reading imposed on the text — it is David's own, three months later: because we did not seek him according to the rule (1 Chron. 15:13). We.

And who Uzzah was. A son of Abinadab, in whose house the ark had stood for twenty years. He very likely grew up walking past the throne of God; it was furniture. That is not an accusation, it is the most ordinary danger there is: the thing you live closest to is the thing you stop seeing, and nobody handles a familiar object carefully.

The instinct was backwards. He put his hand out to keep God's throne out of the dirt — which assumes the ark needed him, that a pothole endangered it, and that holy things are fragile while human hands are safe. It is the reflex of every religious person who has tried to protect God's reputation by means God never authorised. That ark had already flattened a god face down on his own threshold.

Examine the unfairness rather than burying it. Uzzah was almost certainly sincere, and sincerity was not the question. What the sense of injustice measures is not God's harshness but how small a thing we take holiness to be — that we assume without deciding it that God's presence is basically safe, that good motives cover plain commands, and that a nation with the instructions in writing stands where Philistines stood. Israel had watched seventy men die at Beth-shemesh for looking into this same box (1 Sam. 6:19) and learned nothing in twenty years. None of that makes the verse comfortable, and the narrator comforts nobody either.

Anger, then fear (vv. 8-9). David is furious with God and is not rebuked for it, here or anywhere. Scripture is not squeamish about this — Job, Jeremiah, Habakkuk and a good many psalms, several of them his. Anger brought into God's presence is a way of dealing with him; it is not the same as walking away. And his fear asks the right question, the same one Beth-shemesh asked: how can the ark of the LORD come to me? The difference is what each does next. Beth-shemesh passed it on. David spent three months finding out how it was supposed to be done, and came back.

Obed-edom the Gittite (vv. 10-11). A man of Gath — Goliath's city, the city David hid in twice — and the writer keeps the label. The same ark, in the same country, in the same season, killed a careless Israelite and filled a foreigner's house with blessing until the neighbours were talking about it. The presence of God is neither a hazard to be managed nor a convenience to be used.

Repentance that reads the instructions (vv. 13-15). Those who bore — no cart, no oxen. Chronicles supplies the three months: Levites, poles, shoulders, as Moses had commanded (1 Chron. 15:2, 15). That is what repentance looks like when it is real and not merely felt. And a sacrifice after six steps: the last time this ark moved a man died, so before it goes six paces there is blood. They will not take another step on the assumption that it is safe.

The linen ephod (v. 14). A priest's garment, the plain one — what the boy Samuel wore at Shiloh. He has taken off the clothes that say king and put on the clothes that say worshipper, and danced in them in front of his own capital. Then he hands bread, meat and raisin cake to every person present, both men and women — not the officials or the fighting men. Everyone.

Michal is owed something the chapter does not give her. She loved him — the narrator says so, and it is the only place in the Old Testament where a woman is said to love a man. She let him down through a window on a rope, put an idol in his bed and lied to her father's face to save his life. He ran, and did not come back for her. Her father gave her to a man who loved her enough to follow her weeping for twelve miles; and David demanded her return as a clause in a treaty, at the exact moment being married to Saul's daughter helped him with the northern tribes — not in the seven years before. Nobody ever asked her anything. Her contempt is genuinely wrong and she has genuinely been wronged, and both are true at once.

The answer, and what is wrong with it (vv. 21-22). It was before the LORD is unanswerable: she assumed an audience of servant girls, and he says the audience was God. But above your father and above all his house is aimed, and he knows where the wound is; he could have defended the dancing without mentioning Saul, and mentions him twice. This is not the man who wrote a lament for that father with nothing in it for himself. What is great in the reply is I will make myself yet more contemptible than this — he does not deny looking ridiculous, he agrees and offers to go further. There is a Son of David who emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7-8); the distance is not comparable, and the direction is the same.

What verse 23 says and does not say. It states that she had no child and gives no reason. Readers reach at once for divine judgment or for David's withdrawal; the text supplies neither and it is not honest to choose. What it certainly does is close a door: a child of David by Saul's daughter would have united both houses in one person and been the obvious heir, and there is none. And she is called the daughter of Saul for the fifth time in twenty-three verses — the writer's epitaph in a phrase. It is a bleak ending to the happiest day of the reign, and it is placed there on purpose: the ark is home, the nation has eaten in God's presence, and inside the house there is a finished marriage and a woman nobody asked.
6.examples:
Then: A nation moved the throne of God on a brand-new cart built specially for the purpose, copying a method invented by pagans who had never read the instructions — and when an ox stumbled and a man reached out to steady it, he died on the spot, and the king who had organised the whole day went home angry with God.

Now: Two things, and the chapter refuses to let either one go. Uzzah is about the sufficiency of sincerity, and the answer is that it is not sufficient: the cart was built with care, by people who meant well, in a country that had the instructions in writing, and good intentions did not convert a Philistine method into an obedient one. The question worth asking is which of your own well-meant arrangements has never actually been checked against what God said. And the second is David's three months. He was furious, then frightened, and then he went and found out what the rule actually was and did that instead — which is what repentance looks like when it is more than a feeling. He came back and did the same thing the right way, and danced.

7.title: The Throne Forever
