And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant."<sup>7</sup>And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always."<sup>8</sup>And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"<sup>9</sup>Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson.<sup>10</sup>And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.<sup>11</sup>Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons.<sup>12</sup>And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants.<sup>13</sup>So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.
9.overview:
Nobody asked him. There is no petition, no delegation, no political pressure — the kingdom is secure and the wars are won, and one day the king asks whether anybody is left of the family that hunted him for a decade. And the reason he gives is a conversation in a field years ago with a man now dead on a mountain: do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David (1 Sam. 20:14-15). Jonathan named the exact moment — the moment a new dynasty cleans out the old one — and asked David to break the rule.

The promise was made to a dead man, about a person David had never met, with no witnesses and no legal force, at a time when David was a fugitive with nothing. He remembers it.

What comes is Saul's grandson — a rival claimant with a better hereditary title than the man on the throne, dropped by a nurse running from the news of Gilboa when he was five years old and lame ever since. He arrives on his face, brought by soldiers, expecting the one normal outcome of such a summons. And the king says his name, and do not fear, and gives him the estate and a permanent seat at the royal table. Mephibosheth calls himself a dead dog — which is the phrase David shouted at Saul from a hillside about himself.

Four times the writer says he ate at the king's table, and then ends the chapter somewhere else: now he was lame in both his feet. The shape of the story is the shape of the gospel, and the last clause is why it is worth more than a tidier ending.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Is There Still Anyone Left?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" (v. 1). Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, is brought in and asked whether anyone remains to whom I may show the kindness of God (v. 3). There is: a son of Jonathan, crippled in his feet, living at Lo-debar in the house of Machir (vv. 3-4). David sends and brings him (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody asked him to do this. He initiates it, and the word he uses twice is hesed — the covenant love that keeps going after the reason for keeping it has gone. The second time he calls it the kindness of God, which is the standard he is measuring by.
verseByVerse.examples: And he is keeping a promise made in a field years ago to a man now dead: show me the steadfast love of the LORD... and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David (1 Sam. 20:14-15). Jonathan named the exact moment — the moment a normal king cleans out the old dynasty.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David. And the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "I am your servant." And the king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan; he is crippled in his feet." The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar." Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?"'

Nobody asked him. That is the first thing to see.

There is no petition in front of him, no delegation, no political pressure. The kingdom is secure, the wars in chapter 8 are won, the treasury is full, and one day the king asks whether anybody is left from the family that tried to kill him for a decade.

And the question has a reason attached: for Jonathan's sake.

Now go back and find where this comes from, because it is one of the most striking promise-keepings in Scripture.

Years ago, in a field outside Gibeah, Jonathan said this: if I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die; and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth (1 Sam. 20:14-15).

Read what he actually asked for. Not protection while he lived — he adds that almost as an afterthought. What he asks for is kindness to his descendants at the precise moment David has no reason on earth to give it: when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David.

Jonathan knew exactly what he was asking. When a new dynasty is secure, it removes the old one. That is not cynicism about ancient kings; it is simply what happened, every time, in every kingdom around them, and Jonathan was the crown prince of the house being replaced. He was asking David to break the rule.

Here is David, years later, with the man dead on a mountain and the house of Saul finished, raising the subject himself.

Consider what that means about promises. This one was made to a man who has been dead for years, about a person David has never met, in a conversation that had no witnesses and no legal force, at a time when David was a fugitive with nothing. There is not one external reason to remember it.

He remembers it.

'Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David. And the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "I am your servant."'

They have to go and find a former servant of Saul's household to answer the question, which tells you how completely that house has disappeared.

Watch Ziba through this chapter and remember him, because he comes back twice, and both times he is working an angle (16:1-4; 19:24-30).

'And the king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan; he is crippled in his feet."'

The king asks the same question again and raises the standard while doing it: the kindness of God.

That is what he is measuring by. Not ordinary generosity and not political magnanimity — the sort of kindness God shows, which in the Old Testament means kindness to people who have no claim on it, sustained after the relationship that produced it has ended.

Ziba's answer is odd in its shape. Asked whether anyone is left, he says yes, there is a son of Jonathan, and then immediately volunteers the disability. He is not asked about it.

It may be an honest attempt to be helpful — you should know he cannot walk. It may be something less generous: a suggestion that this one is not worth troubling about, no threat, no use. The text does not say. But the writer records that the first fact anyone offers David about this man is what is wrong with him.

How he came to be crippled is told earlier, in one sentence, and it is a terrible one. When the news came from Gilboa that Saul and Jonathan were dead, the household panicked: his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth (4:4). He was five years old. Somebody dropped him while running for their lives, and he never walked again.

He has been disabled since the day his father died.

'The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar."'

Lo-debar is across the Jordan, out in Gilead, well away from anywhere that matters.

The name has been much preached on and a little care is in order. It most likely means something like no pasture, or simply no thing. It is a real village with a real man living in it, and the writer is not making a point about the name. But notice where the grandson of a king of Israel has been living: in somebody else's house, in a place on the far side of the river, for about twenty years.

Note also the man he is living with. Machir the son of Ammiel appears once more in this book, and it is the last place you would expect — when David is fleeing from Absalom, broken and hungry, three men bring food across the Jordan to him at Mahanaim, and Machir of Lo-debar is one of them (17:27-29). The man who sheltered Saul's grandson feeds David in his worst hour.

'Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.'

David sends. Mephibosheth does not come and ask.

State that plainly, because the whole chapter runs on it. This man has been keeping his head down in a village across the river for two decades, expecting nothing, asking for nothing, and almost certainly hoping the king had never heard of him. Soldiers arrive at Machir's door with an order to bring him to Jerusalem.

Everything in this chapter is initiated by the king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — A Dead Dog Such as I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mephibosheth comes and falls on his face, and David says his name (v. 6). Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always (v. 7). And he answers: what is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I? (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Understand what he expects walking in. He is Saul's grandson — a rival claimant with a better hereditary title than the man on the throne — summoned by that man's soldiers from a village on the far side of the Jordan. There was one normal outcome to a journey like that.
verseByVerse.examples: A dead dog is not a figure Mephibosheth invented. It is what David called himself, shouting up a hillside at Saul: after whom has the king of Israel come out? After a dead dog! After a flea! (1 Sam. 24:14). The hunted man's phrase comes back from the grandson of the man who hunted him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and paid homage. And David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant." And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always." And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and paid homage. And David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant."'

Take in what this arrival looks like from his side of the room.

The writer gives his full pedigree in the verse — the son of Jonathan, son of Saul — and that is the whole problem. He is not a private citizen. He is the direct male descendant of the previous king, which makes him, in the eyes of anybody who cared about hereditary right, the legitimate claimant to the throne he is being carried into.

He is at Jerusalem because armed men came for him. He is on the floor, on his face, and he cannot get up without help.

He has grown up hearing one version of David: the man who broke his grandfather, who took the kingdom, who fought a seven-year war against his uncle's regime. Whatever else he expects from this interview, he does not expect to survive it.

The king says his name.

Mephibosheth. Not son of Saul, which is what the writer called Michal five times in chapter 6. Not a title, not a charge. His name.

'And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always."'

Do not fear. Which tells you what was in the room.

Then three things, and each one is larger than the last.

The first is the reason: for the sake of your father Jonathan. Not for anything Mephibosheth is or has done or might be useful for. He is receiving all of this on account of somebody else, and he is told so to his face at the start, before anything is given.

The second is the land. All of Saul's estate, restored — which had presumably reverted to the crown, as a defeated dynasty's property does. That is a fortune, and it is also a statement: the house of Saul is not to be treated as forfeited.

The third is the table, and it is the one that costs David something and matters most. You shall eat at my table always.

Not a pension paid to a man in a distant village. Not permission to live quietly. A permanent seat in the king's own household, at the king's own meals, every day, for the rest of his life.

Now hold that against a proverb this same book gave us four chapters ago.

When David took Jerusalem, the Jebusites jeered that the blind and the lame could hold the place against him, and out of that day came a saying: the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (5:8).

And here, into the house, into the palace, to the king's own table, comes a man who is lame in both feet, and stays there.

'And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"'

His answer is the sentence everybody remembers, and the phrase in it has a history.

A dead dog.

Dogs in that world were not pets; they were scavengers on the edge of a village, and a dead one was refuse. It is about as low as a person can put himself in that language.

But those exact words have been spoken before in this story, and they were spoken by David.

Standing on a hillside above the cave at Engedi, holding a corner of Saul's robe, shouting down at the king who was hunting him: after whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea! (1 Sam. 24:14).

David said it about himself, to Saul. Now Saul's grandson says it about himself, to David.

The wheel has come completely round, and the man on the throne is hearing his own words of self-abasement from the family that made him say them. If anybody in Israel understood what it felt like to speak that sentence, it was the man being spoken to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — He Ate Always at the King's Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David gives Mephibosheth everything that belonged to Saul, and puts Ziba and his fifteen sons and twenty servants to work farming it for him (vv. 9-10). So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons (v. 11). He has a young son, Mica, and the whole of Ziba's household are his servants (vv. 12-13a). And the chapter's last clause: now he was lame in both his feet (v. 13b).
verseByVerse.theology: Like one of the king's sons. Not a pensioner, not a guest, not a hostage kept close — a place at the family table, permanently, four times stated in eight verses.
verseByVerse.examples: And the writer ends on the disability rather than the honour, and it should not be tidied away. Nothing in this chapter heals him. He is fed, restored, and seated at the king's table for the rest of his life, and he is carried there.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson. And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons. And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants. So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson."'

Note the phrase David uses about Mephibosheth when speaking to Ziba: your master's grandson.

Ziba has just been re-assigned. He came in as a free agent, a man who used to serve a household that no longer exists, and he leaves as a steward with a master again.

'"And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.'

The arrangement is complete and it is generous, and the last sentence tells you it is also substantial.

Ziba is not a poor man. Fifteen sons and twenty servants is a considerable operation, and that whole establishment is now put to work farming Saul's estate on behalf of a man who cannot walk out to inspect it.

It should be said that this is a great deal to ask of Ziba, and the writer plants the detail on purpose. Seven chapters from now, when David is running from Absalom, Ziba meets him on the road with two hundred loaves and a story: Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get the kingdom back. David believes him on the spot and hands him the entire estate (16:1-4). And when David returns, Mephibosheth comes to meet him having not washed his feet or trimmed his beard since the day the king left, and says Ziba deceived him (19:24-30).

David never resolves it. He splits the land between them, and Mephibosheth says: oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home.

'Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons.'

Like one of the king's sons.

That is the phrase to stop on, and it is the writer's own, not David's. Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah and Solomon sat at that table, and so did the grandson of the man who threw spears at their father.

He is not a pensioner and not a hostage. He is family.

'And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants.'

A son. The line of Jonathan continues, and the Chronicler follows it down for generations (1 Chron. 8:34-40) — which means Jonathan's request was answered further than he could have known. He asked for kindness to his house, and his house went on.

'So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.'

Four times in this chapter the writer says the man ate at the king's table, and then he ends the chapter on something else.

Now he was lame in both his feet.

That is the last clause, and it is deliberate, and it should not be tidied away into something more triumphant.

Nothing here is healed. Mephibosheth is fed, restored, honoured and given a permanent place among the king's sons, and he is still carried to the table. He will be lame at every meal for the rest of his life. The chapter that could have ended on like one of the king's sons ends on the disability instead.

Now, the shape of this story is the shape of the gospel, and it would be strange not to say so — provided it is said carefully, because the passage is not an allegory and forcing it does it no favours.

What is genuinely there is this. A man who could not come is sent for. He is found in a place far from the king, expecting judgment and receiving the opposite. He is given everything on account of somebody else's covenant, and told so plainly at the start. He is seated at the king's table not as a guest but as a son. And he contributes nothing to the transaction except the acknowledgment that he is a dead dog.

Every one of those is in the text, and the correspondence is not accidental — this is how God has always dealt with people, and the Old Testament keeps showing it.

And the last clause is the honest part, which is why it is worth more than a tidier ending.

He is still lame. Being brought to the table does not undo what happened to him when he was five years old. He eats as a son and he arrives carried, and both of those are permanently true.

Any Christian who has wondered why grace has not fixed the thing that is actually wrong with them — the illness, the memory, the temperament, the damage somebody else did in a moment of panic — is looking at the right verse. The table is real and the lameness is real, and the writer put them in the same sentence on purpose. The healing comes later, and it is not in this chapter, and Scripture never pretends the meantime is comfortable.

9.theology:
A promise with no external reason to keep it (v. 1). Made to a man now dead, about a person David had never met, in a private conversation with no witnesses, when David was a hunted fugitive with nothing to give. Jonathan had asked for kindness to his descendants at the one moment it would be least likely — when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David — because he was the crown prince of the house being replaced and knew exactly what happens to such families. David raises the subject himself, years later, unprompted.

The kindness of God (v. 3). He asks twice, and the second time raises the standard: not ordinary generosity and not political magnanimity, but the sort of kindness God shows — given to people with no claim on it and sustained after the relationship that produced it has ended.

The first fact anybody offers is the disability (v. 3). Ziba is asked whether anyone is left and volunteers the lameness unasked. It may be helpfulness; it may be a hint that this one is no threat and no use. The text does not say, and the writer records that this is how the man was introduced. How he came to be lame is one terrible sentence back at 4:4: the news came from Gilboa, the household ran, and a nurse dropped a five-year-old.

The king initiates everything (v. 5). Mephibosheth does not come and ask. He has been keeping his head down across the Jordan for twenty years, expecting nothing and almost certainly hoping the king had never heard of him, and soldiers arrive at the door with an order to bring him in.

He says his name (v. 6). Not son of Saul — which is what the writer called Michal five times in chapter 6 — not a title and not a charge. And do not fear, which tells you what was in the room. Then three things, each larger: the reason (for the sake of your father Jonathan, stated before anything is given, so the man knows from the start that none of it is on his own account), the estate, and the table.

The proverb undone (v. 7). Out of the Jebusite taunt came a saying: the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (5:8). Into the house, to the king's own table, permanently, comes a man lame in both feet.

A dead dog (v. 8). Scavengers on the edge of a village, and a dead one is refuse — about as low as the language goes. And those exact words were David's, shouted down a hillside at the king who was hunting him: after whom has the king of Israel come out? After a dead dog! After a flea! (1 Sam. 24:14). The man on the throne hears his own self-abasement from the grandson of the man who made him say it.

Like one of the king's sons (v. 11). The writer's phrase, not David's. Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah and Solomon sat at that table, and so did this man. Not a pensioner and not a hostage kept close — family. And Jonathan's request was answered further than he could have known: Mephibosheth has a son, and the Chronicler follows the line down for generations (1 Chron. 8:34-40).

Watch Ziba. Fifteen sons and twenty servants is a substantial establishment, now set to farm another man's estate for him. Seven chapters on, with David fleeing Absalom, Ziba meets him with two hundred loaves and a story that Mephibosheth has stayed behind hoping to get the kingdom back — and David hands him the whole estate on the spot (16:1-4). Mephibosheth's answer on the king's return, unwashed and untrimmed since the day David left, is that Ziba deceived him. David never resolves it; he splits the land, and Mephibosheth says oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (19:24-30).

The last clause, and why it is the honest one (v. 13). Four times the writer says he ate at the king's table, and then ends on now he was lame in both his feet. The shape of the chapter is the shape of the gospel and it would be strange not to say so — a man who could not come is sent for, found far from the king, expecting judgment and receiving the opposite, given everything on account of somebody else's covenant, seated as a son, contributing nothing but the admission that he is a dead dog. All of that is genuinely in the text. And so is this: nothing here is healed. He eats as a son and he arrives carried, and both are permanently true. Anyone who has wondered why grace has not fixed the thing actually wrong with them — the illness, the memory, the damage somebody else did in a moment of panic — is looking at the right verse. The table is real and the lameness is real, and the writer put them in the same sentence on purpose.
9.examples:
Then: A king sent soldiers across the Jordan for the one surviving male heir of the dynasty he had replaced — the man with a better hereditary claim to his throne than he had — carried him into the palace, gave him back his grandfather's entire estate, and sat him down at the royal table with the princes for the rest of his life, because of a promise he had made in a field to that man's father before he was born.

Now: Two things. The first is about promises. Nothing whatever enforced this one: the person it was made to was dead, there were no witnesses, the circumstances that produced it had vanished, and no one alive would have known if David had quietly let it go. Most promises that get broken are broken exactly there — not repudiated, just allowed to lapse once the reason for them is gone. That is precisely what hesed means and precisely where it is tested. And the second is the last clause. Mephibosheth eats as a son and is still carried to the table, and Scripture puts both facts in one sentence without apologising for either. The seat is not provisional on the legs being fixed, and the legs are not fixed.

10.title: War with Ammon and Aram
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me." So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites.<sup>3</sup>But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?"<sup>4</sup>So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away.<sup>5</sup>When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."<sup>6</sup>When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men.<sup>7</sup>And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men.<sup>8</sup>And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country.<sup>9</sup>When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.<sup>10</sup>The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you.<sup>12</sup>Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."<sup>13</sup>So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him.<sup>14</sup>And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together.<sup>16</sup>And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.<sup>17</sup>And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him.<sup>18</sup>And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there.<sup>19</sup>And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.
10.overview:
Chapter 9 began with David asking whether anyone was left of Saul's house so that he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake. This one begins with the same word — hesed — extended to the son of a dead Ammonite king. Nahash is not a stranger to this book: he is the man who offered Jabesh-gilead a treaty on condition of gouging out every right eye in the town. At some point he showed David kindness, and the text never says when or how.

Hanun's counsellors talk him out of accepting it in a single sentence, with no evidence at all — only a theory that sounds shrewd and the flattering assumption that they are too clever to be taken in. And it is not entirely unreasonable, which is the point; the trouble is that they act on a suspicion as though it were a certainty. So the envoys are shaved on one side of the face and their robes cut off at the hips, and sent home to walk through their own country like that. It is calculated to be seen. David intercepts them at Jericho and tells them to stay out of sight until their beards grow — rather than parade them through Jerusalem to raise the nation, which is what a king who wanted a war would do.

Then Joab walks into a two-front trap and answers it by splitting his force, keeping the harder enemy for himself, and agreeing mutual reinforcement before either side engages. And he says the best sentence in the chapter: let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him. Fine theology, from the man who murdered Abner at the gate.

David crosses the Jordan himself against the Syrian relief army and destroys it. Note that, because the next chapter opens by saying the opposite about him. The coalition quits, the Ammonites are left alone — and Rabbah is still standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — As His Father Dealt Loyally with Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nahash king of the Ammonites dies, and David says: I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me (vv. 1-2). But the Ammonite princes tell Hanun the envoys are spies: has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it? (v. 3). So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away (v. 4). David meets them at Jericho: remain at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Two chapters running, David initiates hesed on account of somebody who is dead — and this time the dead man is a foreign king. When and how Nahash showed him kindness the text never says.
verseByVerse.examples: The humiliation is precise and it is aimed at David. A shaved beard was a disgrace a man hid for months, and cutting the robes off at the hips left grown men exposed on a public road. David's response is to send word ahead and let them stay out of sight until they can face people again.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me." So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites. But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?" So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away. When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me."'

Chapter 9 began with David asking whether anyone was left of Saul's house so that he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake. Chapter 10 begins with him showing kindness to the son of a dead Ammonite king, for the same reason.

It is the same word both times. Hesed — loyalty that outlasts the reason for it. And here he extends it to a foreigner.

The father's name is worth a moment. Nahash the Ammonite is not a stranger to this book. He is the man who besieged Jabesh-gilead at the start of Saul's reign and offered the town terms: he would make a treaty with them on condition that he gouge out every right eye in the place, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel (1 Sam. 11:2). That is the atrocity that brought the Spirit on Saul and made him king in fact as well as name.

And this man, at some point, showed David kindness.

The text never says when or how. Perhaps during the fugitive years, when any enemy of Saul had a claim on Ammonite sympathy. It is not explained, and it is better to leave it unexplained than to invent something. What we are told is that David remembered it and intended to repay it to the man's son.

'So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites.'

'But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?"'

The counsellors talk him out of it in a sentence.

Look at how the suspicion works, because it is a permanent feature of human affairs. There is nothing in the evidence to support it. A delegation of condolence has arrived, exactly as delegations of condolence do. The princes have no information; what they have is a theory that sounds shrewd, and the flattering assumption that they are too clever to be taken in.

And it is not entirely unreasonable, which is the point. David has spent the last two chapters subduing everybody within reach — Moab, Zobah, Damascus, Edom. A young and untested king receiving envoys from that man might well be nervous.

The trouble is what they do with the suspicion. Not investigate it, not watch the envoys, not politely accelerate their departure. They act on it as a certainty.

'So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away.'

Read what is done here, because it is designed, not impulsive.

Half the beard of each man is shaved. Not the whole beard, which would be a mourning custom and could be borne; half, so that every face is a joke that cannot be explained. A beard in that world was a man's dignity; the law of Israel even regulated how it might be trimmed, and to have one forcibly cut was among the deepest shames available.

And the robes are cut off at the hips, which left them exposed on a public road for the whole journey home.

Then they are sent away, deliberately, to walk back through their own country like that.

This is not violence and it is worse than a beating in one respect: it is designed to be seen, and to be carried home and displayed to the man who sent them. Hanun is not hurting the envoys. He is using them to insult David, and the insult is meant to be public.

'When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return."'

David's response to it is the best thing in the chapter.

He does not summon them to court to hear their report. He does not require them to walk into Jerusalem in that state so the nation can see the outrage and be roused by it, which is precisely what a king interested in a war would do.

He sends a message to intercept them at Jericho, the first town on the road, and tells them to stay there until they can face people again.

For the men were greatly ashamed. That is the narrator's explanation of the order, and it is the whole of it. The king's first thought is their humiliation, and his first act is to spare them the rest of it.

It costs him nothing, and notice it anyway: how a man treats people who have been made ridiculous in his service is a real test, and it does not usually get recorded.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Let Us Be Courageous for Our People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ammonites see they have become a stench to David and hire thirty-three thousand Syrian troops (v. 6). Joab arrives to find the enemy in front of him and behind — Ammonites at the city gate, Syrians in the open field (vv. 8-9). He splits the army, taking the best against the Syrians and giving the rest to Abishai against the Ammonites, with an agreement that each will come to the other's help (vv. 9-11). Then: be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him (v. 12). The Syrians flee, and the Ammonites see it and run into the city (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab is a professional and this is professional work: a two-front trap answered by splitting the force, keeping the elite for the harder enemy, and arranging mutual reinforcement before either engages.
verseByVerse.examples: And the speech is genuinely good theology — duty done as hard as it can be done, and the outcome left with God — from the man who murdered Abner at the gate of a city of refuge. Both are true of him, and the writer never reconciles them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men. And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country. When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians. The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites. And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you. Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him." So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him. And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men.'

Hanun knows what he has done, and buys an army.

Thirty-three thousand hired troops from four sources, which is an enormous outlay. Note who the main supplier is: the Syrians of Zobah, whose king Hadadezer David defeated two chapters ago. This is the whole northern coalition getting a second attempt, paid for by Ammon.

'And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men.'

'And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country.'

Now the tactical situation, and it is as bad as it can be.

The Ammonites are drawn up in front of their own city gate. The hired Syrians are somewhere out in the open country behind Joab. He has walked into the classic trap: an enemy in front and an enemy behind, with the two able to close on him at a signal.

'When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.'

'The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites.'

He splits the army, which takes nerve, and the allocation tells you he knows his trade.

He takes the picked men himself and faces the Syrians — the professionals, the hired troops, the harder fight in open ground. Abishai gets the remainder and the Ammonites, who are defending a gate and can retreat into it.

'And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you."'

Then the agreement, made before either force engages: whichever of us is losing, the other comes.

That is a plan for the situation actually in front of them rather than the one they would prefer, and it removes from both commanders the temptation to look after their own front and let the other manage. Neither can win separately.

'"Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."'

Here is Joab's sentence, and it is a good deal better than Joab.

Take it in two halves, because the balance in it is what makes it worth having.

The first half is duty. Let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God. He names what they are fighting for, and it is not the king, not the empire, not plunder, and not their own reputations. The people, and the cities of our God. He puts the theological frame round the whole thing: this is God's territory and these are God's people.

The second half is submission. May the LORD do what seems good to him.

Notice what he does not say. He does not promise victory, or claim God is on their side, or assert that the LORD will certainly give the enemy into their hand. He has done everything a competent general can do — split the force, weighted it correctly, arranged mutual support — and then he hands the result over without a guarantee.

That is the right shape for anybody's work, and it is genuinely hard to hold. Do the thing as well as it can be done, fight as if it depends on you, and then leave the outcome with God on the understanding that what seems good to him may not be what seems good to you.

It comes out of the mouth of a murderer.

This is the man who called Abner aside at the gate of Hebron as though to speak privately with him and put a knife in his stomach, in a city of refuge, in peacetime, and was cursed for it in public by his own king. He will kill Absalom against a direct royal order, and Amasa the same way he killed Abner, and he will die holding the horns of the altar.

Both are true of him and the writer never reconciles them. He does not explain how a man can speak like this and behave like that, or suggest the words are hypocrisy. He puts the speech in the record and moves on.

It is a fair warning about how little a true sentence proves about the person saying it — and equally, that a true sentence is still true. Joab was right. He was right about the people and the cities of God and about leaving the outcome with the LORD, and he was a murderer, and both things went into the same battle.

'So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him.'

'And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.'

The hired men break first, which is what hired men do, and the Ammonites go back inside their walls the moment they see it.

Note that Joab does not besiege the city. He has beaten the field army and he goes home. That matters, because the war is not over — Rabbah is still standing, and somebody will have to come back for it next spring.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Afraid to Save the Ammonites Anymore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Syrians regroup and Hadadezer brings troops from beyond the Euphrates under Shobach (vv. 15-16). David crosses the Jordan himself, and the Syrians lose seven hundred chariot teams and forty thousand horsemen; Shobach dies on the field (vv. 17-18). And the vassal kings make peace with Israel and serve them, so the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Note that David goes out himself here, and wins. That matters for the sentence at the start of the next chapter, which describes him doing the opposite.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends with the coalition broken and the Ammonites alone. Their capital is Rabbah, and it has not been taken. The war is unfinished, and it is the war Joab is still fighting when the next chapter opens.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together. And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head. And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him. And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there. And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together.'

'And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.'

This has now stopped being about Ammon.

Hadadezer calls up troops from the far side of the Euphrates, which means the whole Aramean world is being mobilised, and his commander-in-chief takes the field in person. What began as a diplomatic insult in a small kingdom has become a war for control of the north.

'And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him.'

David goes himself.

Mark that sentence and keep it, because in eleven verses' time the writer is going to say the opposite about him in a way that will define the rest of the book. Here, when the enemy is a serious army under a serious commander, the king gathers all Israel, crosses the river, and stands in the line.

'And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there.'

The Syrian army is destroyed and its commander killed on the field.

'And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.'

The coalition collapses, and the last clause is the one that matters for what comes next.

The Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.

Ammon is now alone. The hired army is gone, the great power that was paying attention has been beaten twice and has decided this is no longer its quarrel, and the men who shaved the beards of David's envoys are sitting inside the walls of Rabbah with nobody coming.

And the city has not been taken.

That is the position at the end of chapter 10, and it is the reason chapter 11 opens the way it does. Campaigning stopped for the winter, as it always did. In the spring the army went back out to finish the job, under Joab, to besiege Rabbah.

The first verse of the next chapter says so: in the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah.

And then five words that are the hinge of the whole book.

But David remained at Jerusalem.

This chapter is why that sentence is an accusation. There is a war on, it is his war, it started because his own envoys were humiliated, he fought the northern half of it in person and won, and the army is now in the field finishing it without him.

10.theology:
Two chapters running, faith kept with the dead (v. 2). Jonathan in chapter 9, Nahash here, and the same word both times — loyalty that outlasts the reason for it. This time the beneficiary is a foreign dynasty, and the kindness being repaid was shown by a man whose one other appearance in Scripture is an atrocity (1 Sam. 11:2). The writer does not explain the debt, and inventing one is not a service.

How suspicion works (v. 3). There is no evidence in it. A delegation of condolence has done exactly what such delegations do, and the princes have no information — only a clever-sounding theory and the assumption that they are too shrewd to be fooled. And it is not unreasonable on its face: David has spent two chapters subduing everyone within reach, and a young untested king might well be nervous. The fault is not in having the thought; it is in acting on it as a certainty rather than watching, testing, or simply hastening the envoys home.

An insult built to be seen (v. 4). Half a beard, not the whole — a full shave was a mourning custom and could be borne, while half makes every face a joke that cannot be explained. Robes cut off at the hips left grown men exposed on a public road. Hanun is not hurting the envoys; he is using them to insult David, and the insult is meant to travel.

The king's first thought (v. 5). He does not march them into Jerusalem so the nation can see the outrage and be roused — which is precisely what a king who wanted a war would do. He sends word ahead to the first town on the road and tells them to stay there until they can face people. The narrator gives the reason: for the men were greatly ashamed. How a man treats people who have been made ridiculous in his service is a real test, and it usually goes unrecorded.

Joab's speech, and Joab (v. 12). Two halves, and the balance is what makes it worth having. Duty: for our people, and for the cities of our God — not the king, not the empire, not plunder, not their own names. And submission: may the LORD do what seems good to him, which promises nothing, claims nothing, and does not assert that God is on their side. He has done everything a competent general can do and then hands over the result without a guarantee. That is the right shape for anybody's work and it is hard to hold.

And it comes from a murderer. This is the man who called Abner aside at a gate as though to speak privately and knifed him in the stomach, in a city of refuge, in peacetime; who will kill Absalom against a direct order and Amasa the same way he killed Abner, and die holding the horns of the altar. The writer never reconciles it, never calls the words hypocrisy, and never explains how the same man does both. It is a fair warning about how little a true sentence proves about the person saying it — and equally that a true sentence is still true. Joab was right, and he was a murderer, and both went into the same battle.

David went himself (v. 17). When the enemy is a serious army under a serious commander, the king gathers all Israel, crosses the Jordan, and stands in the line. Keep that sentence. In eleven verses the writer will say the opposite about him, in the words that define the rest of the book.

Why this chapter exists (v. 19). The Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore — the coalition is broken, Ammon is alone, and Rabbah has not been taken. Campaigning stopped for the winter as it always did, and in the spring the army went back to finish it. That is the war in 11:1, and that is why but David remained at Jerusalem is an accusation rather than a detail. It is his war, it began with his own envoys being humiliated, he fought the northern half of it in person and won — and the army is now in the field completing it without him.
10.examples:
Then: A king's counsellors decided, on no evidence whatever, that a delegation of condolence was a reconnaissance party — and their king shaved off half of each envoy's beard, cut their robes off at the hips, and turned them out to walk home through their own country. The war it started ran for two campaigning seasons and cost the lives of an entire allied army and its commander.

Now: Two things. The princes of Ammon are the study in what a plausible suspicion costs when it is acted on as a certainty. They were not stupid and their theory was not absurd; they simply never checked it, and by the time anybody could have checked it the envoys had been mutilated and there was no way back. And Joab's line is the one to carry into ordinary work: do the thing as well as it can be done, for the people it is actually for, and then leave the result with God — on the honest understanding, which Joab states and most of us quietly omit, that what seems good to him may not be what seems good to you.

11.title: The Great Fall
11.text: <sup>1</sup>In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful.<sup>3</sup>And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"<sup>4</sup>So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house.<sup>5</sup>And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."<sup>6</sup>So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.<sup>7</sup>When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going.<sup>8</sup>Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king.<sup>9</sup>But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.<sup>10</sup>When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"<sup>11</sup>Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing."<sup>12</sup>Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.<sup>13</sup>And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.<sup>14</sup>In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.<sup>15</sup>In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die."<sup>16</sup>And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men.<sup>17</sup>And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.<sup>18</sup>Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting.<sup>19</sup>And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king,<sup>20</sup>then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?<sup>21</sup>Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"<sup>22</sup>So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell.<sup>23</sup>The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.<sup>24</sup>Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."<sup>25</sup>David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him."<sup>26</sup>When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband.<sup>27</sup>And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
11.overview:
Everything is in the last sentence of verse 1, and the previous chapter spent nineteen verses loading it. This is the second season of the Ammonite war — his own war, started when his envoys were shaved and stripped and sent home — and he fought the hard half of it in person, crossing the Jordan to destroy a Syrian army and kill its commander. Joab is at Rabbah. Uriah is at Rabbah. All Israel is at Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.

The seeing is not the sin; he looked out from the tallest roof in a small city. The turn comes in verse 3, and it is the answer to a question he asked: she has a name, she is the daughter of one of his own thirty, and she is the wife of another — and both men's names are given him. He had every fact he needed and could still have stopped. Then the verbs, and they are all his: he sent, he took, he lay. Took is the word the narrator used at 5:13 without a syllable of comment.

The cover-up gets worse at every step. Uriah will not sleep at home while the ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths — a Hittite mercenary more careful of the ark than the king who danced it into the city — and swears he will not, by the life of the man arranging it. Drunk, he still walks past his own street. So David writes the order in his own hand and sends it by the one man certain not to open it: his loyalty is the mechanism. Joab improves on the method, because a visible withdrawal would be remembered and a costly assault buries one name in a casualty list.

Twenty-six verses, and the narrator says nothing at all. Then seven words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — But David Remained at Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel... But David remained at Jerusalem (v. 1). Late one afternoon he walks on the roof and sees a woman bathing (v. 2). And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?" (v. 3). So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her (v. 4). Then five words that change everything: and she conceived — and a message: I am pregnant (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the second season of the Ammonite war — his own war, begun when his envoys were humiliated, the northern half of which he fought in person and won (10:17). Everyone he commands is in the field. He is not.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 is the point of no return, and it is the answer to a question he asked. He was told she was married and told the husband's name, and he sent anyway. And took is the same verb the narrator used at 5:13 without a word of comment.

verseByVerse.quote: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful. And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?" So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house. And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.'

Everything that follows is in that last sentence, and the writer has spent the whole previous chapter loading it.

Take the pieces in order.

The time when kings go out to battle. Campaigning stopped over the winter, when the roads were mud and there was nothing in the fields to live on. In the spring, armies moved. That is simply how the year worked, and the phrase is not sarcasm; it is a calendar note that becomes an accusation because of what comes after it.

And this is not some optional foreign adventure. It is the second season of the Ammonite war, which began when Hanun shaved the beards of David's own envoys and sent them home half-dressed. It is his war. Rabbah is unfinished business from chapter 10, and the coalition that was propping the Ammonites up has already quit.

More than that: he fought the hard half of that war in person. When the Syrians brought up an army from beyond the Euphrates, David gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan (10:17) and destroyed them and killed their commander. He knows how to do this and he has just done it.

He sends Joab, and his servants, and all Israel.

But David remained at Jerusalem.

The whole army is in the field. Uriah is in the field. Joab is in the field. And the man who has been asking God before every battle since he came out of a cave is at home with nothing to do.

Nothing in the verse says he was wrong to delegate; kings did delegate. What the verse does is put him in the one place where the next verse can happen, at the one time of year when there is nobody around, with no responsibility on him for the first time in his adult life.

He is somewhere in his early fifties. He has won everything. And the writer, who has spent five chapters showing us a man who asks God about everything, now shows us a man with an afternoon free.

'It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful.'

He gets up from a nap in the late afternoon and walks about on his roof.

The palace was the highest building in a very small city built on a steep ridge, and the houses below were packed close. From that roof you could see into a good many courtyards. There is no indication anywhere in the text that she is doing anything improper — the bathing is most likely the purification the law required after a period, which is a detail the writer supplies in the next verse and which matters because it establishes the pregnancy is not her husband's.

The seeing is not the sin. It should be said plainly, because a great deal of preaching has made this chapter about a glance. He saw something from his own roof.

What happens next is the sin.

'And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"'

Here is the point of no return, and it is not verse 4.

He asks. And the answer he gets back is not a name but a warning, and it is delivered in the form of a question — is not this...? — which is how a servant tells a king something he does not want to say.

The answer contains three pieces of information and every one of them is a wall.

She has a name: Bathsheba. She is not an anonymous body on a roof; she is a person, and people in this city know her.

She is the daughter of Eliam. And Eliam is on the list at the end of this book — one of the thirty, David's own elite (23:34). More than that, the list makes Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, which would make Bathsheba the granddaughter of David's greatest counsellor. If that is right — and it is the natural reading — it explains something that otherwise makes no sense at all: why, years later, Ahithophel abandons David for Absalom without a word of hesitation (15:31), and why his advice to Absalom is so ferocious. The wisest man in the kingdom had a granddaughter.

And she is the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Married. And the husband is also on the list at the end of the book — the very last name on it (23:39). He is not a stranger. He is one of the king's own thirty, and he is at this moment sleeping in a field outside Rabbah on David's orders.

David asked a question and was told, in one sentence, that the woman was somebody's daughter and somebody's wife, and given both men's names, and both men were his.

He went ahead.

That is where this chapter turns. Not on the roof. In the half minute after the servant answered him, when he had every fact he needed and could still have stopped.

'So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house.'

Read the verbs, because the writer has chosen them and they are all David's.

He sent. He took. He lay. She came and she returned, and those are the only two things attributed to her in the entire verse, and both of them are responses to being summoned.

Took is the word to stop on. It has appeared before, in a sentence the narrator laid down without a syllable of comment: David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem (5:13), immediately after the finest thing ever said about him. And behind that stands the law about Israel's king, and its stated reason: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17).

A man who has spent twenty years lawfully taking women when he wanted them has practised something, and here it is.

Now, about Bathsheba, and this needs care, because commentators have gone both ways for centuries and the text supports neither confidently.

Some have made her a temptress who bathed where she could be seen. There is nothing whatever in the passage to support it; she is washing in her own courtyard, and the man looking is on the roof of the tallest building in the city.

Others have written her a full interior life of terror or of complicity. The honest position is that the narrator does not tell us her mind at any point, and filling the silence in either direction is invention.

What the text does establish is the situation. She is the wife of a serving soldier, in a small city, summoned by the king of Israel, by messengers, to the palace. There is no version of that scene in which she is a free party to a negotiation. Whatever she felt, the power in that room was entirely on one side, and Scripture's own verdict — delivered by Nathan in the next chapter — assigns the guilt to one person and describes her as a lamb that was taken.

The prophet's parable has a rich man, a poor man, and a ewe lamb. The lamb does not get blamed.

'And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."'

Two words in Hebrew, and they end the private phase of this.

She sends, which is the one action she initiates in the chapter, and the message is three words long in English and unanswerable. The purification note in verse 4 has already told the reader what David is about to work out for himself: the child cannot be Uriah's, because Uriah has been at Rabbah, and the whole city will be able to count.

Everything from here is a cover-up, and it gets worse at every step.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Shall I Then Go to My House?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David recalls Uriah from the siege, asks after the war, and tells him to go home and wash his feet, sending a present after him (vv. 6-8). But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house (v. 9). Challenged, he answers: the ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing (v. 11). So David keeps him another day and gets him drunk — but he did not go down to his house (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A Hittite mercenary will not sleep under his own roof while the ark of God is in a field shelter. The king of Israel, who danced that ark into the city, is sleeping in a palace and has just taken this man's wife.
verseByVerse.examples: And drunk, he still will not go. Whatever David hoped the wine would loosen, the loyalty underneath it did not move.

verseByVerse.quote: So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David. When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going. Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house. When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?" Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing." Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next. And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.'

The first plan is the obvious one, and if it had worked nobody would ever have known.

Bring the husband home for a night. The dates will be close enough. The child will be assumed to be his, Uriah will go back to the siege, and the whole thing disappears.

Note that David has to pull a named officer out of an active siege to do it, which Joab will certainly have noticed.

'When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going.'

And here is the small talk, and it is repulsive.

Three questions: how is Joab, how are the men, how is the war. Every one of them the right question for a king to ask a soldier just in from the front, and every one of them a delay while the man stands there waiting to be told why he has been summoned a day's journey from a siege.

He is asking after the welfare of the army he is about to have this man killed by.

'Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king.'

Go down to your house and wash your feet is an ordinary phrase for going home and resting, with a plain enough implication attached. And then the present, sent after him — food from the palace, most likely, for a homecoming meal.

The king is furnishing the evening.

'But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.'

He sleeps on the doorstep with the palace staff.

The plan has failed and David does not yet know why. Neither does the reader, until Uriah is asked.

'When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"'

'Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing."'

This is the moral centre of the chapter and it is spoken by a foreigner.

Go through what he actually says.

The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths. He begins with the ark. Not the army, not his commander, not his own comfort — the ark of God is out in a field shelter, and while it is there he will not sleep under a roof.

That is the same ark David danced into this city in a linen ephod, having spent three months learning how to carry it properly. The Hittite is more careful of it than the man who brought it home.

My lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. His officers and his mates are sleeping in the dirt outside Rabbah. He will not take a comfort they cannot have.

Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? Three things, and the third is the one David needs him to do.

As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing.

He swears it. And he swears it by the life of the king who is standing in front of him trying to arrange exactly that thing, which is the cruellest accident in the passage.

Now set the two men side by side, because the writer has arranged this and means it to be seen.

Uriah is a Hittite — a foreigner, from a people Israel was told to drive out, serving in Israel's army under an Israelite name that means the LORD is my light. He will not sleep in his own bed because the ark of God is in a tent.

David is the anointed king of Israel, the man after God's own heart, who wrote about the ark and danced in front of it. He has slept in a palace, taken this man's wife, and is now trying to get him drunk enough to go home so the arithmetic will work.

Neither man knows what the other knows. Uriah is being honourable in front of a king who is counting days, and every honourable thing he says makes his own death more certain.

There is a question worth asking here that the text leaves open: did Uriah suspect? Some have thought so — the palace was small and servants talk, and his refusal is very firm. It is possible, and the text gives no answer. What it gives is a soldier's principle stated twice and kept under pressure, and that is enough.

'Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.'

'And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.'

So David gets him drunk.

Read that as what it is: the king of Israel sitting at a table with a loyal officer, filling his cup, working on him for an evening, in order to lower the man's guard enough to send him home to a wife the king has already slept with.

And it does not work. Drunk, at the end of a long evening, Uriah walks past the turning to his own street and lies down on the floor with the servants.

Whatever the wine loosened, it did not reach the thing underneath. Some men are not different when their guard is down; they are simply the same men, more slowly. That is a harder integrity than David has at this moment, and the king can see it.

He has now tried decency, hospitality and alcohol, and the man will not be moved. There is one thing left, and he does it in the morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — Set Uriah in the Forefront
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah (v. 14): set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die (v. 15).
