Joab does not do exactly that — he assigns Uriah to a place he knows is defended by hard men, sends the assault in against the wall, and loses a number of the king's servants along with him (vv. 16-17). Then he coaches the messenger: if the king is angry about the casualties, mention Abimelech and the millstone at Thebez — then you shall say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also" (vv. 18-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Uriah carries his own death warrant across the country, sealed, in his hand, and hands it to the man who will execute it. He is chosen as the courier because he is the one man certain not to open it.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab quietly improves on the instruction. A withdrawal that exposed one man would have been visible to the whole army; a costly frontal assault kills Uriah and buries him inside a casualty list. And Joab now knows something about the king that cannot be unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah. In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die." And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men. And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died. Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting. And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king, then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall? Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.'

Read that sentence again and let it be as bad as it is.

He writes the order for the man's death, in his own hand, and gives it to the man to carry. Uriah walks the whole way back to Rabbah with his own execution sealed in his belt, and delivers it to his commanding officer himself.

The reason he is chosen as courier is the reason he is being killed. He is the one man in the kingdom who is certain not to open it.

His loyalty is the mechanism.

'In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die."'

The instruction is precise and it is murder, and it is murder of a kind that leaves no body to explain and no blood on anybody's hands.

Note what David is willing to spend. A deliberate withdrawal from a man in contact with the enemy would be seen by every soldier in the line; it would need Joab to give an order that would be remembered. He does not care. He also does not seem to consider that the manoeuvre will cost other men, which it does.

He is no longer covering a pregnancy. He is disposing of a witness who has done nothing but behave well.

'And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men.'

And Joab does it differently, and the difference tells you a great deal about Joab.

He does not stage a withdrawal. He puts Uriah where he knows the defenders are hard, and then sends the whole assault in against the wall.

Why? Because Joab is a professional and he can see what David, sitting in Jerusalem, has not thought about. A visible abandonment of one named officer would be talked about in the army for twenty years and would eventually reach somebody who would ask why. A costly assault on a fortified wall is a normal military disaster, and one dead officer in a casualty list is invisible.

Joab's method is safer and it kills more people.

'And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.'

Some of the servants of David among the people fell.

Other men die. The writer does not say how many and does not name them, and their families were told they fell in an assault on Rabbah, and that was true, and it was not the reason.

Then, at the end of the verse, as though it were an afterthought: Uriah the Hittite also died. Which is the only part of the operation David was interested in.

'Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting.'

'And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king,"'

'"then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?'"'

'"'Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"'

And this is the most chilling piece of stage management in the book, and it is entirely Joab's.

He briefs the messenger on the king's likely reaction, anticipates the exact rebuke — including the historical example David will reach for, the death of Abimelech under a millstone thrown by a woman at Thebez (Judg. 9:53) — and gives the man the sentence that will make the anger stop.

Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.

Joab has understood the letter completely. He knows that the casualties are irrelevant to the king and that one name will settle everything, and he has arranged for a junior messenger to say it out loud in the throne room without knowing what he is saying.

He is also, in the same breath, establishing something. He has the letter. He has done the thing. And he has now demonstrated to himself that the king will accept a report of unnecessary dead soldiers as long as the right man is among them.

From this morning, Joab owns David.

Everything the man does for the next thirty years sits on top of this. He kills Absalom against a direct, public, repeated royal order and suffers nothing. He murders Amasa in the road exactly as he murdered Abner and suffers nothing. He speaks to the king with a contempt no other subject would survive. And David, dying, has to ask Solomon to do what he could never do himself (1 Kings 2:5-6).

A man who has helped you do something you cannot admit is not your servant afterwards.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Sword Devours Now One and Now Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messenger reports; David's reply is do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it (vv. 22-25). Bathsheba mourns her husband (v. 26). And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The sword devours now one and now another is a commander's shrug at the cost of war, and the man saying it arranged this particular death and knows the name of the man in the casualty list. It is the coldest sentence David ever speaks.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter has offered no judgment for twenty-six verses. It has simply reported. And then the last clause arrives, and it is the only comment in the whole account.

verseByVerse.quote: So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell. The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate. Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also." David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him." When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband. And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell.'

'The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate."'

'"Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."'

The messenger delivers the whole thing at once and never gets to find out whether the king would have been angry.

'David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it,' and encourage him."'

And here is the coldest sentence David ever speaks.

The sword devours now one and now another.

On any other day that is a decent thing for a commander to say to a commander who has taken losses. War is like that; men die; do not carry it. It is the sort of thing that keeps an army functioning.

Said by this man, on this morning, it is obscene. He knows precisely which one the sword devoured and why, because he wrote the instruction. He is telling the executioner not to feel bad about the execution, using a proverb about the randomness of war to describe a death he arranged in advance, in writing.

And note the last two words of the message: encourage him. Buck Joab up.

The phrase will come back. Abner shouted across a valley at this same Joab, years ago: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? (2:26). The sword does not stop, and it is bitter in the end, and Nathan is about to tell David that it will never leave his house.

'When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband.'

She is not given her name in this verse.

The writer has called her Bathsheba once, in verse 3, in the servant's warning. Here, and in the next verse, she is the wife of Uriah — and the New Testament does the same thing at the head of the Gospels, where Matthew declines to name her at all and writes that David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6).

That is not an accident in either place. She is identified by the man who was killed, in the sentence recording that she mourned him.

And she lamented over her husband is all we are told about what this did to her. Seven days, in a house, for a man she was married to and who would not come home to her while the ark was in a field.

'And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son.'

David sent. The same verb again, for the fourth time in the chapter. He sent for Joab, he sent for the woman, he sent for Uriah, he sends now.

And from the outside it is a decent act. A king marries the widow of an officer killed at the siege of Rabbah, quickly, before anybody counts months. The child arrives inside a marriage. The mathematics are covered, the household is provided for, and the whole business is closed.

Twenty-six verses, and the narrator has not said one word of judgment. He has reported a walk on a roof, a question and its answer, a summons, a pregnancy, three failed attempts to arrange a paternity, a letter, a battle, a casualty list, a piece of coaching, a shrug, and a wedding. No comment at all.

'But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.'

And there it is, at the very end, in one clause.

The Hebrew is stronger than the English: the thing was evil in the eyes of the LORD.

Everything in the chapter has been about eyes. David saw a woman from a roof. He arranged matters so that nobody else would see what had happened. The mathematics were made to look right, the marriage was made to look decent, the death was made to look like the ordinary attrition of a siege, and the messenger did not know what he was carrying and neither did Uriah.

It worked. Every person in Jerusalem who mattered saw exactly what David wanted them to see.

One did not.

That single sentence is the writer's whole method. He has refused to editorialise for a full chapter, letting the reader watch it happen and feel the sickness of it without being told what to think, and then he puts the verdict down in seven words and stops.

There is no punishment in this verse, no lightning, no visible consequence. There is a year of silence coming — the child is born, the household settles, the siege goes on — and Psalm 32 is probably David's own record of what that year was like from the inside: when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me (Ps. 32:3-4).

And then a man walks into the room with a story about a lamb.

11.theology:
Why verse 1 is an accusation. Not because delegating a siege is wrong — kings delegated. Because it is his war, unfinished from chapter 10, whose northern half he fought in person and won (10:17); because everyone he commands is in the field; and because it puts him in the one place, at the one season, where he has nothing to do and no responsibility on him for the first time in his adult life. The writer has spent five chapters showing a man who asks God about everything, and now shows him with an afternoon free.

The point of no return is verse 3, not verse 4. He asked, and the answer came back as a warning phrased as a question — which is how a servant tells a king something he does not want to say. Three facts, each a wall: a name, a father who is one of the thirty, and a husband who is another. Eliam is the son of Ahithophel (23:34), which would make Bathsheba the granddaughter of David's greatest counsellor — and that is the only thing that explains why Ahithophel later joins Absalom without hesitating (15:31). Uriah is the last name on the list of the mighty men (23:39), which is the writer's own quiet memorial. David was told all of it and went ahead.

The verbs are all his (v. 4). He sent, took, lay; she came and returned, and both are responses to a summons. Took is the verb of 5:13 and behind it stands the law about Israel's king and its stated reason: lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). Twenty years of lawfully taking women when he wanted them is a practised thing.

What can and cannot be said about Bathsheba. Some have made her a temptress; there is nothing in the passage to support it — she is washing in her own courtyard and the man looking is on the roof of the tallest building in the city. Others write her a full interior life of terror or complicity. The narrator reports her mind at no point, and filling that silence in either direction is invention. What the text does establish is the situation: a serving soldier's wife, in a small city, summoned by the king by messengers. There is no version of that in which she is a free party to a negotiation. And Scripture's own verdict comes next chapter, in a parable with a rich man, a poor man, and a ewe lamb — and the lamb is not blamed.

The moral centre is spoken by a foreigner (v. 11). He begins with the ark — not his commander, not his comfort. It is the same ark David danced into the city in a linen ephod after three months learning to carry it properly, and the Hittite is more careful of it than he is. Then his officers and his mates in the dirt outside Rabbah, and a comfort he will not take that they cannot have. And he swears it by the life of the king standing in front of him arranging exactly that thing. Whether he suspected, the text does not say; what it gives is a principle stated and kept under pressure, and every honourable sentence he speaks makes his death more certain.

Drunk, he still would not go (v. 13). The king of Israel sat at a table filling a loyal officer's cup for an evening to lower his guard enough to send him home to a wife the king had already slept with — and it failed. Some men are not different when their guard is down; they are the same men, more slowly.

The loyalty is the mechanism (v. 14). He writes the death warrant in his own hand and sends it by the condemned man, and the reason Uriah is chosen as courier is the reason he is being killed: he is the one man certain not to open it.

Joab improves on the instruction (v. 16). A staged withdrawal from a man in contact would be seen by the whole line and remembered for twenty years; a costly frontal assault is a normal military disaster and hides one name in a casualty list. Joab's method is safer and it kills more people — some of the servants of David among the people fell, unnamed, whose families were told they died attacking Rabbah, which was true and was not the reason.

From this morning, Joab owns David (vv. 19-21). He briefs the messenger on the king's likely anger, anticipates the exact rebuke down to the historical example (Abimelech and the millstone at Thebez, Judg. 9:53), and supplies the one sentence that will stop it. He has understood the letter completely: the casualties are irrelevant and one name settles everything. Everything Joab does for thirty years sits on this — killing Absalom against a direct public order, murdering Amasa exactly as he murdered Abner, speaking to the king with a contempt no other subject would survive. A man who has helped you do what you cannot admit is not your servant afterwards, and a dying David has to ask Solomon to do what he never could (1 Kings 2:5-6).

The coldest sentence he ever speaks (v. 25). The sword devours now one and now another is a decent thing for one commander to say to another who has taken losses — on any other day. Here it is a proverb about the randomness of war used to describe a death arranged in advance in writing, with encourage him attached. And the phrase has a history: Abner shouted at this same Joab across a valley, shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? (2:26). Nathan is about to say it will never leave his house.

She is named once (vv. 26-27). After verse 3 she is the wife of Uriah — and Matthew does the same thing at the head of the Gospel, declining to name her and writing that David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6). She is identified by the man who was killed, in the sentence recording that she mourned him.

Seven words, at the very end. The Hebrew is stronger than the English: the thing was evil in the eyes of the LORD. And the whole chapter has been about eyes — he saw a woman from a roof, and then arranged matters so nobody would see what followed. The arithmetic was made to look right, the marriage decent, the death like ordinary attrition; the messenger did not know what he was saying and neither did Uriah. It worked. Everyone in Jerusalem saw exactly what David meant them to see. One did not. There is no lightning in the verse and no visible consequence — only a year of silence, which Psalm 32 probably records from the inside: when I kept silent, my bones wasted away... day and night your hand was heavy upon me (Ps. 32:3-4). And then a man walks in with a story about a lamb.
11.examples:
Then: A king wrote out the order for a man's death in his own hand, sealed it, and gave it to that man to carry a day's journey across country and hand to the general who would carry it out — choosing him as the courier for the same reason he was killing him, because he was the one officer in the kingdom certain not to open it.

Now: Two things. The first is where the chapter actually turns. Not the roof — verse 3, the half minute after the servant answered, when David had every fact he needed and the information was doing its work and he sent anyway. Almost nobody walks into a disaster without being told first; what happens is that the telling arrives and gets overridden, and everything afterwards is momentum. And the second is Joab. The cover-up required an accomplice, and from the moment he had one, David was never free of him again. There is no such thing as a person who helps you hide something and then goes back to being an ordinary subordinate.

12.title: You Are the Man
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor.<sup>2</sup>The rich man had very many flocks and herds,<sup>3</sup>but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him.<sup>4</sup>Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."<sup>5</sup>Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die,<sup>6</sup>and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."<sup>7</sup>Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.<sup>8</sup>And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.<sup>9</sup>Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.<sup>10</sup>Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'<sup>11</sup>Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.<sup>12</sup>For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"<sup>13</sup>David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die.<sup>14</sup>Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die."<sup>15</sup>Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.<sup>16</sup>David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.<sup>17</sup>And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them.<sup>18</sup>On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm."<sup>19</sup>But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."<sup>20</sup>Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate.<sup>21</sup>Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food."<sup>22</sup>He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?'<sup>23</sup>But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."<sup>24</sup>Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him<sup>25</sup>and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD.<sup>26</sup>Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city.<sup>27</sup>And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters.<sup>28</sup>Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name."<sup>29</sup>So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it.<sup>30</sup>And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.<sup>31</sup>And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
12.overview:
About a year of silence, and nothing happened. The marriage held, the household ran, the siege went on, and nobody in Jerusalem said a word. Psalm 32 is probably his own account of that year from the inside: when I kept silent, my bones wasted away... day and night your hand was heavy upon me. Then the LORD sends Nathan — the same prophet who brought the promise in chapter 7, now walking in to say what will happen to the house.

And he does not accuse. He brings a case. That is why it works: this is the supreme judge of Israel doing the exact job 8:15 credits him with, and the verdict is out of his mouth under oath before he knows who the defendant is. He sets the sentence himself — death, and fourfold, which is the law's penalty for a stolen sheep — and four of his sons will die. And the sharpest clause is his own: because he had no pity.

The indictment is built out of gifts, not laws, and the worst line in it is if this were too little, I would add to you as much more. There was more available and he never asked. Then God's account of the killing, straight through the Ammonite arrow that did it: you have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. Every layer of distance David built bought him a year with the neighbours and nothing here.

He says four words and is forgiven in the next sentence — and then told the sword will never leave his house. Both stand, and neither cancels the other. The child dies. He prays for seven days against a word he has been given plainly, on the ground that who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me?, and when it is over he washes and goes to worship. And at the end of the worst chapter of his life, four words about the next son: and the LORD loved him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — There Were Two Men in a Certain City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD sends Nathan, and he brings the king a case: a rich man with very many flocks, a poor man with nothing but one little ewe lamb that he had brought up with his own children — it used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him (vv. 1-3). A traveller comes to the rich man, who spares his own flock and takes the poor man's lamb (v. 4). Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man: as the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die, and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: This is not a story with a moral. It is a legal case brought to the supreme judge of Israel — exactly the work 8:15 says he did — and the king hears it and gives judgment. That is why it works: the verdict is out of his mouth before he knows what he has done.
verseByVerse.examples: And he sets his own tariff. Death, and fourfold restitution, which is the penalty the law prescribes for a stolen sheep (Ex. 22:1). Four of his sons will die: this child, Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor. The rich man had very many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him. Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him." Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die, and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor."'

About a year has passed. The child in 11:27 has been born, which means roughly nine months of silence at least, and probably more.

Nothing happened in that year. The marriage held, the household ran, the siege of Rabbah continued, and no one in Jerusalem said anything. David got away with it completely.

Psalm 32 is very probably his own account of what that year was like from the inside: when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer (Ps. 32:3-4).

The LORD sent Nathan. Not the court, not a rival, not a rumour. And it is the same prophet who brought the covenant promise in chapter 7 — the man who told him his house would stand forever now walks in to tell him what is going to happen to it.

Now watch what Nathan does, because the method is as instructive as the message.

He does not accuse. He brings a case.

'"The rich man had very many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him."'

Every detail in that sentence is doing work, and the effect is cumulative.

One little ewe lamb, against very many flocks and herds. He bought it, so it cost him. It grew up in the house with his children. It ate his food and drank from his cup and slept in his arms.

And then: it was like a daughter to him.

The Hebrew word for daughter is bat, and the woman's name is Bath-sheba. It is very likely deliberate, and even if it is not, the picture is exact: not a possession, a member of the family, loved.

'"Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."'

The occasion is trivial. That is the point.

It is not famine, not desperation, not a debt. A visitor arrives and a meal has to be made, and the rich man will not spend one animal out of many, so he takes the one animal a poor man owns.

The disproportion between what he needed and what he destroyed is the whole case.

'Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die,"'

And now the trap closes, and it closes because David does his job.

This is not a king being taken in by a clever story. Nathan has brought him a legal matter, which is exactly what the king of Israel was for: David administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15). A man with no standing has been robbed and has no redress, and the case has come up to the supreme court, and David hears it and does what he is supposed to do. He gets angry, and he gives judgment.

That is why the parable works. It is not a moral tale that he happens to identify with; it is a verdict he pronounces in office, under oath — as the LORD lives — before he knows who the defendant is.

And note how far he goes. Nobody has died in the story. A sheep was taken. And the king's instant, furious sentence is capital.

'"and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."'

Then the restitution, and it is straight out of the law: if a man steals an ox or a sheep and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep (Ex. 22:1).

David sets the tariff himself: fourfold.

Hold that number, because the rest of this book pays it out. Four of his sons die. The child in this chapter. Amnon, murdered by his brother at a sheepshearing. Absalom, killed in an oak tree against David's explicit order. Adonijah, executed by Solomon. Four sons, and the man who set the figure was the boy's father.

And listen to the last clause of his own verdict, because it is the sharpest thing in the chapter: because he had no pity.

Not because he broke the law. Because there was nothing in him that stopped.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nathan said to David, "You are the man!" (v. 7). Then the indictment, and it is built out of gifts: I anointed you, I delivered you, I gave you your master's house and your master's wives — and if this were too little, I would add to you as much more (vv. 7-8). Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites (v. 9). The sentence: the sword will never depart from his house, and evil will be raised up against him out of his own house — done in secret, answered before all Israel and before the sun (vv. 10-12). David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge is not that he broke a rule. Every clause of it is something God gave him, and the worst line is the one about how much more was on offer: if this were too little, I would add to you as much more. There was another way to get anything he actually needed, and he did not ask.
verseByVerse.examples: And God names the murder as David's own, straight through the Ammonite arrow that did it: you have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. The distance David built into the arrangement does not exist in God's account of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul. And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more. Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.' Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'" David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die." Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Nathan said to David, "You are the man!"'

Three words in Hebrew. Attah ha-ish.

There is nothing else like it in Scripture for sheer compression. No preamble, no softening, no appeal to the king's better nature. The judge has passed sentence and the prophet identifies the defendant.

Consider what Nathan is risking. He is standing alone in front of a man who has, within the last year, arranged the death of a decorated officer and several other soldiers to conceal a pregnancy, and got away with it. Nathan knows this, because God has just told him. And he says it anyway.

'"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.'"'

'"'And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.'"'

Read the indictment carefully, because of what it is made of.

It is not a list of laws. It is a list of gifts.

I anointed you — in your father's house, when you were the eighth son out with the sheep. I delivered you out of the hand of Saul — through the spears, the window, the caves, the three thousand men, twice. I gave you your master's house, and Israel, and Judah.

Every clause begins with God as the giver, exactly as chapter 7 did.

And then the line that is worse than any accusation.

And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.

There was more available. If the man had needed something, or wanted something, or found himself at fifty-something with an empty afternoon and an appetite he could not manage, the door was open and the giver was generous and had never once refused him.

He did not ask. He went and took.

That is the shape of this sin, and it deserves precision. Not a starving man stealing bread. A man with everything, who had never been refused anything, helping himself to the one thing that was not on offer, from a household that had nothing else.

'"'Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.'"'

Now God's account of the killing, and every word of it should be felt.

You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword.

David never touched him. He was in Jerusalem. An Ammonite archer on a wall at Rabbah killed Uriah, in an assault ordered by Joab, and David's only involvement was a sentence in a letter.

God says: you struck him down with the sword.

And then, so that nobody can miss what is being said: you have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. The instrument is named. The arrangement is named. And the killer is named, and it is not the archer and it is not Joab.

Every layer David built into that operation — the distance, the deniability, the fact that the actual weapon belonged to an enemy of Israel in the middle of a legitimate siege — is simply set aside. It bought him a year with the neighbours. It bought nothing here.

'"'Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'"'

The sword shall never depart from your house.

He used a sword to solve a problem, and the sword is going to live in his family. Amnon killed at a feast, Absalom run through in a tree, Adonijah executed, and a rebellion in between that costs twenty thousand men in one day.

'"Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.'"'

'"'For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"'

And the correspondence is exact, which is how the judgments in this book generally work.

He took a wife in secret; wives will be taken from him in public. He worked in the dark from a roof; this will happen before the sun. And it does, on that same roof, when Absalom pitches a tent on it in front of the whole city (16:22) — on the advice, as it happens, of Ahithophel.

Out of your own house. That is the hardest clause in the sentence. The judgment is not an invasion or a plague; it is his own sons.

'David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD."'

Five words in English, four in Hebrew, and that is the whole of it.

No excuse. No explanation of the pressures. No mention of Bathsheba, or Joab, or the difficulty of the situation, or what the alternatives would have cost. No attempt to distinguish what he did from what the man in the story did. No request for time.

And the direction is right: against the LORD. He has wronged Uriah beyond repair, and Bathsheba, and the other men who died on that wall, and he will say so — but he names first the one against whom the offence is finally committed.

Which is exactly what the psalm says. Psalm 51 is headed as David's, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba, and it contains the same sentence at greater length: against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Ps. 51:4).

The whole psalm belongs here. Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love... blot out my transgressions... create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me... cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me (Ps. 51:1-11). That last line is not a formula; he had watched the Spirit leave Saul.

And the psalm knows what the man cannot bring: for you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps. 51:16-17).

He had good reason to know that. There was no sacrifice in the law for premeditated murder or adultery. Those carried the death penalty and no offering covered them. The man had nothing to bring.

'And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die."'

The answer comes in the same breath as the confession.

There is no interval. No period of proving it, no probation, no series of works to be completed first. He says I have sinned and is told, in the next sentence, that it is dealt with.

Put away is the language of removal — the sin taken off him and carried elsewhere.

And you shall not die is a direct reversal of the verdict David gave in verse 5. He said the man deserved to die. He was right; the law agreed with him twice over. And he does not die.

Somebody else does, and the whole Bible is about how that comes to be just.

'"Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die."'

And then, immediately after the pardon, the consequence — and the two must be held together, because this verse is where a great deal of shallow teaching about forgiveness breaks.

The sin is put away and the sword still comes. Both are said by the same prophet in the same conversation, and neither cancels the other.

Forgiveness is not the removal of consequence. It is the removal of the sin. David is not going to be cut off as Saul was, not going to lose the covenant, not going to be abandoned — and his family is going to be torn apart for the rest of his life, and it starts with a baby.

Anybody who has come to God with something genuinely destructive and been genuinely forgiven, and then found that the wreckage was still there in the morning, is standing in this verse. The relationship is restored. The consequences run their course. Scripture never offers the second as part of the first.

'Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.'

The prophet goes home, and the writer calls her Uriah's wife one last time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — I Shall Go to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The child falls ill, and David fasts and lies all night on the ground; his servants cannot raise him or make him eat (vv. 16-17). On the seventh day the child dies and they are afraid to tell him (v. 18). He sees them whispering, asks, is told, and gets up — washes, changes, worships in the house of the LORD, and eats (vv. 19-20). The servants cannot understand it (v. 21). While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, "Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?" But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven days on the ground while there was any possibility, and not one day after. He is not callous and he is not resigned; he prayed as long as praying could change anything, and when it could not, he got up and went to worship.
verseByVerse.examples: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me. He does not say the child will come back. He says he is going where the child is — and it is spoken in hope, by a man on the worst week of his life, about a baby who died in a judgment on his own sin.

verseByVerse.quote: David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground. And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them. On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm." But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead." Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate. Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food." He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?' But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.'

He has been told what will happen, by a prophet, plainly.

And he prays anyway.

Sit with that, because it is unusual and it is not disobedience. He does not argue with Nathan or deny the word. He goes into a room and lies on the floor and asks God to change his mind, on the basis he states himself two verses further on: who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me?

He is not claiming a promise. He is appealing to a character.

'And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them.'

Seven days of this. His household cannot get him off the floor and cannot get him to eat.

'On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm."'

His own staff are frightened of what this news will do to him.

They have watched a man lie on the ground for a week refusing food, and they conclude, reasonably, that the death will break him completely. They stand in the corridor whispering and cannot make themselves go in.

'But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."'

'Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate.'

He gets up.

Read the order of what he does, because it is deliberate and it is not what anybody expected. He washes. He anoints himself. He changes his clothes. He goes into the house of the LORD and worships. Then he goes home and asks for food and eats it.

Worship comes before the meal. The first place he goes after seven days on the floor and the death of his son is into God's presence, to worship the God who had told him this would happen.

'Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You ate no food while the child was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food."'

They ask, and it is a fair question, and it is exactly backwards from what they expected.

'He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?'"'

Here is his account of the seven days, and it is the honest one.

Who knows? He never had a promise. He had a word of judgment and a knowledge of God's character, and on the strength of the second he spent a week begging against the first. There was always a possibility, and while there was a possibility he prayed with everything he had.

'"But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."'

Here is the sentence people come to this chapter for, and it should be handled slowly and without a trace of glibness, because the people who need it are usually holding something unbearable.

Take the first half first. Can I bring him back again?

What David is refusing is the thing grief most wants to do, which is to keep going with the protest after the outcome is settled. He is not being cold; he wept on a floor for a week. He is saying that the fasting had a purpose, the purpose is finished, and continuing it would be doing something to himself rather than for the child.

There is a hard-won wisdom in that and it belongs to people who have prayed properly. He gave everything he had while it could matter. He is not going to punish himself now that it cannot.

Then: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.

Notice what the sentence actually says, and what it does not.

It does not say the child will be restored to him in this life; that is the clause he explicitly denies. What he says is that he is going where the child is. The movement is one way, and it is David who is travelling.

Now, the honest position on how much weight that will bear. Some read it as no more than a statement about death — I shall die as he has died, and go to the grave where he is. That reading is possible and it should be admitted. But it is difficult to account for the effect it has on the man. He has been on the ground for a week; this sentence is what gets him up, washed and into the house of God to worship. A remark that everybody dies eventually is not a comfort, and it does not explain the change in him.

What is certain is this. David, who knew as much about God as anybody in the Old Testament, faced with the death of an infant — and an infant who died under a stated judgment on his own sin — looked forward and not back, and expected to be with him, and got up and worshipped.

That is what the passage gives, and it is a great deal.

Two things stand beside it. The first is that David's whole hope in this chapter rests on the character of God rather than on the child's record, which is the only ground anybody has ever had. His question was who knows whether the LORD will be gracious?, and the answer he received about himself was that the LORD had put away his sin. The God who does that is the God he expects to find the child with.

And the second is the Lord Jesus, who said let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God (Mark 10:14) — and who was indignant with the disciples for getting in the way.

Scripture does not give a systematic doctrine on this, and pretending otherwise is not kindness. What it gives is these two things, and the settled conviction of a grieving father who knew God well, and the character of the God who put away his sin the moment he named it.

Anybody standing where David stood should be given exactly that, and no less, and nothing invented.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — And the LORD Loved Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him (v. 24). And he sends word by Nathan to name him Jedidiah, because of the LORD (v. 25). Meanwhile Joab, still at Rabbah, has taken the water supply and sends for the king: gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name (vv. 26-28). David goes, takes the city and its crown, and brings out great spoil, and sets the people to labour (vv. 29-31).
verseByVerse.theology: And the LORD loved him. Four words at the end of the worst chapter in David's life, about the child of this marriage — and the name God sends back through the prophet means beloved of the LORD. Solomon inherits the throne and the covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: And Joab, who knows exactly what he holds over this king, sends him a message that is half loyalty and half a summons. He has finished the war David should have been fighting in verse 1 of the previous chapter, and he tells him to come and put his name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD. Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city. And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters. Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name." So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it. And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount. And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him,'

Two things in this verse, and both of them are grace.

The first is small and easy to miss: David comforted his wife, Bathsheba.

It is the first time in two chapters that she is called by her name and not the wife of Uriah. And it is the first indication anywhere in the account that anybody thought about what this had been like for her. She has been summoned by a king, made pregnant, widowed, married inside a mourning period, and has now buried a baby, and the verbs in her story until this moment have all belonged to somebody else.

He comforts her. It does not repair anything and it is not nothing.

The second is four words, and they arrive at the end of the worst chapter in the man's life.

And the LORD loved him.

This is the child of this marriage — a marriage that began in adultery and a murder, in a household under an announced judgment, born to the woman whose first husband David killed.

And God loves him.

Not tolerates. Not permits. Loves — and the writer says it flatly, without explanation, in the same sentence that gives his name.

Solomon will inherit the throne. He will build the house David was not allowed to build. He will be the son through whom the covenant of chapter 7 runs. And Matthew, opening the New Testament with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, writes it into the line with the fact still attached: and David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6).

The New Testament refuses to tidy this up. It puts the murdered man's name in the family tree of the Messiah.

'and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD.'

God sends the prophet back with a name.

Nathan's last visit was you are the man and a sentence of judgment. He comes this time carrying a name for the baby, and the name is Jedidiah, which means beloved of the LORD.

The same prophet, the same house, the same God. That is the shape of the chapter in two visits.

'Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city.'

'And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters."'

Meanwhile the war has been going on the whole time.

Joab has taken the water supply, which means the city cannot hold out, and he sends word.

'"Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name."'

Here is Joab, and it is impossible to read this message straight.

On the surface it is loyalty: come and finish it, so the credit is yours and not mine. Kings were touchy about this and generals were wise to be careful.

Underneath it is something else, and the sentence is a small masterpiece. Lest I take the city and it be called by my name. He is telling the king, in writing, that he could take the city himself and let everyone know who did it — and that he is choosing not to.

Remember what has passed between these two men since the last time we saw them corresponding. David sent Joab a letter. Joab carried it out and improved on the method and coached a messenger on how to manage the king's anger. Nothing was ever said about it afterwards.

This message is from a man who knows exactly what he holds, telling his king to come out to the war he should have gone to in the first place.

'So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it.'

He goes.

The chapter that began with a prophet and a lamb ends with the king finally doing what the first verse of chapter 11 said kings do at this time of year.

'And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.'

A talent is something like seventy-five pounds, which is not a weight a man wears; it was presumably held above him, or the figure refers to the value of it.

'And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.'

This last verse is genuinely disputed and it is better to say so than to choose confidently.

The Hebrew can be read as forced labour — the population put to work with saws and picks and axes and at the brick kilns, which is how the ESV and most modern versions take it and how the Chronicler's parallel reads most naturally. It can also be read as the population being killed with those implements, which is how the older English versions took it, and which would make this an atrocity.

The difference turns on a preposition and a single letter in one verb, and honest scholars have divided on it for a long time. Given that the same writer reported the measuring of the Moabites in chapter 8 without flinching, he would not have hidden this one either; and given that forced labour is what conquerors normally did with a defeated population, that reading is at least as likely. It is not possible to be certain, and pretending to be would be worse than the difficulty.

What can be said is that the chapter ends with the war finished, the crown on the right head, and the king back in Jerusalem — and with everything Nathan said still ahead of him.

12.theology:
Nathan brings a case, not an accusation (vv. 1-6). The parable is not a moral tale the king happens to identify with — it is a legal matter brought to the supreme court by a man with no standing, and David hears it in office and gives judgment under oath. That is exactly the work 8:15 says he did. Nobody in the story has died; a sheep was taken; and his instant sentence is capital. Every detail of the lamb is cumulative — one against very many, bought, raised with his children, eating from his plate, sleeping in his arms, like a daughter to him. The word is bat, and the woman is Bath-sheba. And the occasion is trivial: not famine, not need — a visitor arrived and a meal had to be made.

He set his own tariff (v. 6). Fourfold is the law's penalty for a stolen sheep (Ex. 22:1), and this book pays it out: this child, Amnon at a sheepshearing, Absalom in an oak tree, Adonijah executed. The man who fixed the figure was their father. And his own last clause is the sharpest sentence in the chapter — not because he broke the law, but because he had no pity: there was nothing in him that stopped.

An indictment made of gifts (vv. 7-8). I anointed you, I delivered you, I gave you your master's house and Israel and Judah — every clause with God as the giver, exactly as in chapter 7. And then the line that is worse than any accusation: if this were too little, I would add to you as much more. The door was open and the giver had never once refused him. He did not ask; he took. This is not a starving man stealing bread. It is a man who had never been refused anything helping himself to the one thing not on offer, from a household that had nothing else.

God's account of the murder (v. 9). David never touched him; an Ammonite archer killed Uriah in an assault Joab ordered, and David's whole involvement was one sentence in a letter. God says you have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and then names the instrument so nobody can miss it: you have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. The distance, the deniability, the enemy weapon in the middle of a legitimate siege — all of it bought a year with the neighbours and counted for nothing here.

The judgments match the crime (vv. 10-12). He used a sword to solve a problem, and the sword will live in his family. He took a wife in secret, and wives will be taken from him before the sun — which happens on that same roof, in front of the whole city, on Ahithophel's advice (16:22). And the hardest clause is out of your own house: the judgment is not an invasion or a plague. It is his sons.

Four words, and nothing else (v. 13). No excuse, no explanation of the pressures, no mention of Bathsheba or Joab or what the alternatives would have cost, no attempt to distinguish himself from the man in the story, no request for time. And the direction is right — against the LORD — which is Psalm 51 at greater length: against you, you only, have I sinned. That psalm belongs here entire, including take not your Holy Spirit from me, which is not a formula from a man who watched the Spirit leave Saul; and including its knowledge that he has nothing to bring, since the law provided no sacrifice at all for premeditated murder or adultery. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.

The pardon arrives in the same breath. No interval, no probation, no works to complete first. Put away is the language of removal — the sin taken off him and carried elsewhere. And you shall not die directly reverses the verdict he gave in verse 5, which was correct; the law agreed with him twice over. He does not die. Somebody else does, and the whole Bible is about how that comes to be just.

Forgiveness is not the removal of consequence (vv. 13-14). The same prophet says both things in the same conversation and neither cancels the other. The sin is put away and the sword still comes; David keeps the covenant and loses his family. Anyone who has brought God something genuinely destructive, been genuinely forgiven, and then found the wreckage still there in the morning is standing in this verse. The relationship is restored; the consequences run their course; Scripture never offers the second as part of the first.

He prayed against a word he had been given (v. 16). Not disobedience and not denial — he states his own ground two verses later: who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me? He is not claiming a promise. He is appealing to a character. Seven days on the floor while there was any possibility, and not one day after; and the first place he goes when it is finished is into the house of the LORD, to worship the God who told him this would happen. Worship comes before the meal.

I shall go to him (v. 23). This is where readers with dead children come, and it deserves care and no glibness. The first half refuses what grief most wants — to keep protesting after the outcome is settled. He gave everything while it could matter and will not punish himself now that it cannot. The second half says he is going where the child is; the movement is one way, and it is David who travels. How much weight will it bear? Some read it as no more than a statement that everybody dies, and that reading is possible and should be admitted — but it does not explain the effect, because a remark about mortality does not get a man off the floor after a week and send him to worship. What is certain is that David, who knew as much about God as anyone in the Old Testament, facing the death of an infant under a stated judgment on his own sin, looked forward rather than back and expected to be with him.

Two things stand beside it: his whole hope here rests on God's character rather than on any record — the God who put away his sin the moment he named it is the God he expects to find the child with — and the Lord Jesus, indignant with the disciples, saying let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God (Mark 10:14). Scripture gives no systematic doctrine here and pretending otherwise is not kindness. It gives these, and the settled conviction of a grieving father who knew God well — which is a great deal, and should be given whole, with nothing invented on top.

And the LORD loved him (v. 24). Two graces in one verse. She is called Bathsheba for the first time since 11:3 rather than the wife of Uriah, and somebody finally considers what this has been like for her — summoned, made pregnant, widowed, married inside a mourning period, and now burying a baby, with every verb in her story until now belonging to someone else. He comforts her. It repairs nothing and it is not nothing. And then four words about the child of that marriage, in a house under an announced judgment: not tolerates, not permits — loves. God sends the prophet back with a name, and Nathan, whose last visit was you are the man, arrives carrying Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD. Solomon inherits the throne, builds the house, and carries the covenant — and Matthew opens the New Testament by putting it in the genealogy with the fact still attached: David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6). The New Testament refuses to tidy this up.

Joab's message (v. 28). On the surface it is loyalty: come and finish it so the credit is yours. Underneath, lest I take the city and it be called by my name tells the king in writing that he could take it himself and let everyone know — and is choosing not to. The last time these two corresponded, David sent a letter and Joab carried it out, improved the method, and coached a messenger on managing the king's anger, and nothing was ever said afterwards. This is a man who knows exactly what he holds, telling his king to come out to the war he should have gone to in the first place.

The last verse is disputed (v. 31). The Hebrew can be read as forced labour — the population set to work with saws, picks, axes and brick kilns, which is how most modern versions take it and how the Chronicler's parallel reads most naturally — or as the population being killed with those implements, which is how the older English versions took it. The difference turns on a preposition and a single letter in one verb, and honest scholars have divided for a long time. This writer reported the measuring of the Moabites in chapter 8 without flinching and would not have hidden this; and forced labour is what conquerors normally did with a defeated population. Certainty is not available, and manufacturing it would be worse than the difficulty.
12.examples:
Then: A prophet walked into a throne room with a lawsuit about a stolen lamb, and the king — doing his job, in office, under oath — lost his temper and sentenced the defendant to death and fourfold restitution before he was told the defendant's name. Four of his own sons died.

Now: Three things. Nathan's method is the first: he did not accuse a man who had already killed to protect this secret — he got him to pronounce his own verdict, on a case where his judgment was not clouded because he could not see himself in it. Anybody who has to tell someone something true and unwelcome should study that. The second is verse 13 and verse 14 held together: the sin was put away in the same breath as the confession, with no probation and nothing to complete first — and the sword still came. Forgiveness is not the removal of consequence, and anyone who has been genuinely pardoned and then found the wreckage still there in the morning is reading the right chapter. And the third is verse 23, for anybody who is carrying it: he prayed with everything he had while it could still matter, and he stopped when it could not, and what got him off the floor was not resignation but the expectation that he was going where the child had gone.

13.title: Amnon, Tamar, Absalom
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her.<sup>2</sup>And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.<sup>3</sup>But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man.<sup>4</sup>And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."<sup>5</sup>Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'"<sup>6</sup>So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."<sup>7</sup>Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."<sup>8</sup>So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.<sup>9</sup>And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him.<sup>10</sup>Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.<sup>11</sup>But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."<sup>12</sup>She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing.<sup>13</sup>As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."<sup>14</sup>But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.<sup>15</sup>Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!"<sup>16</sup>But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.<sup>17</sup>He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her."<sup>18</sup>Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her.<sup>19</sup>And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.<sup>20</sup>And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house.<sup>21</sup>When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.<sup>22</sup>But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar.<sup>23</sup>After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons.<sup>24</sup>And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."<sup>25</sup>But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing.<sup>26</sup>Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"<sup>27</sup>But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.<sup>28</sup>Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant."<sup>29</sup>So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.<sup>30</sup>While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left."<sup>31</sup>Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments.<sup>32</sup>But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar.<sup>33</sup>Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead."<sup>34</sup>But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain.<sup>35</sup>And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about."<sup>36</sup>And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.<sup>37</sup>But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.<sup>38</sup>So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.<sup>39</sup>And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
13.overview:
Nathan said the sword would not depart from this house and that evil would rise out of your own house, and it begins here, with the correspondence exact. David saw a woman who was not his and took her; his firstborn does the same. David arranged a killing to cover it; his third son arranges one too.

The narrator diagnoses Amnon before Amnon acts. Verse 1 calls it love, which is what Amnon would have called it; verse 2 calls it torment and names the obstacle — and the obstacle is not that she is his sister but that she is guarded. The problem, as he experiences it, is logistical. Then Jonadab, described as clever rather than wicked, hears that a prince is consumed with wanting his own half-sister and supplies a method within a sentence. He never lays a hand on anybody.

Tamar's speech is the best thing in the chapter and she makes it with a hand already on her: the law, what it will do to her, what it will make of him — and then a way out that costs her everything, speak to the king. Twice the writer records that he would not listen. And then verse 15, which is one of the most penetrating sentences in the Old Testament: the hatred was greater than the love, and it arrives immediately, because what he had was never love and satisfied appetite does not become affection. She tears the robe that says she is a virgin daughter of the king and walks through the city so that nobody can pretend.

Her brother tells her to be quiet. Her father is very angry and does nothing at all — and every sentence he might have said to Amnon had already been said to him, by a prophet, in that palace, about Bathsheba. Absalom says neither good nor bad for two years, which is not restraint but a murder being planned. And the chapter ends with a father who has stopped grieving the murdered son and aches for the murderer.
13.theology:
The judgment of chapter 12, arriving (vv. 1-2). This is the household of 3:2-5 and 5:13 producing what such a household produces, in a kingdom whose law had warned its king in advance. And the writer diagnoses Amnon before he moves: what verse 1 calls love, verse 2 calls torment, and the thing standing in his way is not the relationship but the guard. A man frustrated by the difficulty of reaching a person rather than by the wrongness of wanting to is not in love.

Jonadab supplies the method (v. 5). Told that a prince is eaten up with wanting his half-sister, he does not argue, warn anybody, or walk away — he designs an operation. It uses David's affection as the lever, requires Tamar to come unaccompanied because the king himself is sending her, and puts her in a private room with a plausible reason.
