Nobody has to be deceived except David, and David will not examine it. He never touches her; he does not have to.

Tamar's arguments, in her order (vv. 12-13). She gives him back his own word, my brother, and starts not with herself but with the nation: such a thing is not done in Israel, and the term is nebalah, the word used of the atrocity at Gibeah. Then herself — where could I carry my shame? — which is not a figure of speech but an accurate description of the rest of her life. Then him: she takes the trouble, in a locked room with a man twice her strength, to tell him what this will make of him, using nabal, which does not mean a silly man but a moral idiot. And then the way out: speak to the king. She offers to spend her life married to the man holding her down, if only he will not do it this way. Whether such a marriage was lawful is debated (Lev. 18:9, 11); what it cost her to say it is not.

Twice, in three verses (vv. 14, 16). He would not listen to her voice, and then, when she protests the second wrong, he would not listen to her. The writer will not let it be missed. And the act itself is reported in three flat clauses with no description at all, which is a kind of respect.

Verse 15, and why the hatred is immediate. Not later, not after reflection — the sentence puts it directly on top of the act. Because what he had was never love, and appetite that has been satisfied does not turn into affection; it turns into disgust, and the disgust has to go somewhere. It cannot go to himself, so it goes to her. She is the evidence, and he hates the sight of what he did and calls that hating her. A man will wreck a family to get a thing and find it turned to ash four seconds after he has it, and the person he obtained becomes intolerable precisely because she is proof.

She goes public (v. 19). Ashes, the torn robe, the hand on the head, the loud crying — every one a formal act of mourning, performed in the street. And the writer stops the narrative to say what she is wearing, because it is a uniform: the garment of the king's virgin daughters, recognisable across a street. She tears it because she is no longer one, and makes it impossible for the household to pretend. It is the last free act she performs in the book.

Silenced by her protector (v. 20). Absalom already knows — he names Amnon without being told. He takes her in, and that is real. And his instruction is hold your peace: not I will get justice, not we are going to the king. Part of that is a brother sparing her more exposure, and part is a man who has already decided what he will do and needs the matter quiet for two years. A desolate woman is the writer's own word, and the last thing said of her; she has one further mention, when Absalom names a daughter after her (14:27). The word is shomemah, which is used of ruined cities and of land laid waste after an army has gone through it. She is the only person in the chapter who behaves well throughout, and she is the one whose life is over. The narrative moves on because its subject is the house of David — but the book records her arguments in full, calls the deed nebalah, and calls her desolate. It does not treat her as a plot device even when the plot does.

Very angry, and nothing else (v. 21). No summons, no judgment, no protection ordered, no recorded word to Amnon — from the king whose one stated qualification was that he administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15). The Septuagint and a Qumran manuscript add the reason the Hebrew omits: because he loved him, for he was his firstborn. And under the favouritism is something everyone in that palace could have named. What was he going to say? That a son of the king may not take a woman he has decided he wants? That a man may not use power to get a woman into a private room? Every sentence available to him had already been spoken to him by a prophet, in that palace, about Bathsheba. He is not silent because he does not care; he is silent because he has disqualified himself, and his sons know it. That is what chapter 12's judgment actually looks like — not God striking David, but David unable to act.

Neither good nor bad (v. 22). Not a word in either direction for two full years — no accusation, no quarrel, no conspicuous avoidance. Civil at every family occasion. The writer gives the reason in the same sentence: for Absalom hated Amnon. That is a man who has decided on murder and understands that the way to arrange one is to leave nobody any reason to remember you had a grievance. It is colder than a rage.

Battlefield words for a stabbing (v. 28). Do not fear. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant — the vocabulary spoken to soldiers before an engagement, used to steady servants for the murder of a drunk man at a table. It gives them cover and gives him cover: not an assassination, a brave deed under orders. And note who takes the risk. He commands and they do it, exactly as David wrote a letter and Joab did it. Note too that David asks the right question — why should he go with you? — and then does not press it, having twice in one chapter handed over a child to a request he would not examine.

Jonadab knew (v. 32). He has the true casualty figure before a single survivor arrives: the number, the name, whose command it was, and the motive dated exactly — from the day he violated his sister Tamar. This is the man who wrote the plan that put her in that room. So he spent two years watching a silence he understood perfectly and said nothing, to David or to Amnon, who was his friend and could have been warned — and then steps forward with the right information at the moment it makes him indispensable to a grieving king. He never acts and never touches anybody. He arranges, observes, and is present with the correct sentence.

The last verse (v. 39). Three years, the grief for Amnon fades as grief does, and what is left is longing for the son who is alive. Set it beside the rest: very angry about his daughter and did nothing; mourned his firstborn and stopped; and aches for the murderer. There is no justice anywhere in it. Amnon was never punished and is beyond it; Absalom has been neither tried, charged, pardoned nor condemned, merely out of the country; Tamar is in a house and nobody has mentioned her since verse 20. And the next chapter is Joab noticing that longing and deciding to use it.
13.examples:
Then: A young woman argued for her life in a locked room — from the law, from what it would cost her, from what it would make of the man holding her, and finally by offering to marry him if he would only ask her father first — and when he had finished she tore the robe that marked her as a king's daughter, put ashes on her head, and walked through the capital city crying aloud so that nobody could pretend it had not happened. Her father was very angry and did nothing.

Now: Three things. Verse 15 is the one to carry: the hatred that arrives on top of the act, because appetite satisfied turns to disgust and the disgust has to land somewhere, and it never lands on the person responsible. Anyone tempted to believe that getting the thing will settle it should read that verse and notice how fast it turns. Second, Jonadab — who never lifts a hand, never lies, never strikes, and is present at both catastrophes with the useful sentence. Some people do all their damage by supplying a method to someone who had only an appetite. And third, David's silence, which is the most sobering thing in the chapter. He did not lose his son's obedience; he lost the standing to say this is wrong and be heard saying it, and he lost it years earlier, in a different room, over a different woman.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom has a beautiful sister, Tamar, and Amnon — David's firstborn, her half-brother — is so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her (vv. 1-2). His friend Jonadab, a very crafty man, sees him wasting away and asks why (vv. 3-4). And supplies the plan: pretend to be ill, ask the king to send Tamar to make food in your sight and feed you by hand (v. 5). Amnon does it, and David sends her (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator diagnoses it before Amnon acts. What he calls love in verse 1 he calls torment in verse 2, and the obstacle named is not that she is his sister but that she is guarded.
verseByVerse.examples: Jonadab is the one who turns a sick obsession into an operation. He is a nephew of David's, he is described as clever rather than wicked, and he will appear once more — two years later, knowing exactly what has happened before anybody else does (v. 32).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her. And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her. But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man. And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister." Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'" So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her.'

Three of David's children in one verse, and the writer names the relationship each time: Absalom, David's son; Amnon, David's son. They are half-brothers and half-sister, sons and daughter of the same father by different mothers.

That is what the household described at 3:2-5 and 5:13 actually produced. Six sons at Hebron by six women, eleven more at Jerusalem, and a law that had warned Israel's king in advance not to multiply wives.

Nathan said the sword would not depart from this house and that evil would be raised up out of your own house (12:10-11). It begins here, and the reader should see what kind of correspondence it is. David saw a woman who was not his and took her. His firstborn is about to do exactly that. David arranged a killing to cover it. His third son will do exactly that.

'And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.'

The narrator has already told us what this is, in the space of one verse.

Verse 1 called it love, which is what Amnon would have called it. Verse 2 calls it torment, and then names the obstacle — and note carefully what the obstacle is not.

It is not that she is his sister. It is that she is a virgin daughter of the king, which means she is guarded and not accessible. The problem, as Amnon experiences it, is logistical.

A man who is frustrated by the difficulty of getting at a person rather than by the wrongness of wanting to is not in love, and the writer establishes it before anything happens.

'But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man.'

Here is the man who makes this happen.

He is David's nephew, a cousin of the princes, and the word used of him is not wicked but wise in its shrewd sense — clever, sharp, able to see how a thing can be arranged. The translation crafty is well judged.

Keep him in view. He is going to reappear at the end of the chapter knowing more than anybody else in the room.

'And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."'

Hear Amnon's own description: my brother Absalom's sister.

Not my sister. He locates her by the brother, which is either an attempt to put a little distance between himself and the relationship, or simply how the household worked — full siblings by the same mother, half-siblings otherwise.

'Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'"'

And there is the plan, worked out in a sentence.

Look at the craft in it. A sick prince is visited by the king. A sick man's request for particular food from a particular hand is exactly the sort of thing an ill man asks and a father grants without thinking. It uses David's affection as the lever, it requires Tamar to come unaccompanied because she is being sent by the king himself, and it puts her in a private room with a plausible reason.

Nobody has to be lied to except David, and he will not examine it.

It is also worth being clear about what Jonadab has done. He has been told by a prince that the man is consumed with wanting his own half-sister, and his response is not to talk him out of it, or to warn anybody, or to walk away. He immediately supplies a method.

He does not lay a hand on her. He does not have to.

'So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."'

The plan is executed word for word, and the king walks straight into it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–19 — He Would Not Listen to Her
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tamar comes and bakes in front of him, and he refuses to eat and sends everyone out (vv. 8-9). He tells her to bring the food into the bedroom and takes hold of her (vv. 10-11). She answers: no, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel... as for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you (vv. 12-13). But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her (v. 14). Then: then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her (v. 15). He has her thrown out and the door bolted (vv. 16-18). She puts ashes on her head, tears the long robe she is wearing, and goes away crying aloud (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Her speech is the most intelligent thing anybody says in this chapter. She argues from the law, from what it will do to her, from what it will do to him — and then offers him a way out that costs her everything and saves them both: ask the king.
verseByVerse.examples: He would not listen to her voice, and two verses later, when she pleads again, he would not listen to her. The writer says it twice. And the robe she tears is the garment worn by the virgin daughters of the king; she is telling the city what has happened, in the street, without a word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him." So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes. And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him. Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother. But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister." She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing. As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you." But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her. Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!" But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her. He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her." Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her. And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."'

The father sends her.

He suspects nothing, which is not much of a defence, because the whole scheme depended on his not asking a single question about why an adult prince needed his half-sister to come and cook in his bedroom. He has never had to think hard about Amnon.

'So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.'

She goes because the king sent her and does what she was told to do.

'And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him.'

He refuses the food, which was never the point, and clears the room.

Note that there were other people present until this moment — servants, at least — and that a prince ordering a room emptied is not questioned. Every stage of this has used ordinary authority to arrange something that could not survive being looked at.

'Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.'

'But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."'

My sister. He uses the word while he is doing it.

'She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing."'

Now listen to her, because this is the best speech in the chapter and it is made by somebody with a hand already on her.

She begins where he began: my brother. She gives him back the word.

And then the first argument, and it is not personal. Such a thing is not done in Israel. She appeals to what the nation is. The word translated outrageous thing is nebalah — the strong term used of the worst offences in Israel, the same word used of the atrocity at Gibeah in Judges 19 and of Achan's sin. She is naming the category.

'"As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."'

Three more arguments, and watch the order she puts them in.

First herself: where could I carry my shame? A woman in her position, in that society, had no future after this. It is not a figure of speech; she is describing the rest of her life, and she is right, as verse 20 will confirm.

Then him: you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. She is arguing for his good. Standing in a locked room with a man twice her strength, she takes the trouble to tell him what this will make of him. The word is nabal — the same word that was Nabal's name, the fool of 1 Samuel 25, and it does not mean a silly man; it means a moral idiot, a man with nothing in him that works.

And then the way out. Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.

That is the remarkable one. She offers to marry him.

Whether such a marriage was possible is debated — Leviticus forbids a man to marry his half-sister (Lev. 18:9, 11; 20:17), and it may be that she is simply saying anything to stop him, or that royal practice in that period differed from the law, or that she believes David would arrange it. What is not in doubt is what it costs her to say it. She is offering to spend her life married to the man currently holding her down, if only he will not do it this way.

She has given him law, consequence, his own reputation, and an alternative that would get him what he says he wants. There is nothing left to say.

And none of it reaches him, because appetite that has already decided does not hear counsel. Proverbs has a whole chapter on a young man walking a road he has been warned about, deaf the entire way, as an ox goes to the slaughter (Prov. 7:22). It could have been written about this room.

'But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.'

The Hebrew is he would not listen to her voice, and it is the first of two.

The rest of the verse is three facts in the order the writer chose: he was stronger, he violated her, he lay with her. There is no description and no lingering. It is stated the way a report is stated, and the brevity is a kind of respect.

'Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!"'

Stop here, because this is one of the most penetrating verses in the Old Testament and it is easy to read as mere brutality.

The hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her.

It happens immediately. Not later, not after reflection — the sentence structure puts the hatred right on top of the act.

Why? Because what he had was never love, and the writer told us so in verse 2. It was appetite, and appetite that has been satisfied does not become affection; it becomes disgust, and the disgust has to go somewhere. It cannot go to himself, because he will not have it. So it goes to her.

She is now the evidence. Every time he looks at her he sees what he did, and he hates the sight of it, and he calls that hating her.

This is a permanent feature of that kind of sin and Scripture states it here once, exactly. A man will wreck a family to get a thing and find it has turned to ash four seconds after he has it, and the person he obtained becomes intolerable precisely because she is proof.

Get up! Go! Two words in Hebrew, barked at her.

'But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.'

And she speaks again, and the second refusal is recorded in the same words as the first.

Her argument is legal and it is correct. The law of Israel required a man who violated an unbetrothed virgin to marry her and never divorce her (Deut. 22:28-29), and harsh as that provision sounds to modern ears, its purpose was to protect the woman — to give her a household and a standing rather than leave her discarded. Being put out of the door is a second destruction on top of the first, and she says so.

But he would not listen to her. Twice in three verses. The writer will not let it be missed.

'He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her."'

This woman. He will not use her name and does not speak to her directly; he gives an order about an object to a servant, in her hearing.

And the door is bolted behind her.

'Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her.'

The writer stops the narrative to tell us what she is wearing, which means it matters.

It is a distinctive garment — the same phrase used of Joseph's coat — and it is a uniform: this is what the unmarried daughters of the king wore, and everyone in Jerusalem would have recognised it at a distance.

'And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.'

And she goes public.

Everything she does here is a formal act of mourning, performed in the street: ashes on the head, the garment torn, the hand laid on the head, and the loud crying that was the recognised sound of grief.

She tears the robe that says she is a virgin daughter of the king, because she is not one any more, and she walks through the city letting everybody see it.

She had every reason to go home quietly. Instead she made it impossible for the household to pretend. Whatever was going to be done about this, it was not going to be done in the dark.

That is a brave thing and it is the last free act she performs in the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — Absalom Spoke to Amnon Neither Good Nor Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom meets her: has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart. And she lives in his house, a desolate woman (v. 20). When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry (v. 21) — and that is all. But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar (v. 22). Two years later he holds a sheepshearing at Baal-hazor and presses the king to send all his sons (vv. 23-27). His servants have their orders: when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, "Strike Amnon," then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant (v. 28). They do it, and the king's sons flee on their mules (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The father is very angry and does nothing at all. The Septuagint and a Qumran manuscript supply the reason the Hebrew leaves out: because he loved him, for he was his firstborn. There is a deeper disablement than favouritism, and everybody in the palace could have named it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the brother says nothing for two years, which is not restraint. Neither good nor bad is the sound of a murder being planned. Note also the orders he gives — be courageous and be valiant — which is the language of a commander sending men into battle, used for stabbing a drunk man at a party.

verseByVerse.quote: And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house. When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry. But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar. After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons. And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant." But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing. Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?" But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him. Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant." So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house.'

Her brother's first response is to tell her to be quiet.

Read the sentence carefully, because it is doing several things at once and only one of them is kind.

He already knows. The question has Amnon your brother been with you? is not really a question; the torn robe and the ashes have told him, and the fact that he names Amnon without being told suggests he had some idea this was coming.

He takes her in, and that is real. She lives in his house from this day.

And then: hold your peace... do not take this to heart. He has just watched his sister walk through the city tearing her clothes, and his instruction is silence. Not I will get justice for you. Not we are going to the king. Be quiet.

Two things are probably true of that at once. Part of it is a brother trying to spare her more public exposure. And part of it is a man who has already decided what he is going to do and needs the matter to go quiet so that he can do it in two years' time.

Either way, she is silenced by the person protecting her.

A desolate woman. That is the writer's own word for her, and it is the last thing said about her in Scripture. The Hebrew is shomemah, and it is not a word about feelings. It is used of ruined cities and of land laid waste after an army has been through it. Tamar is the town Amnon sacked, and she stays that way. She has one more mention: Absalom names a daughter after her, and she was a beautiful woman (14:27). Nothing else. No marriage, no children, no restoration.

She is the only person in this chapter who behaves well throughout — who argues rightly, warns the offender for his own sake, offers a way out, protests the second wrong as well as the first, and refuses to let it be hidden — and she is the one whose life is over.

The narrative moves on to what her brothers do, because the narrative is about the house of David and the judgment on it. That is the writer's subject. But she should not be left behind without saying plainly that the book knows what was done to her, records her arguments in full, calls it nebalah, and calls her desolate. It does not treat her as a plot device even when the plot does.

'When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.'

And that is the whole of the father's response.

Anger, and nothing after it. No summons, no judgment, no protection ordered for Tamar, no punishment, not even a recorded conversation with Amnon. The king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) hears that his firstborn has raped his daughter, becomes very angry, and does nothing.

The Hebrew text stops there. The Greek Septuagint and a manuscript of Samuel found at Qumran both carry an additional clause at this point, and it supplies the reason: but he would not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn.

Whether or not that sentence belongs in the text, it describes what happened.

And there is something under the favouritism that everybody in that palace could have named.

What exactly was David going to say to Amnon? That a son of the king may not take a woman he has decided he wants? That a man in power may not use that power to get a woman into a private room? That there are consequences for arranging your desires around what you can get away with?

Every sentence available to him had already been spoken to him, by a prophet, in this same palace, about a woman called Bathsheba.

He is not silent because he does not care. He is silent because he has disqualified himself, and his son knows it, and his other sons know it. The judgment of chapter 12 is not that God struck David; it is that David can no longer act.

That is what a father loses. Not the love of his children and not their obedience, necessarily, but the standing to say this is wrong and be heard saying it.

'But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar.'

And here is the other silence, and it is worse.

Neither good nor bad. Not a word, in either direction, for two full years. He does not accuse him, or quarrel with him, or avoid him conspicuously. He is civil. He behaves, at every family occasion, exactly as a brother behaves.

The writer explains it in the same sentence: for Absalom hated Amnon.

That is not restraint and it is not forgiveness. It is a man who has decided on murder and understands that the way to arrange one is to give nobody the slightest reason to remember that you had a grievance.

Two years of speaking neither good nor bad is a colder thing than a rage.

'After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons.'

Sheepshearing was the great festival of the pastoral year — a harvest feast, with a great deal to eat and more to drink. Nabal was holding one when David's men came for provisions.

'And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."'

'But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing.'

He asks for the king first, and there is some debate about whether he meant it. What is certain is that he needed a refusal, because David's presence would have made the thing impossible, and he needed the refusal to look like reluctance on the king's side.

'Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"'

And David asks the right question.

Why should he go with you? Somewhere in the man there is still an instinct that this is odd — that of all the sons, this is the one Absalom has singled out, and that there is a reason these two should not be alone together in the country.

He asks the question and then does not press it.

'But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.'

He gives way, as he gave way over the cakes.

Twice in this chapter David has been asked for something that should have made him uneasy, and twice he has handed over a child to a request he did not examine.

'Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant."'

Now hear the language of the order.

The plan itself is squalid: wait until the man is drunk, and stab him at the table.

And Absalom dresses it in the vocabulary of the battlefield. Do not fear. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant. Those are the words spoken to soldiers before an engagement — the words Joshua was given, the words Joab used at Rabbah — and they are being used here to steady a group of servants for the murder of an unarmed man at a party.

He is giving them cover, and he is giving himself cover. This is not an assassination; this is a brave deed done under orders.

Note also who takes the risk. He commands, and they do it. Exactly as David wrote a letter and Joab did it.

'So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.'

The other princes get on their mules and ride, and they are right to. They have just watched their brother stab their brother, and none of them knows where it stops.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–39 — The Spirit of the King Longed to Go Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A report reaches David that Absalom has killed all the king's sons, and he tears his clothes and lies on the ground (vv. 30-31). Jonadab corrects it at once: let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar (vv. 32-33). The sons arrive and everybody weeps (vv. 34-36). Absalom flees to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, and stays three years (vv. 37-38). And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: Jonadab knows. He knows the true casualty figure before the survivors arrive, and he knows the motive, and he says it has been settled from the day he violated his sister. The man who designed the first crime has been watching the second one coming for two years and said nothing to anybody.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends with a father grieving a murdered son and longing for the murderer, and the next four chapters come out of that sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left." Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments. But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar. Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead." But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain. And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about." And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly. But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day. So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years. And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left."'

The report arrives before the survivors do, and it is wrong.

'Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments.'

He tears his clothes and lies on the ground.

That is the posture from chapter 12, when the baby was dying. He has spent a night on the floor before, over a child, and the writer is not likely to have chosen the detail by accident.

'But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar."'

And Jonadab walks back into the story, and what he says should stop a reader cold.

He knows the true casualty figure before any survivor has arrived. He knows the number is one. He knows the name. He knows whose command it was. And he knows the motive, and dates it exactly: from the day he violated his sister Tamar.

This is the man who wrote the plan that put Tamar in that bedroom.

So he has spent two years watching Absalom say neither good nor bad, understanding perfectly well what the silence meant, and he said nothing. Not to David. Not to Amnon, who was his friend and whom he could have warned. Nothing.

And now he steps forward with the correct information at the moment when producing it makes him look indispensable to a grieving king.

The writer calls him crafty in verse 3 and then shows us what the word means over a span of two years. He never once acts. He arranges, he observes, and he is present with the right sentence at the right moment. He is one of the most quietly frightening figures in the book, and he never touches anybody.

'"Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead."'

He says it twice, which is the only kindness he offers.

'But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain.'

'And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about." And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voices and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.'

As your servant said, so it has come about. He cannot help pointing out that he was right.

Then the house of David weeps together, which is the only thing in this chapter they do together.

'But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.'

Geshur is a small Aramean kingdom north-east of the Sea of Galilee, and Talmai is Absalom's grandfather — his mother Maacah was Talmai's daughter (3:3).

So the murderer goes to his mother's father, a foreign king, beyond David's reach. He has a place to go because his father married a foreign princess for political reasons twenty years earlier.

'So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.'

'And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.'

The last verse of the chapter, and it is one of the saddest sentences about David anywhere.

Three years pass. The grief for Amnon fades — the writer says so flatly, and it is simply what grief does — and as it fades, what is left is longing for the son who is alive.

He wants Absalom back.

Now hold that against what he did about Tamar, because the two belong in the same sentence. He was very angry about his daughter and did nothing. He mourned his firstborn and then stopped. And what remains, three years on, is a father's ache for the son who murdered the other one.

There is no justice anywhere in this. Amnon was never punished and is now beyond punishment. Absalom has not been tried, charged, pardoned or condemned; he is simply out of the country. Tamar is in a house, desolate, and nobody has mentioned her since verse 20.

And the king of Israel, whose one recorded qualification for the job was that he administered justice and equity to all his people, cannot bring himself to do anything at all about a rape and a murder in his own family, and misses the murderer.

The next chapter is Joab noticing that longing and deciding to use it.

14.title: Joab's Stratagem; Absalom's Return
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom.<sup>2</sup>And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead.<sup>3</sup>Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth.<sup>4</sup>When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king."<sup>5</sup>And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.<sup>6</sup>And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him.<sup>7</sup>And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."<sup>8</sup>Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."<sup>9</sup>And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."<sup>10</sup>The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again."<sup>11</sup>Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."<sup>12</sup>Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."<sup>13</sup>And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again.<sup>14</sup>We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.<sup>15</sup>Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.<sup>16</sup>For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God.'<sup>17</sup>And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!"<sup>18</sup>Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."<sup>19</sup>The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant.<sup>20</sup>In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on the earth."<sup>21</sup>Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom."<sup>22</sup>And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."<sup>23</sup>So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.<sup>24</sup>And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence.<sup>25</sup>Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.<sup>26</sup>And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight.<sup>27</sup>There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.<sup>28</sup>So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence.<sup>29</sup>Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come.<sup>30</sup>Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.<sup>31</sup>Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"<sup>32</sup>Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still." Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.'"<sup>33</sup>Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
14.overview:
Joab notices that the king's heart has gone out to Absalom, and acts on it. He hires a wise woman from Tekoa, dresses her as a mourner and scripts her — and what she brings the king is a case that turns out to apply to himself. A reader who has been paying attention recognises it at once: this is Nathan's method exactly. The difference is the sender. Nathan came because the LORD sent Nathan to David; this woman comes because Joab put the words in her mouth. The technique is identical and the results could hardly be more different.

Her case is built with care, and every detail softens it in ways Absalom's case is not soft — a quarrel in a field, no witnesses, no premeditation. And she will not leave without an oath, pressing him through three stages to get one. Then she turns it: the king has sworn to protect a stranger's fratricide while his own son sits in a foreign country under no sentence at all.

And she says one of the great sentences of the Old Testament, in borrowed mourning clothes, reciting Joab's script. We are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God... devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast. Every word of it is true, and it is being used to procure the unconditional return of a man who has never once been recorded as sorry. The theology is right and the application is wrong, and holding both is the lesson of the chapter.

Then David does the one thing worse than either justice or mercy: let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence. Home but not received, neither tried nor pardoned, with a household and time on his hands and a grievance that grows daily. Two years of it — and when he finally forces a meeting by burning Joab's barley, the chapter ends in a kiss with not one word spoken by either man.
14.theology:
Nathan's method, Joab's purpose (vv. 1-3). A petitioner, a case that is not what it appears, a king who gives judgment and finds the judgment applies to him. It is chapter 12 repeated deliberately, and the only variable is who sent her. That is the point of the whole chapter: the technique is not what made Nathan's parable work.

The case is built to be softer than the real one (vv. 6-7). A widow with nobody to protect her interest; two sons and now one; a quarrel in a field with nobody to separate them and no witnesses — ambiguity where Absalom's case has none. Absalom planned it for two years, gave the order to servants, and did it at a feast in front of the family. And my coal that is left is beautifully judged: a household banked its coals overnight, and if the last one went out there was no fire in the morning. It is an argument about the dead husband as much as the living son.

She would not leave without the oath (vv. 8-11). Three stages — a promise to consider, a promise to intervene, and finally a sworn undertaking in the name of the LORD that cannot be withdrawn. Nathan needed only a verdict; she needed something David could not take back.

Verse 14, and why it is one of the great sentences. Pour a jug of water on dry ground and try to collect it — not most of it, not some of it. That is death, exactly, and everyone knows it and spends a lifetime not thinking about it. Then it turns: God devises means. He plans, contrives, engineers — and what he engineers is a way to get the banished one home. The whole human problem is in the first half of the verse, and every religion that ever existed is an attempt to gather up the water. The second half says God did not accept the loss and did not leave it to us. He devised a means; it took most of the length of the Bible to arrive and it cost him his Son, and Paul puts it in these terms — alienated and hostile in mind, and now reconciled by his death (Col. 1:21-22).

And what her argument leaves out. The means God devises are not a shrug. They involve a price paid and a sin dealt with, and on the human side they involve repentance — David is the proof, restored in chapter 12 through I have sinned against the LORD. Absalom says nothing of the kind here or anywhere. So a true sentence about God's mercy is quoted accurately in the service of an outcome God has not authorised, and that is far more common than open error. The sentence is genuine; the use of it is not.

He works it out, and it changes nothing (vv. 19-20). David asks straight whether Joab's hand is in this, and she admits it straight — give her that. And then he knows the widow is not a widow, the sons never existed, and his general has manoeuvred him into an oath. Nathan's parable ended with I have sinned. This one ends with a shrug and an instruction to Joab. He has been handled and lets it stand, because he wanted the outcome anyway. Nathan told him what he did not want to hear and he submitted; Joab told him what he did want to hear and he went along. The first produced repentance; the second produces a rebellion. There is also a bleak accidental joke in it: the man being told twice that he is like the angel of God to discern good and evil has spent ten verses failing to notice that the woman in front of him is an actress.

The decision that makes everything else (v. 24). Neither charge nor acquittal — a house in Jerusalem and a closed door. He did not exercise justice: there was never a trial, never a verdict, and Tamar has not been mentioned by anybody since 13:20, from a king whose one recorded qualification was administering justice to all his people. And he did not extend mercy: if the man was to be forgiven, then receive him and eat with him, which is exactly what Mephibosheth got for nothing more than being Jonathan's son. Instead, the third option, which is the worst available. David's instinct is not hard to understand — he cannot execute his son and cannot sit across a table from the man who killed his other son — and the in-between that feels like a reasonable compromise is the one course that guarantees disaster. Anybody who has managed a broken relationship by keeping the person at arm's length, neither confronting nor restoring, is looking at where that policy ends.

Why the description is placed here (vv. 25-26). No blemish in him is sacrificial language; it means physically perfect, and there is nobody in the country better looking. The reader has been here: Saul was the handsomest man in Israel and a head taller than anyone (1 Sam. 9:2), and Samuel looked at Eliab and was told the LORD sees not as man sees (1 Sam. 16:7). The narrator puts it directly after the closed door, because the country is about to choose this man. And the hair is weighed — five pounds of it, cut only when it grew too heavy to carry, with the figure known. A man who weighs his own hair annually is telling you something. The detail is planted without comment and picked up in chapter 18.

He named his daughter after his sister (v. 27). The three sons are not named; the daughter is, and she is Tamar, and she is beautiful. That is the only memorial his sister gets in this book, and her brother gave it to her. Whatever else is true of Absalom, he did not forget what was done to her.

Arson gets a meeting (v. 30). Two polite requests ignored; a burned crop brings the commander of the army to his door within the hour. Absalom has just learned something, and a man who learns it at thirty is dangerous. Note the pattern, third time now: Amnon killed by Absalom's servants on Absalom's order, the field burned by Absalom's servants on Absalom's order. He gives instructions and other people carry the risk. And his complaint is fair on its own terms — exile was a definite condition and this is not, and he was better off in Geshur. David created that.

Not repentance, a challenge (v. 32). If there is guilt in me, put me to death is often read as courage. There is guilt in him; he arranged a murder in front of witnesses and fled for three years, and nobody has ever disputed it. So the offer is not an offer. It is a man who has watched his father fail to act about Tamar and fail to act about Amnon, calling it: try me, or receive me. He never says he did wrong — not here, not anywhere.

The kiss (v. 33). Not one word is spoken by either man — no question, no accusation, no confession, no condition. He comes in, goes to the floor, and is kissed. It looks like everything a reader wants, the gesture of the father running down the road; and there is no repentance underneath it and no justice on top of it, and both men know. What has been achieved is that the form is now correct: the prince is received, the awkwardness is over, nobody has to explain anything, Tamar is still in a house somewhere and Amnon is still dead. The very next verse is after this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.
14.examples:
Then: A general hired an actress, dressed her as a widow and wrote her a speech, and she manoeuvred the king of Israel into swearing a public oath about an imaginary son — and in the middle of the performance said one of the truest sentences in the Old Testament about the mercy of God, in order to get a murderer home without a trial.

Now: Two things, and both are uncomfortable. The first is that a true statement about God can be deployed for an end God has not authorised, and the more true it is the better it works. He devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast is the gospel — and the means he devises deal with the sin rather than waving it through, which is the part the speech omits. Test the application, not just the doctrine. And the second is verse 24, which is the practical heart of the chapter: David could not bring himself to punish and could not bring himself to forgive, so he chose the middle course, and it looked like restraint and was in fact the only option that could not work. Distance maintained and never discussed is not peace. It is a wound with a lid on it, and the lid comes off.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab sees that the king's heart went out to Absalom and sends to Tekoa for a wise woman, dresses her as a mourner, and puts words in her mouth (vv. 1-3). She comes to the king with a case: a widow with two sons, one of whom struck and killed the other in a field; and now the whole clan demands the killer's life, and so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant (vv. 4-7). David tells her to go home and he will give orders; she presses him twice more until he swears: as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The method is Nathan's, exactly — a case brought to the supreme judge, engaging the king's judicial instinct on a matter he cannot see himself in, until he pronounces a verdict he will not be able to escape. The difference is who sent the petitioner.
verseByVerse.examples: Note that she has to press him three times. He gives a vague answer, then a firmer one, and only under repeated pressure does he swear an oath — which is what she came for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom. And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead. Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth. When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king." And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead. And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him. And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth." Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you." And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless." The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again." Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom.'

Joab notices, and that is how the chapter starts.

The last verse of chapter 13 said the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom. Joab has worked it out, and Joab is a man who acts on what he works out.

Why he wants Absalom back is not stated, and the honest answer is that we do not know. It may be simple concern for a grieving king he has served for thirty years. It is more likely political: an heir in exile is an unresolved succession, and Amnon is dead, and a general has an interest in knowing who will be on the throne. Chapter 18 will show what Joab thinks of Absalom when the man becomes inconvenient, and it does not suggest affection.

'And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead."'

Tekoa is a village about ten miles south of Jerusalem — the same place Amos came from two centuries later.

She is a wise woman, which in that world was something like a recognised office; there is another at Abel of Beth-maacah in chapter 20 who talks Joab out of destroying a town. These were women known locally for judgment and for the ability to speak well.

And Joab hires her, costumes her, and scripts her.

'"Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth.'

Now, before she speaks, see what is being set up, because a reader who has been paying attention will recognise it immediately.

A petitioner comes to the king with a case that is not what it appears to be. The king hears it, gives judgment, and the judgment turns out to apply to himself.

That is exactly chapter 12. Nathan did this two chapters ago and it broke David open.

The difference is the sender. Nathan came because the LORD sent Nathan to David (12:1). This woman comes because Joab put the words in her mouth.

Hold that distinction through the whole chapter. The method is identical and the results could hardly be more different, and the reason is not the technique.

'When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king."'

'And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead."'

'"And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him."'

The story is constructed with great care, and every element is chosen.

She is a widow, so there is no man to protect her interest. There were two sons and now there is one. The killing happened in a field with nobody present, which makes it ambiguous — a quarrel that went wrong rather than a planned murder, and no witnesses to establish which.

Every one of those details softens the case in a way Absalom's case is not soft. Absalom planned his brother's death for two years, gave the order to servants, and did it at a feast in front of the whole family.

'"And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also."'

The clan is invoking the law of blood vengeance, which was real and which the law of Israel regulated rather than abolished. There were cities of refuge precisely for the case she describes — a death without premeditation — and the clan is refusing to allow the distinction.

'"Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."'

And there is the picture that does the work: my coal that is left.

A household kept a fire going and banked the coals overnight, and if the last coal went out there was no fire in the morning. One surviving son is the last live coal in a dead man's house. Put that out and the family is finished — no name, no inheritance, nothing on the earth to show that the man ever lived.

It is an argument about the dead husband as much as the living son, and it is beautifully judged.

'Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."'

And David gives a vague answer, and she does not accept it.

'And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."'

'The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again."'

Better, and still not enough. She presses a third time.

'Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."'

There it is: the oath.

She would not leave without it, and she pushed him through three stages to get it — a promise to consider, then a promise to intervene, and finally a sworn undertaking in the name of the LORD that cannot be taken back.

David has now publicly sworn that a man who killed his brother will not be put to death.

He does not yet know what he has done. It took Nathan three verses; it has taken her eight, and she has been more thorough, because she needed an oath and Nathan only needed a verdict.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She asks leave to speak once more, and turns it: why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again (vv. 12-13). Then the great sentence: we must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast (v. 14). She flatters him — my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil (v. 17) — and then, asked directly, admits Joab sent her (vv. 18-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament and it is entirely true. Death is irreversible, like water poured out on dry ground; and God, faced with that, does not simply accept the loss — he devises means. He engineers a way to get the banished back.
verseByVerse.examples: And it is being used to procure the unconditional return of an unrepentant murderer, for a general's political convenience. The theology is right and the application is wrong, and the chapter is the standing proof that those two can come apart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak." And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again. We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast. Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant. For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God.' And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!" Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak." The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant. In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."'

She asks permission, having already got what she came for.

'And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again."'

The trap closes, and it is a good one.

The argument is that David has just sworn to protect a fratricide he has never met, in a village he has never visited, on the ground that a family should not lose its last son — while his own last son sits in a foreign country under no sentence at all.

By his own judgment, in his own mouth, under oath, the king is inconsistent. That is what convicts himself means.

And she widens it: against the people of God. It is not a private family matter. The succession of the house of David is a national question, and everybody in Israel knows there is now one obvious heir and he is in Geshur.

'"We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast."'

Now stop, because this is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament and it is spoken by a hired actress in the middle of a manipulation.

Take the first half. We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again.

She is arguing that Amnon cannot be brought back, so killing Absalom achieves nothing. But the image is bigger than her argument. Pour a jug of water onto dry ground and try to collect it: you cannot. Not most of it, not some of it. It is gone into the dust and there is no method by which a human being can retrieve it.

That is death, and it is exact. Everybody knows it and everybody spends their life not thinking about it.

Then the second half, and it turns.

But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.

The Hebrew is difficult in places and translations vary a little, but the heart of it is not in doubt. God devises means. He plans, he contrives, he engineers — the verb is about working something out deliberately.

What does he work out? A way to get the banished one home.

That sentence is the gospel in Old Testament clothing, and it should be said plainly.

The whole human problem is in the first half of the verse: the water is spilled, the loss is irreversible, and nobody can gather it up. Every religion that ever existed is an attempt to gather up the water. And the second half says that God did not accept the loss and did not leave it to us; he set about devising a means.

He devised one. It took most of the length of the Bible to arrive, and it cost him his Son, and Paul describes it in exactly these terms — that we were alienated and hostile in mind and have been reconciled, brought back, by the death of Christ (Col. 1:21-22). The banished one does not remain an outcast, because God took the trouble to arrange it.

Every word of that is true.

And it is being said, at this moment, by a woman in borrowed mourning clothes, reciting a speech written by Joab, in order to procure the unconditional return of a man who murdered his brother and has never once been recorded as sorry.

Both of those things are the case, and holding them together is the whole lesson of the chapter.

Because here is what her argument leaves out. God devises means so that the banished one need not remain an outcast — and the means he devises are not a shrug. They involve a price paid and a sin dealt with, and on the human side they involve repentance. David himself is the proof: he was restored in chapter 12, and the restoration went through I have sinned against the LORD.

Absalom has not said anything of the kind. He does not say it in this chapter either. When he finally speaks, in verse 32, what he offers is not repentance but a challenge.

So the theology is right and the application is wrong, and a reader should take the warning seriously, because this is a great deal more common than open error. True things about God's mercy can be quoted accurately in the service of an outcome God has not authorised. The sentence is genuine. The use of it is not.

'"Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.'"'

'"For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God."'

'"And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!"'

Then the flattery, and it is laid on thickly.

Like the angel of God to discern good and evil. She says it here and says it again in verse 20. It is the kind of thing a king hears often enough to stop noticing, and she is using it to close the deal.

There is a bleak joke in it that she cannot have intended. The man being told he is like an angel of God at discerning good and evil has been sitting there for ten verses failing to discern that the woman in front of him is an actress.

'Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."'

'The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant."'

He works it out, and asks straight, and she admits it straight.

Give her that: challenged, she does not brazen it out. She names Joab immediately.

And notice how little David's discovery changes. He knows now that the whole thing was staged, that the widow is not a widow, that the two sons never existed, and that his general has manoeuvred him into an oath. Nathan's parable ended with I have sinned. This one ends with a shrug and an instruction to Joab.

He has been handled, and he lets it stand, because he wanted the outcome anyway.

That is the real difference between the two parables. Nathan told David something he did not want to hear, and David submitted to it. Joab told him something he wanted to hear, and David went along with it. The first produced repentance. The second is going to produce a rebellion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–27 — Let Him Not Come Into My Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David tells Joab to bring the young man back, and Joab falls on his face and blesses him and goes to Geshur (vv. 21-23). And then: let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence. So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence (v. 24). The narrator pauses on his looks: no one so much praised for beauty in all Israel, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him (v. 25) — and his hair, cut once a year because it was heavy, weighing two hundred shekels (v. 26). He has three sons and a daughter named Tamar (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the sentence that makes the rebellion. Home but not received; in the city but not forgiven; neither tried nor pardoned. A full pardon would have been wrong and a trial would have been right, and David does neither — and the arrangement he chooses is the one guaranteed to feed a proud man's grievance for two years.
verseByVerse.examples: The hair is not a decorative detail. The writer weighs it and records the annual cutting, and leaves it there, and four chapters later Absalom's head catches in an oak.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom." And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant." So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence. Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him. And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight. There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom."'

The young man Absalom. He is a grown man with three children and a murder behind him, and his father calls him a boy.

'And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."'

Joab is effusive, and it costs him nothing.

'So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.'

'And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence.'

Here is the decision that makes everything that follows.

Look at what David has actually done. He has brought home a man who arranged the murder of the crown prince, and has neither tried him nor pardoned him. There is no charge and no acquittal. There is a house in Jerusalem and a closed door.
