Consider the two things he did not do.

He did not exercise justice. Absalom killed Amnon and there was never a trial, never a hearing, never a verdict. Tamar has never been mentioned again by anybody. A king whose one recorded qualification was that he administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) has now failed to administer any at all, twice, in his own family.

And he did not extend mercy. If the man was to be forgiven, forgive him: receive him, restore him, eat with him. That is what forgiveness is, and Mephibosheth got it from this same king for nothing more than being Jonathan's son.

Instead there is a third thing, which is the worst available. The man is home, at liberty, in the capital, with a household and time on his hands and a grievance that grows every single day, and no way to resolve anything because he cannot get into the room.

Two years of that are coming.

David's instinct here is not hard to understand. He cannot execute his son and he cannot bring himself to sit across a table from the man who killed his other son. So he does something in between, which feels like a reasonable compromise and is in fact the only option that guarantees disaster.

Anybody who has ever managed a broken relationship by keeping the person at arm's length — not confronting, not restoring, just maintaining a distance that never gets discussed — is looking at the outcome of that policy. Surface arrangements over unresolved wrongs hold for a while and then come apart, and they come apart worse than the original problem.

'Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.'

The narrator stops and describes him, which he rarely does.

No blemish in him is the language used of a sacrificial animal, and it means physically perfect. There is nobody in the country better looking.

And the reader has been here before. Saul was a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people (1 Sam. 9:2). And when Samuel came to Bethlehem he looked at Eliab and thought, surely this is the one — and was told the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7).

The writer puts the description here, immediately after the sentence about the closed door, because the country is about to choose this man.

'And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight.'

Then the hair, and the writer weighs it.

Two hundred shekels is around five pounds, which is a great deal of hair, and the note that he cut it only when it became too heavy to carry is not admiration. A man who weighs his own hair annually and lets people know the figure is telling you something about himself.

The detail is planted, and it is left there without comment. It will be picked up in chapter 18.

'There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.'

He named his daughter after his sister.

Nothing else is said. The three sons are not named, and an earlier note says they died (18:18), but the daughter has a name, and it is Tamar, and she is beautiful.

That is the only memorial his sister gets in this book, and her brother gave it to her. Whatever else is true of Absalom — and a great deal is — he did not forget what was done to her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–33 — So He Set the Field on Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two full years in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face (v. 28). He sends for Joab twice and Joab will not come (v. 29). So he tells his servants: see, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire (v. 30). Joab arrives at once, and Absalom's complaint is that he would rather be back in Geshur — now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, put me to death (vv. 31-32). Joab carries the message, the king summons him, and Absalom bows to the ground — and the king kissed Absalom (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: He burns a crop to get a meeting. It is entirely characteristic: he is not a man who waits, and he has just discovered that destroying something valuable brings people to him immediately.
verseByVerse.examples: If there is guilt in me, put me to death. That is not a confession. It is a challenge from a man who knows perfectly well that his father will not do it — and David does not answer it. He kisses him instead, which settles the form of the matter and none of its substance, and four verses later Absalom buys a chariot.

verseByVerse.quote: So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence. Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come. Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire. Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?" Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still." Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.'" Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence.'

Two years, in the same city, a few hundred yards away.

Add it up. Three years in Geshur, two years in Jerusalem behind a closed door: five years since he killed Amnon, and in all that time not one conversation with his father about any of it.

Nobody has ever told him he is forgiven. Nobody has told him he is condemned. There has been no hearing, no sentence, no reconciliation, no explanation. He has simply been managed.

What that does to a proud man over two years is the whole of the next chapter.

'Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come.'

Joab, who went to Geshur to fetch him, will not now cross the city to see him.

Which tells you what the errand in chapter 14 was worth. Joab wanted the heir back in the country; having achieved it, he has no further use for the man and does not answer his messages. Twice.

'Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.'

So he burns the barley.

Take it in. He is a prince of Israel who cannot get a meeting, and his solution is arson against the commander of the army, destroying a standing crop belonging to a man who has just done him a considerable favour.

And note the pattern, because it is the third time. Amnon was killed by Absalom's servants on Absalom's order. The field is burned by Absalom's servants on Absalom's order. Absalom gives instructions and other people carry the risk.

'Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"'

Joab comes immediately.

Which is exactly what Absalom has just learned. Two polite requests were ignored; destroying something valuable produced the commander of the army on his doorstep within the hour.

A man who discovers that at thirty is dangerous.

'Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still."'"'

Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still.

And that complaint, on its own terms, is entirely fair. Exile was a definite condition; this is not. He was better off in a foreign country than in his father's capital with the door shut.

David created this. Absalom is describing accurately what the half-measure feels like from inside.

'"Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, put me to death."'

This is the sentence often read as courage or even repentance, and it is neither.

If there is guilt in me, put me to death.

There is guilt in him. He arranged a murder in front of witnesses and fled the country for three years. It is not a debatable point, and no one has ever disputed it.

So the offer is not an offer. It is a challenge, made by a man who knows exactly what his father will do, which is nothing. He has watched David fail to act about Tamar and fail to act about Amnon, and he is calling it: try me, or receive me.

He is not saying I did wrong. He is saying either kill me or stop pretending. Nowhere in this chapter, or anywhere else in the book, is Absalom recorded as being sorry for anything.

'Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.'

And the chapter ends with a kiss, and it is the most ambiguous gesture in the book.

Look at what does not happen. Nothing is said. There is no recorded word from either man — not a question, not an accusation, not a confession, not a condition. Absalom comes in, goes down on the floor, and is kissed.

The kiss looks like everything a reader wants. It is the gesture of the father in the parable running down the road. And there is no repentance underneath it and no justice on top of it, and both men know it.

What has been achieved is that the form of the thing is now correct. The prince is received at court. The awkwardness is over. Nobody has to explain anything to anybody, and Tamar is still in a house somewhere, and Amnon is still dead, and nothing whatever has been dealt with.

The very next verse begins: after this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.

A surface peace laid over a wound that was never cleaned does not hold. It holds long enough for everyone to relax, and then it comes apart, and it takes the kingdom with it.

15.title: Absalom's Rebellion and David's Flight
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.<sup>2</sup>And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel,"<sup>3</sup>Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you."<sup>4</sup>Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice."<sup>5</sup>And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him.<sup>6</sup>Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. 15.overview:
After this — after the kiss — Absalom buys a chariot, horses and fifty runners, which is not transport but a royal progress. Then he gets up early, every day, for four years, and stands beside the road into the gate. And what he says there is a masterpiece with almost nothing false in it. Every man is told his claim is good and right, without evidence and without a hearing. And there is no man designated by the king to hear you is probably true: the kingdom now runs from Egypt to the Euphrates and one man cannot hear its cases, so people walk three days and go home unheard. He does not accuse his father of injustice, which could be disputed. He points at a real administrative failure and lets each man conclude that the king does not care about him. A true grievance, aimed. And in four years he never judges a single case — the permanent advantage of the man responsible for nothing.

Hebron is chosen with care, and a vow is the cover, because it is the one errand a king cannot examine without looking impious. David says go in peace, having asked nothing, for the third time in three chapters. Ahithophel goes over — and he is almost certainly Bathsheba's grandfather, which means nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

David walks out of a defensible city rather than have Israelites fight over its walls. Ittai the Gittite, who arrived yesterday and has no stake in any of it, answers Ruth's words in a soldier's mouth and brings his children with him. And the ark is sent back — by the man who knows what happened at Aphek, and who learned chapter 6 the hard way — because he will not use God as a talisman even to save a throne.

Then a barefoot king with his head covered goes up the Mount of Olives weeping, having crossed the Kidron, betrayed by a man who ate at his table. He prays one short sentence about the one thing that will decide the war. And the next verse begins behold.
15.theology:
A true grievance, aimed (vv. 3-4). Absalom never calls the king unjust, which would be a lie anyone could refute. He names a genuine failure — 8:15 was the summary of David's whole reign, and an empire's caseload has outgrown one man — and lets every litigant draw the conclusion himself. And he tells each of them their claim is good without hearing the other side. Notice what is missing across four years: he never judges one case, never weighs evidence, never gives a ruling that disappoints anybody. He promises what nobody could deliver to all of them and is never tested, because in every real dispute somebody loses.

The kiss, and where he learned it (v. 5). A man bows and the prince catches him before he gets down, takes his hand and kisses him: not to me, we are the same. It is a man refusing the distance his position gives him, and it is entirely calculated — and the last chapter ended with a kiss that settled the form of a thing and none of its substance. He learned what a kiss can be made to do. And the writer's verdict is one word: stole. Not won, not earned — taken from somebody it belonged to.

Religion as cover (v. 8). A vow is unverifiable, private between a man and God, and impossible to refuse without appearing irreligious. He picked the one request his father could not examine. And go in peace is the third time in three chapters that David has handed over something precious to a request he would not look at — Tamar to Amnon's house, Amnon to the sheepshearing, and now the son who has been holding court at his own gate for four years, sent to his own first capital with a blessing. (The Hebrew's forty years cannot fit this reign; the Greek, Syriac and Josephus read four.)

Why Ahithophel went (v. 12). The book never says, and it lays the pieces where a careful reader will find them. He is of Giloh; one of the thirty is Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite (23:34); and the woman on the roof was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (11:3). That makes him her grandfather, and Uriah — also on the list of the thirty — the grandson-in-law he lost. He gave faultless advice to the man who did it for years and said nothing, and left the moment there was an alternative king.

He gives away a city he could have held (v. 14). Jerusalem is defensible; he took it himself and fortified it, and he has the Cherethites, the Pelethites and six hundred professionals from Gath. His stated reason is that a siege would be Israelites killing Israelites over walls he built, and the people inside would pay. That has been read as panic — but a panicking man does not then send the ark back with a reasoned speech, post two priests as intelligence, identify the single decisive threat, pray about it, and plant a double agent, in that order.

Ittai, and the pattern (v. 21). He is from Gath, commands six hundred men — David's own wilderness number — and has been in the country days. David tries to release him, honestly: you came only yesterday, and I go I know not where. And the answer is Ruth's, almost word for word, with death named before life. Set him against who is not there: Ahithophel gone, the king's son leading the rebellion, two hundred men of Jerusalem at Hebron, David's own nephew commanding the rebel army. And he brings all the little ones — not a mercenary taking a contract, a man moving his household onto the losing side. The book keeps doing this: Uriah the Hittite would not sleep at home while the ark was in a field; Obed-edom the Gittite housed the ark when Israel was afraid of it; Ittai walks into exile with a king he has known a week. Each foreigner is set beside an Israelite who failed at the same point.

The ark goes back (vv. 25-26). Israel did the other thing once: at Aphek the elders sent to Shiloh so that it may come among us and save us, and the whole camp shouted, and they lost thirty thousand men and the ark itself in one afternoon (1 Sam. 4). David knows that story, and learned chapter 6 the hard way — and here, running for his life with no idea where he is going, the one thing that would look most like divine endorsement is put in his hands and he sends it home, into Absalom's keeping. And he will not claim the outcome either: he wants to come back and says so, and then let him do to me what seems good to him — which is Joab's sentence between two armies at Rabbah (10:12). He does not remind God of chapter 7, and he could.

Both at once (vv. 27-28). In the same breath he refuses to manipulate God and sets up an intelligence network: two priests who can legitimately stay with the ark, two sons nobody watches, and a king waiting at the fords. Neither cancels the other, and the chapter will not let a reader choose between them.

The correspondence is structural (v. 30). He crossed the Kidron and went up the Mount of Olives, betrayed by a man who ate at his table — and he wrote the psalm about it: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9), which the Lord Jesus quoted in the upper room about Judas (John 13:18). Jesus went out over the Kidron (John 18:1) and up the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). And Ahithophel set his house in order and hanged himself (17:23), the only person in Scripture to die that way apart from the man who betrayed Christ (Matt. 27:5). The greater Son of David went up that slope in anguish with a small group of bewildered followers and prayed not my will, but yours, be done, which is what David has just said to Zadok in other words.

One sentence, aimed at where it will be decided (v. 31). Short, specific, no rehearsal of the injustice and no general request that the rebellion fail. David can count: Absalom has the numbers, the capital, the ark and the momentum, and what he lacks is a good decision — and the man who can supply one has just arrived. Chapter 17 shows the advice, and it would have worked. So he prays about the counsel, not the army. Anyone who has prayed vaguely because a crisis was too big to think about should study that sentence.

And the next verse begins behold (v. 32). The writer sets them side by side and says nothing. Hushai arrives in mourning, to grieve with a friend, with no idea what he is walking into — and David immediately sees how his own prayer is going to be answered. Not by lightning: by an old man with dirt on his head being asked to walk into a captured city, swear a false oath to a usurper, and sit in a council where one wrong word is death. That is normally how. And the two men enter Jerusalem at the same moment from opposite directions — a prince with an army and the finest mind in Israel, and an elderly man in a torn coat who has agreed to lie for a living. The kingdom turns on the second one.
15.examples:
Then: A king who could have defended the strongest city in the country walked out of it barefoot with his head covered, weeping, and when the priests brought the ark of God out to go with him he sent it back inside — into the hands of the son who wanted him dead — because he would not carry God about as a lucky charm even to keep his throne.

Now: Two things. Recognise Absalom's method, because it is still the whole of it: find a real failure, tell everyone their complaint is justified without ever examining it, promise what you will never be required to deliver, and abolish the distance between yourself and the crowd. It works because the grievance is genuine. The test of the man offering to fix it is whether he has ever decided anything that cost him a supporter. And verse 31 is the practical one: when everything is going wrong at once, most people pray about the whole of it, which is another way of praying about none of it. David worked out where the thing would actually be decided, prayed for that single point, and then walked up the hill and met the answer coming down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — So Absalom Stole the Hearts of the Men of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom gets a chariot and horses and fifty men to run before him (v. 1). He rises early and stands beside the road into the gate, and stops every man with a lawsuit: see, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you... Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice (vv. 2-4). And when anyone bows to him he takes him by the hand and kisses him (v. 5). So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel (v. 6). After four years he asks leave to pay a vow at Hebron, and David says go in peace (vv. 7-9). Messengers go through all the tribes; two hundred invited guests go with him in their innocence, and knew nothing; and he sends for Ahithophel (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The pitch is 8:15 failing. He never says the king is unjust — he says there is nobody appointed to hear you, which is probably true, and converts an administrative failure into a reason for disloyalty. Note that in four years at that gate he never actually judges a single case. He only says he would.
verseByVerse.examples: Hebron is chosen with care: David's first capital, the place of his own anointing, and the town where Absalom was born. And a vow is the cover, because religion is the one errand nobody questions. David asks nothing, for the third time in three chapters.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him. And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel," Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you." Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice." And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him. Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. And at the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron. For your servant vowed a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will offer worship to the LORD.'" The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron. But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron!'" With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem who were invited guests, and they went in their innocence and knew nothing. And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.'

After this — after the kiss.

The reconciliation of the last verse of chapter 14 is followed immediately by a man buying the equipment of a king. A chariot, horses, and fifty runners going ahead of him through the streets is not transport; it is a royal progress, and everyone who saw it understood what it meant.

Note also that the writer has recorded exactly this before. When Samuel told Israel what a king would do to them, the first thing on the list was: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen, and they shall run before his chariots (1 Sam. 8:11).

'And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel,"'

He gets up early, every day, and stands by the road.

That is the detail to hold on to, because whatever else Absalom is, he is not lazy. The gate of the city was where cases were heard and business was done, and he is there before anyone else, intercepting people on their way in.

And his opening question is personal. From what city are you? He asks a man where he is from before he asks what he wants, which is the oldest technique there is and it works every time.

'Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you."'

Now look very carefully at what he says, because it is a masterpiece and almost nothing in it is a lie.

First: your claims are good and right. He tells every man who comes that his case is a winner, without having heard the other side, without evidence, and without the slightest intention of deciding anything. Every litigant in Israel walks away from that gate having been told by a prince that he was in the right.

Second: there is no man designated by the king to hear you.

And that is probably true.

Here is the sentence that made David's reign: so David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15). That was the summary of the whole kingdom — not the conquests, not the tribute, but that people could get a hearing.

By now the kingdom stretches from Egypt to the Euphrates, and one man cannot hear its cases. The system has not kept up. There are almost certainly people at that gate who have walked three days and will go home unheard, and their complaint is real, and Absalom has found it.

That is the craft of it. He does not accuse his father of injustice, which would be a lie anybody could dispute. He points at a genuine administrative failure and lets each man draw the conclusion that the king does not care about him personally.

A true grievance, aimed.

'Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice."'

The offer costs him nothing, because it is entirely hypothetical.

Read the whole passage again and notice what is missing. In four years standing at that gate, Absalom never judges a single case. Not one. He never hears both parties, never weighs evidence, never gives a ruling that disappoints anybody, never does the actual work.

He tells every man his claim is good and says how much better things would be if he were in charge. That is the complete extent of it.

It is the permanent advantage of the man who is not responsible for anything: he can promise everyone what nobody could deliver to all of them, and never be tested. The moment he has to actually judge, half the people at that gate become his enemies, because in every dispute somebody loses.

'And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him.'

And the physical touch, every time.

A man bows to a prince, as he should, and the prince catches him before he gets down, takes him by the hand, and kisses him. It says: not to me, we are the same. It is the gesture of a man refusing the distance his position gives him, and it is completely calculated.

There is another kiss behind it, four verses' worth of chapter ago, and Absalom has learned exactly what a kiss can be made to do.

'Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.'

Stole. The writer's own verdict, in one word.

Not won. Not earned. Took, from somebody it belonged to.

'And at the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron."'

Four years of standing at a gate. The Hebrew as it stands says forty, which cannot be right in this reign; the Greek, the Syriac and Josephus all read four, and every modern version follows them.

And the cover story is a vow.

'"For your servant vowed a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will offer worship to the LORD.'"'

He invents a piece of piety.

It is well chosen, because a vow is the one errand nobody questions. It is between a man and God; it is unverifiable; and refusing it would be an act of irreligion by the king. Absalom has picked the only request his father cannot examine without looking impious.

'The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron.'

Go in peace. And that is the third time.

He sent Tamar to Amnon's house without a question. He let Amnon go to the sheepshearing after asking one question and not pressing it. And now he sends the son who has been holding court at his own city gate for four years off to his own first capital, with a blessing, having asked nothing.

'But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron!'"'

The gate work has not been random. He has four years of names, and he can reach every tribe at once.

Hebron is the choice that gives the game away. It is where David was anointed king of Judah, and then king over all Israel; it is the ancient covenant town where Abraham is buried; and it is where Absalom himself was born (3:2-3). Proclaiming a king there says: the throne has moved back to where it started.

'With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem who were invited guests, and they went in their innocence and knew nothing.'

Two hundred men from the capital, invited to a religious observance, who found out what they were part of when the trumpet sounded.

The writer says it twice in one clause: in their innocence, and knew nothing. They are hostages of a kind — two hundred prominent men of Jerusalem publicly at Absalom's side, whose presence tells the country that the capital has gone over.

'And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.'

Ahithophel comes.

This is the worst news in the chapter, and chapter 16 will say why: the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God (16:23). He is the finest political mind in Israel and he has been David's for years.

Why does he go? The book never says, but it lays out the pieces and leaves them where a careful reader will find them. Ahithophel is from Giloh. One of David's mighty men is Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite (23:34). And the woman on the roof was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (11:3).

Which makes Ahithophel her grandfather, and Uriah — who is also on that list of the thirty — the grandson-in-law he lost.

He has sat in that council chamber giving faultless advice to the man who did it, for years, and said nothing. And the moment there is an alternative king, he is gone before he is asked twice.

Nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Wherever My Lord the King Shall Be
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Word comes that the hearts of Israel have gone after Absalom, and David tells his servants to flee at once, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword (vv. 13-14). They go out on foot, leaving ten concubines to keep the house (vv. 15-16). David tells Ittai the Gittite to turn back — you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home... you came only yesterday (vv. 19-20). And Ittai answers: as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be (v. 21). All the country weeps aloud as the people pass over the brook Kidron (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: He leaves rather than let Jerusalem be fought over. Whatever else is true of these chapters, that decision costs him a kingdom and saves a city.
verseByVerse.examples: Ittai arrived yesterday, from Gath, with no stake in any of it — and his answer is Ruth's, almost word for word, in a soldier's mouth. The pattern holds all through this book: Uriah the Hittite, Obed-edom the Gittite, Ittai the Gittite. The foreigners keep faith while the insiders defect.

verseByVerse.quote: And a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom." Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Go quickly, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword." And the king's servants said to the king, "Behold, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king decides." So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house. And the king went out, and all the people after him. And they halted at the last house. And all his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath, passed on before the king. Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home. You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you." But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be." And David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom."'

The same word the writer used in verse 6. What Absalom stole, David has now lost.

'Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Go quickly, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword."'

He decides in a sentence, and the reason he gives is the city.

Jerusalem is defensible. He took it himself against a garrison that thought it could hold out with the blind and the lame, and he has fortified it since. He has the Cherethites and the Pelethites, he has six hundred professional soldiers from Gath, and Joab is somewhere.

He could fight for it, and he says why he will not: lest he... strike the city with the edge of the sword. A siege of Jerusalem would be Israelites killing Israelites over a wall David built, and the people inside it would pay for it.

So he walks out of his own capital and gives it away rather than have it fought over.

That decision has been read as panic. Look at what he does in the next twenty verses — sends the ark back with a reasoned speech, posts two priests as intelligence, identifies Ahithophel as the decisive threat, prays about it, and plants a double agent. A panicking man does not do those things in that order.

'And the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house.'

Ten women left behind to keep the palace, in a sentence that reads like housekeeping.

Remember them. They have done nothing and chosen nothing, and chapter 16 will do to them exactly what Nathan said would be done, in public, on the roof — and 20:3 records what became of them afterwards, which is that they lived shut up until the day they died.

'And the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home."'

Now the finest thing in the chapter, and it is a conversation with a foreigner.

Ittai is a Gittite — from Gath, Goliath's city, the town David hid in twice. He commands six hundred men, which is exactly the number David had in the wilderness, and he has been in the country for a matter of days.

David tries to send him home.

Read what he says: go back and stay with the king. He means Absalom. He is telling this man to go and serve the winner, and he is not being bitter about it; he is releasing a foreign officer from a quarrel that is not his.

'"You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you."'

You came only yesterday. And I go I know not where.

He is being honest about what he is offering: no destination, no plan, no prospect. And he sends him off with a blessing that uses the covenant words — steadfast love and faithfulness — the same pair he sent to Jabesh-gilead on the first day of his reign.

'But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be."'

There it is, and any reader of the Old Testament will hear what it is.

A Moabite woman said it on a road out of Moab: where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried (Ruth 1:16-17).

Ittai says the same thing in a soldier's words. He swears by the LORD — the God of a country he has lived in for about a week — and by the king, and he names the two possibilities in the order that matters: whether for death or for life. He puts death first.

Now set him against the men who are not there.

Ahithophel, the wisest man in Israel, has gone. Absalom, the king's son, is leading the rebellion. Two hundred prominent men of Jerusalem are at Hebron. Amasa, David's nephew, will command Absalom's army.

And a Philistine mercenary who arrived yesterday will not leave.

The book keeps doing this and it is not accidental. Uriah the Hittite would not sleep in his own bed while the ark was in a field. Obed-edom the Gittite took the ark into his house when Israel was afraid of it. Ittai the Gittite goes into exile with a king he has known for a week. Three foreigners, and each of them is put beside an Israelite who failed at the same point.

'Then David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.'

And all the little ones. He has brought his family. He is not a mercenary taking a contract; he has moved his household into the losing side of a civil war.

'And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.'

The whole countryside is standing along the road crying while the king walks out.

And he crosses the Kidron, which is the ravine between the city and the Mount of Olives, on the east side. A thousand years later another son of David went out of that city at night, over that same brook, with a small group of followers, on his way to be betrayed — and John records the crossing specifically: Jesus went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron (John 18:1).

The correspondence is going to get closer before this chapter ends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — Let Him Do to Me What Seems Good to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zadok and the Levites come out carrying the ark, and David sends it back: carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, "I have no pleasure in you," behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him (vv. 24-26). He posts the two priests in the city as his eyes (vv. 27-29). Then: David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went (v. 30). Told that Ahithophel is among the conspirators, he prays: O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the man who learned chapter 6, at the moment when the lesson costs most. Israel once carried this ark into battle as a charm and lost it, and thirty thousand men with it. David is running for his life and will not use it.
verseByVerse.examples: Let him do to me what seems good to him is Joab's sentence at Rabbah (10:12), and it is the whole of submission: he wants to come back, he asks for it, and he will not manufacture the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until the people had all passed out of the city. Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him." The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar. See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me." So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there. But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went. And it was told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until the people had all passed out of the city.'

The priests bring the ark out to go with him.

It is the obvious thing to do, and it is meant kindly, and every instinct in the nation is behind it. The presence of God should go with the true king.

'Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place."'

He sends it back.

Understand what this costs and what it proves.

Israel had done the other thing once, and the writer of this book told the story at length. At Aphek the army was beaten, and the elders said, let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us, and the whole camp shouted when it arrived, and they lost thirty thousand men and the ark itself in a single afternoon (1 Sam. 4).

David knows that story better than anybody. He also knows chapter 6 of this book, where he learned in the hardest possible way that the ark is not a piece of equipment to be moved about at convenience.

So here, running for his life, with a rebel army behind him and no idea where he is going, the one thing that would look most like divine endorsement is offered to him and he sends it home.

It stays in Jerusalem, in Absalom's hands.

He will not use God as a talisman even when it might save his throne, and he says the reason: if God intends to bring him back, God will bring him back, and the box is not what does it.

'"But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him."'

There is the other half, which is harder.

He does not claim the outcome. He would like to come back — he says so in the previous verse — and he will not pretend to know that he will, and he will not arrange matters to force it.

Let him do to me what seems good to him.

That exact sentence has been said once before in this book, by Joab, drawn up between two armies at Rabbah: may the LORD do what seems good to him (10:12). Do everything a man can do, and then leave the result where it belongs.

David is a fugitive from his own son, walking barefoot out of the city he captured, and he is not bargaining. He is not reminding God of chapter 7, and he could. He is saying: I want to come back, I have no claim, and whatever he decides is right.

That is one of the high points of the man's life, and it happens on the worst day of it.

'The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar."'

'"See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me." So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there.'

In the same breath he sets up an intelligence network.

The two priests go back with the ark, which is legitimate and expected, and their two sons will carry messages out to the fords. Nobody will question priests staying in the city with the ark, and nobody watches the sons of priests.

Both things are David at once: he refuses to manipulate God and he makes every arrangement a competent man would make. Neither cancels the other, and the chapter will not let a reader choose between them.

'But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went.'

Now the picture, and it should be allowed to stand for a moment before anything is said about it.

The king of Israel is walking up a hill outside his own capital. He has no shoes on. His head is covered, which is a sign of mourning and of shame. He is crying, out loud, where everyone can see him. And the entire column behind him has covered their heads and is crying too.

He is somewhere past sixty. He captured that city. He built the walls he has just walked out of. And he is going up a hill in his bare feet because his son wants him dead and the country agreed.

Now the correspondence, which is structural and not decorative.

He crossed the Kidron. He is going up the Mount of Olives. He has been betrayed by his closest counsellor, a man who ate at his table — and David wrote a psalm about that: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9). The Lord Jesus quoted that verse in the upper room, about Judas, on the night he was betrayed (John 13:18).

He went out over the Kidron (John 18:1). He went up the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). And two chapters from now, Ahithophel set his house in order and hanged himself (17:23), which is the only other person in Scripture to die that way apart from the man who betrayed Christ (Matt. 27:5).

The greater Son of David went up that same slope, in anguish, with a small group of loyal and bewildered followers, and prayed not my will, but yours, be done — which is what David has just said to Zadok in different words.

'And it was told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."'

One sentence of prayer, on a hillside, and it is exactly right.

It is short. It is specific. It does not inform God of the situation, rehearse the injustice, or ask for the rebellion generally to fail. It identifies the single thing that will decide the war and asks for that one thing.

David can count. Absalom has the numbers, the capital, the ark and the momentum. What he does not yet have is a good decision, and the man who can give him one has just arrived. If Ahithophel's advice is taken, David is dead within two days — and chapter 17 shows the advice, and it is lethal, and it would have worked.

So he prays about the counsel. Not the army. The counsel.

Anybody who has prayed vaguely in a crisis because the crisis was too big to think about should look at that sentence. He works out where it will actually be decided, and prays there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–37 — And Behold, Hushai Came to Meet Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head (v. 32). David sends him back: as a declared servant of Absalom he can defeat Ahithophel's counsel from inside (vv. 33-34). Zadok and Abiathar are there, and their two sons can carry messages out (vv. 35-36). So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: He prays in verse 31 and the answer walks up the hill in verse 32. The writer sets the two sentences next to each other and offers no comment, which is how he does his most serious work.
verseByVerse.examples: And David does both things at once. He prays a specific prayer and then uses every means available — a friend inside the palace, two priests, two runners — without treating the second as a substitute for the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head. David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me. But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant in time past, so now I will be your servant,' then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel. Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. Behold, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son, and by them you shall send to me everything you hear." So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head.'

He prayed in verse 31. Verse 32 begins behold.

The writer puts the two sentences side by side and says nothing at all, which is how he does his most serious work. David asks God to turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness, and before he reaches the top of the hill a man is walking up it who is the only person in Israel capable of doing that.

Hushai comes in mourning — coat torn, dirt on his head — which tells you he has come to grieve with his friend and not to be useful. He has no idea what he is walking into.

'David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me."'

He is an old man, evidently, and David says so kindly enough: on the road you would be a liability.

'"But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant in time past, so now I will be your servant,' then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel."'

There is the answer to the prayer, and David is the one who works out what it is.

He is asking Hushai to go back into a captured city, lie to a usurper's face, take an oath of loyalty he does not mean, and sit in a council chamber where one wrong word means execution — at an age when he cannot keep up with an army on the march.

Then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel. David has already seen exactly how his own prayer is going to be answered, and it is going to be answered through a frightened friend saying the right thing at the right moment in an enemy's council.

That is normally how. The prayer of verse 31 is not answered by lightning; it is answered by an old man with dirt on his head being asked to do something extremely dangerous, and agreeing.

'"Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So whatever you hear from the king's house tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests."'

'"Behold, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son, and by them you shall send to me everything you hear."'

The network is complete: a counsellor in the council, two priests to receive, two runners to carry, and a king waiting at the fords.

Every piece of it will be used in chapter 17, and one of the runners will spend an afternoon hiding in a well with a woman spreading grain over the mouth of it.

'So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.'

The timing of the last verse is the writer's, and it is exact.

Two men walk into Jerusalem at the same moment from opposite directions. One is a prince arriving to take a throne with an army behind him and the wisest counsellor in Israel at his side. The other is an elderly man with a torn coat, alone, who has agreed to lie for a living.

The kingdom turns on the second one.

And the phrase the writer chooses for him is David's friend. It is used of him four times in these chapters, and it may well be a court title — the King's Friend was a recognised office in some ancient courts. It is also simply true, and it is the reason he goes.

16.title: Shimei's Curse and Absalom in Jerusalem
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine.<sup>2</sup>And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink."<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'"<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."<sup>5</sup>When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually.<sup>6</sup>And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.<sup>7</sup>And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!<sup>8</sup>The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood."<sup>9</sup>Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head."<sup>10</sup>But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'"<sup>11</sup>And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.<sup>12</sup>It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today."<sup>13</sup>So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust.<sup>14</sup>And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.<sup>15</sup>Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.<sup>16</sup>And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"<sup>17</sup>And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"<sup>18</sup>And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain.<sup>19</sup>And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you."<sup>20</sup>Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?"<sup>21</sup>Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."<sup>22</sup>So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.<sup>23</sup>Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.
16.overview:
Ziba is waiting past the summit with exactly what an exhausted column needs, having worked out which road the king would take and got there first. And attached to the generosity is a story: Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem expecting the tribes to give him back Saul's kingdom. It is a lie, and chapter 19 proves it — the man had neither washed nor trimmed his beard nor changed his clothes from the day David left until the day he returned safely. It is also absurd on its face, since nobody in Israel was about to crown a man who cannot walk in the middle of Absalom's coup.

David hands over the entire estate in one sentence with no hearing at all. That is the king of 8:15 under pressure — sixty-odd, barefoot, just betrayed by his son and his counsellor, and handed food by the first person all morning to show him any loyalty. Exhaustion, grief and betrayal make a very bad court.

Then Shimei, throwing rocks at a column containing the entire professional army of Israel, and they let him. He is wrong and right in the same speech: the blood of the house of Saul is the one crime David is demonstrably innocent of, and man of blood is exactly true, and its name is Uriah. Abishai offers the usual remedy. And David gives one of the great answers in Scripture — with the hedge that makes it honest: it may be that the LORD will repay me with good. He claims nothing.

And in Jerusalem, on the roof, Nathan's sentence is carried out clause by clause — before all Israel, before the sun, out of his own house — on the advice of the grandfather of the woman he took, in the exact place where he first saw her.
16.theology:
The lie, and why it worked (vv. 3-4). Chapter 19 settles the facts: Mephibosheth was in mourning the whole time, says he asked Ziba to saddle a donkey so he could follow, and that he has slandered your servant (19:24-26). And nobody was going to hand a kingdom to a man crippled in both feet with no faction, no army and no following, in the middle of a coup by David's own son. Ziba timed it perfectly, producing generosity at the exact moment a betrayed man is least able to weigh a story. This is not so much a failure of character as of conditions — a man who has just been deceived by his son and his counsellor is primed to believe he has been deceived by everyone. And the consequence sits unresolved: David never decides who lied, splits the land, and Mephibosheth answers oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (19:30).

Shimei is wrong about the charge (vv. 7-8). David had Saul at his mercy in a cave and was troubled about a corner of a robe; stood over him asleep and would not let Abishai use the spear; executed the Amalekite and the two men who murdered Ish-bosheth; buried the head in Abner's tomb; and fed Saul's last grandson at his own table for twenty years. Shimei has picked the one crime David is demonstrably innocent of, because it is the one a Benjaminite would believe without evidence.

And right about the word. Man of blood is true — not about Saul, but about a Hittite officer at the wall of Rabbah, the unnamed soldiers who died in the same assault so the death would not stand out, and a letter carried by the man it killed. A bitter partisan shouting a false accusation out of tribal spite has landed on exactly the right word, and he does not know it. The writer gives him no credit for insight; he is a man kicking somebody who is finally down. The word lands anyway.

The conditional, and what it does not say (v. 10). If the LORD has said to him, curse David. He does not say Shimei is right, or that the accusation is fair, or that God approves — Shimei will answer for this, and David raises it on his deathbed. He says he will not remove a difficulty before he knows where it came from.

My own son seeks my life (v. 11). Given what my child is doing today, why would a stranger from Saul's tribe throwing rocks surprise me? A man who has taken the measure of the real disaster is not much moved by an insult — and one reason people are so easily wounded by small slights is that they have never honestly faced the large things.

It may be (v. 12). The hedge is what makes the speech honest, and it is easy to read past. He does not announce that God will vindicate him, quote chapter 7 at anybody, or promise himself an outcome. Perhaps God will look at what is being done today, and perhaps repay it with good. That is faith with no guarantee attached, from a man walking downhill barefoot with a stranger throwing dirt at him — and it is exactly what he said about the ark an hour earlier: if I find favor... but if he says, "I have no pleasure in you," behold, here I am. He is at the bottom of his circumstances and the top of his theology, and the two are not unrelated.

The New Testament writes the commentary without naming him. Peter, describing Christ: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23). Not passivity and not agreement — handing the case to a judge who cannot be corrupted and declining to prosecute it yourself. And the Son of David, arrested on that same hillside, told a man with a sword to put it away and said he could have twelve legions of angels for the asking (Matt. 26:53). David had Abishai, who had offered the same service over Saul asleep at Hachilah and is a brave man who solves every problem the same way.

Hushai's answers (vv. 18-19). Not a false word in either, and every sentence means the opposite of what the hearer takes it to mean. Whom the LORD... have chosen — and the LORD chose David. Should it not be his son? — a question, not an argument. As I have served your father, so I will serve you — a promise to do to Absalom exactly what he has been doing for David. It is deception and the book does not pretend otherwise; what it does is set him beside the midwives in Egypt and Rahab at Jericho rather than beside Ziba, who lied for an estate.

Why the counsel is brilliant (v. 21). Absalom's problem is not military. Half the country is waiting to see whether this is a real revolt or a family quarrel that will be patched up next month, and nobody wants to be the man who committed to the son and then had to face the father. Taking the royal harem was the recognised act of a successor, and doing it publicly makes reconciliation impossible — so every waverer now knows Absalom cannot climb down, which makes it safe to join him. It is a plan for burning a bridge, and it works.

Nathan's sentence, clause by clause (v. 22). Out of your own house — his son. Before all Israel — a tent where the whole city can see. Before the sun — in daylight, nothing hidden (12:11-12). And on a roof. The writer does not say the word and does not need to; there is only one roof in this book, and it is the one he was walking on when he saw her (11:2). The place where a man looked down and saw something he wanted is where the judgment is executed, in public, by his own son, on the advice of the grandfather of the woman he took. None of it is stated. It is put where a reader who has been paying attention will find it.

The cost falls on people who did nothing. The ten concubines were left in a sentence that read like housekeeping (15:16). They chose none of it, were not consulted about the arrangement that made them royal property, and are not consulted now; what happens on that roof happens because two men are conducting a political argument through them. The book does not forget them: David provides for them and did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood (20:3). Provided for, and finished at perhaps twenty. Sin rarely confines its damage to the people who committed it, and those who pay most are frequently those with the least say. Uriah did not choose it. Tamar did not choose it. These ten women did not choose it.

What David was up against (v. 23). As if one consulted the word of God — an extraordinary valuation of a man's political judgment, and the writer says both kings held him at it. Which is why the prayer on the hillside was aimed where it was: not that the army would fail or that Absalom would repent, but that this man's advice would be turned into foolishness, because nothing else in the rebellion was going to beat him.
16.examples:
Then: One man walked along a hillside for several miles throwing stones and dirt at the king of Israel and every soldier in the royal bodyguard, shouting that God was paying him back — and the king forbade his officers to touch him, on the grounds that he could not be certain God had not sent him.

Now: Two things, and they sit oddly together in one chapter. Ziba is the warning about judging: David heard one side, from the party who stood to gain, at the moment he was least able to weigh anything, and gave a verdict in a sentence. Grief and exhaustion and a recent betrayal are the conditions in which almost every unjust snap decision gets made, and the remedy is not to be a better person but to refuse to decide anything then. And Shimei is the model for being slandered. David neither agreed with the man nor silenced him; he declined to prosecute his own case, and said it may be — no claim, no promised vindication, no certainty about what God was doing. Notice too what freed him to do it: he was not shaken by an insult because he had already faced the real wound, and his son was the one who had inflicted it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — All That Belonged to Mephibosheth Is Now Yours
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ziba meets David just past the summit with two donkeys loaded with bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine (vv. 1-2). Asked where his master's son is, he answers: behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, "Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father" (v. 3). Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king" (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The story is a lie, and chapter 19 proves it: Mephibosheth had not washed his feet, trimmed his beard or changed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came back safely. It is also absurd on its face — nobody in Israel was going to make a man who cannot walk their king in the middle of Absalom's coup.
verseByVerse.examples: And David hands over the whole estate in one sentence, without hearing the other side. This is the king of 8:15, judging under pressure, about the man who was the recipient of his own greatest act of grace. Exhaustion and betrayal make a bad court.

verseByVerse.quote: When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine. And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink." And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'" Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine.'

Ziba is waiting past the top of the hill with supplies for a fleeing king.

The timing is not accidental. He has worked out which road David will take and got there first, and he has brought exactly what a column of exhausted people needs. Two hundred loaves is the same figure Abigail brought down the mountain to stop a massacre (1 Sam. 25:18), and Ziba may well have the precedent in mind.

'And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink."'

An excellent answer, itemised, thoughtful, and precisely matched to the need.

'And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'"'

There is the payload, and it is a lie.

We know it is a lie because the book tells us. When David comes back, Mephibosheth comes down to meet him, and the writer describes him: he had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back safely (19:24). He had been in mourning the entire time. And his account is that he asked Ziba to saddle a donkey so that he could go with the king, and he has slandered your servant, and that he could not go himself because he is lame (19:26).

It is also absurd on its face if anybody stops to think about it.

The rebellion in progress is Absalom's. Nobody in Israel is proposing to restore the house of Saul. And the candidate Ziba is describing is a man crippled in both feet who has spent twenty years eating at David's table as a pensioner and has no faction, no army and no following of any kind. The idea that the tribes would hand him a kingdom in the middle of a coup by David's own son is not plausible for a moment.

'Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."'

David gives him everything, in one sentence, without asking a single question.

No summons. No hearing. No attempt to check the story against anything. The other party is twelve miles away in a city David has just left, and cannot be reached, and is not sent for — and the entire estate of Saul changes hands on the word of the man who benefits from it.

This is the same king of whom it was written that he administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15). Here is what that looks like on the worst day of his life: he is sixty-odd years old, walking barefoot out of his own capital, has just been told his most trusted counsellor has defected, and is being handed food by the first person all morning who has shown him any loyalty.

Ziba has timed it perfectly. He has produced generosity at the exact moment when a betrayed man is least able to weigh a story, and he has attached his accusation to it.

Take that seriously, because it is not a failure of character so much as a failure of conditions. Exhaustion, grief and betrayal make a very bad court, and a man who has just been deceived by his son and his counsellor is primed to believe he has been deceived by everybody else.

The consequence sits there unresolved. When David finally hears the other side he does not apologise, does not restore the estate, and does not decide who was lying. He splits the land between the two of them — and Mephibosheth answers, oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (19:30).

The man who was given everything for Jonathan's sake loses half of it to a lie, and does not complain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Let Him Alone, and Let Him Curse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Bahurim, Shimei of the house of Saul comes out cursing and throwing stones at the king and all his servants (vv. 5-6): get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man! The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul... See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood (vv. 7-8). Abishai offers to take his head off (v. 9). David refuses: if he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, "Curse David," who then shall say, "Why have you done so?" (v. 10). Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today (vv. 11-12). Shimei keeps pace along the hillside, cursing and throwing dust, until they arrive weary and refresh themselves (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: He is half wrong and half right, and both halves matter. The blood of the house of Saul is simply false — David had two chances to kill Saul and refused, and executed the men who killed Saul's son. But man of blood is true, and its name is Uriah.
verseByVerse.examples: This is David at the bottom of his circumstances and the top of his theology. Note the hedge — it may be. He claims nothing, demands nothing, and predicts nothing. He will not silence the man, and he will not pretend to know what God is doing with him.

verseByVerse.quote: When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually. And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left. And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man! The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood." Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head." But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'" And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today." So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust. And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually.'

Bahurim is a village on the road down to the Jordan, and it is Benjaminite country — Saul's tribe.

It is also, as it happens, where Paltiel stood weeping when Michal was taken back from him (3:16). The same village.

'And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.'

Take in the picture, because it is grimly funny as well as awful.

A man is throwing rocks at a column that contains the entire professional army of Israel — the Cherethites, the Pelethites, the six hundred Gittites, and the mighty men, the ones with names in chapter 23 who killed lions in pits and held fields alone against the Philistines. They are walking on either side of the king, and they let him do it.

'And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!"'

'"The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood."'

Now this needs to be taken apart, because Shimei is wrong and right in the same speech and it matters which is which.

The charge is false. All the blood of the house of Saul — David never shed it. He had Saul at his mercy in a cave and cut a corner off his robe and was troubled about that much. He stood over him asleep with a spear in the ground beside his head and would not let Abishai use it. He executed the Amalekite who claimed to have finished Saul off, and executed the two men who murdered Ish-bosheth in his bed, and buried the head in Abner's tomb. He sought out the last surviving grandson and fed him at his own table for twenty years.

Shimei has picked the one crime David is demonstrably innocent of, and it is the one a Benjaminite would believe without evidence.

And man of blood is true.

Not about Saul. About a Hittite officer at the wall of Rabbah, and the unnamed soldiers who died in the same assault so that the death would not stand out, and a letter carried by the man it killed.

So a bitter partisan, shouting a false accusation out of tribal spite, has accidentally hit the one word that is exactly right. Shimei does not know that.
