He is not a prophet and he is not being noble; he is a man kicking somebody who is finally down, and the writer gives him no credit for insight.

But the word lands.

'Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head."'

Abishai, entirely in character.

He offered the same service over Saul asleep at Hachilah — let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear; I will not strike him twice (1 Sam. 26:8) — and he is offering it again. He is a brave man who solves every problem the same way, and it is his brother Joab who does it when David says no.

Note that he calls Shimei this dead dog. It is the phrase Mephibosheth used about himself, and David used about himself to Saul, and here it is used as pure contempt.

'But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'"'

And here begins one of the great answers in Scripture, and it should be read slowly because it is easy to make it either more or less than it is.

He does not say Shimei is right. He does not say the accusation is fair. He asks a question about where this is coming from.

If the LORD has said to him, "Curse David." That is a conditional — if — and David is entertaining the possibility that a man throwing stones at him is part of something God is doing.

Note what he is not doing. He is not saying God approves of Shimei; Shimei will be judged for this in due course, and David himself brings it up on his deathbed. He is not saying the curse is accurate. He is saying that he is not going to remove a difficulty until he knows where it came from.

'"Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to."'

Here is the argument, and it is devastating in its simplicity.

My own son seeks my life.

He is saying: given what my child is doing to me today, why would I be surprised or offended by a stranger from Saul's tribe throwing rocks? Compared with the actual wound, this is nothing.

A man who has taken the measure of the real disaster is not much moved by an insult, and one reason people are so easily wounded by small slights is that they have not honestly faced the large things.

'"It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today."'

Here is the hedge that makes the whole speech honest, and it is easy to read past.

It may be.

He does not claim it. He does not announce that God will vindicate him, or quote chapter 7 at anybody, or promise himself an outcome. He says perhaps — perhaps God will look at what is being done to me today, and perhaps he will repay this with good.

That is faith with no guarantee attached, offered by a man walking downhill in his bare feet with a stranger throwing dirt at him. It is exactly what he said to Zadok an hour ago about the ark: if I find favor... but if he says, "I have no pleasure in you," behold, here I am.

He is at the very bottom of his circumstances and the very top of his theology, and the two things are not unrelated.

The New Testament writes the commentary on this without mentioning David. Peter, describing Christ: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23). That is precisely the mechanism — not passivity, not agreement, but handing the case to a judge who cannot be corrupted and declining to prosecute it yourself.

And the Son of David, arrested on that same hillside, told a man with a sword to put it away, and said he could have twelve legions of angels for the asking and would not ask (Matt. 26:53). David had Abishai. It is the same refusal at a smaller scale.

'So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust.'

He keeps it up, walking parallel along the slope, for what must have been miles.

'And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.'

They arrive worn out at the river, and the writer lets that be the end of the day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — In the Sight of All Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel, and Hushai greets him: long live the king! Long live the king! (vv. 15-16). Absalom challenges his loyalty, and Hushai answers that he will serve whom the LORD and this people have chosen, and as I have served your father, so I will serve you (vv. 17-19). Then Absalom asks Ahithophel for counsel, and gets it: go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father (vv. 20-21). So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel (v. 22). Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Nathan's sentence, word for word: I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor... For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun (12:11-12). And it happens on a roof — the roof of 11:2, where he was walking when he saw her.
verseByVerse.examples: Hushai's double answer is a small masterpiece: every clause of it is technically about whoever God has chosen and whoever the father's son is, and Absalom hears what he wants. And the last verse measures exactly what David prayed against on the hillside.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!" And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?" And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain. And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you." Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?" Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened." So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.'

The rebellion enters the capital without a fight, exactly as David intended when he left it.

'And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"'

Here is the old man with the torn coat, doing what he agreed on the hillside to do.

He shouts the acclamation twice, which is louder than anybody else in the room, and notice that he does not say which king. That will be his whole technique.

'And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"'

Absalom is nobody's fool, and the question is the right one, and it has a barb in it. He uses the word friend twice, which is Hushai's own title at court.

'And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain."'

'"And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you."'

Read the two answers, because there is not a false word in either of them.

Whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen — and the LORD chose David. Hushai says he will belong to God's choice, and means it, and Absalom hears an endorsement of himself because the people have just acclaimed him.

Should it not be his son? — which sounds like an argument for hereditary legitimacy and is in fact a question. As I have served your father, so I will serve you — which Absalom takes as a transfer of loyalty and which is a promise to do to Absalom exactly what he has been doing for David all along.

Every sentence is technically true and every sentence means the opposite of what the hearer takes it to mean.

It should be said plainly that this is deception, and the book does not pretend otherwise. Hushai is a spy in a rebel court, and there is a real question about it that Scripture does not stop to answer here. What can be said is that he is in a war, that Absalom would kill him on the spot if he answered honestly, and that the writer sets him alongside the midwives in Egypt and Rahab at Jericho rather than alongside Ziba, who lied for an estate.

'Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?"'

'Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."'

This is why David prayed on the hillside.

The advice is cold, brilliant, and correct on its own terms. Absalom's problem is not military; it is that half the country is waiting to see whether this is a real revolt or a family quarrel that will be patched up next month, and nobody wants to be the man who committed to the son and then had to face the father.

Taking the royal harem was the recognised act of a successor claiming a throne. Doing it publicly makes reconciliation impossible — there is no coming back from it — and every waverer in Israel now knows that Absalom cannot climb down, which means it is safe to join him.

It is a plan for burning a bridge, and it works.

'So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.'

On the roof.

Now go back four chapters and hear Nathan again, and match it clause by clause.

Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun (12:11-12).

Out of his own house: his son. Before all Israel: a tent pitched where the whole city can see it. Before the sun: in daylight, publicly, with nothing hidden.

And on a roof.

The writer does not say the word, and he does not need to. There is only one roof in this book. It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing (11:2).

The place where a man looked down and saw something he wanted is the place where the judgment on it is carried out, in public, by his own son, on the advice of the grandfather of the woman he took.

Nothing in that arrangement is coincidental and none of it is stated. It is simply put where a reader who has been paying attention will find it.

And there is a cost in this verse that must not be passed over, because it falls on people who did nothing.

The ten concubines were left to keep the house, in a sentence in the previous chapter that read like a housekeeping detail (15:16). They did not choose any of this. They were not consulted about the arrangement that made them royal property in the first place, and they are not consulted now, and what happens to them on that roof happens because two men are conducting a political argument through them.

The book does not forget them. When David comes back he takes them into a house and provides for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood (20:3).

That is the last thing said about them. Provided for, and finished at perhaps twenty years old, because of a decision on a roof they had nothing to do with.

Sin does that. It rarely confines its damage to the people who committed it, and the ones who pay the most are frequently the ones with the least say in any of it. Uriah did not choose it. Tamar did not choose it. These ten women did not choose it.

'Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.'

And the chapter ends with the writer telling us exactly what David is up against.

As if one consulted the word of God. That is an extraordinary thing to say about a man's political judgment, and the writer says both kings held him at that valuation. When Ahithophel spoke, you did what he said, the way you would do what an oracle said.

Which is why the prayer on the hillside was aimed where it was. David did not pray that the army would fail or that Absalom would repent. He prayed that this man's advice would be turned into foolishness, because he knew that nothing else in the rebellion was going to beat him.

The next chapter is that prayer being answered, in a council chamber, by an old man in a torn coat.

17.title: Ahithophel's Counsel Overthrown
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight.<sup>2</sup>I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king,<sup>3</sup>and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace."<sup>4</sup>And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say."<sup>6</sup>And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak."<sup>7</sup>Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good."<sup>8</sup>Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people.<sup>9</sup>Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.'<sup>10</sup>Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men.<sup>11</sup>But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person.<sup>12</sup>So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left.<sup>13</sup>If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there."<sup>14</sup>And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.<sup>15</sup>Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled.<sup>16</sup>Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'"<sup>17</sup>Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city.<sup>18</sup>But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it.<sup>19</sup>And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it.<sup>20</sup>When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.<sup>21</sup>After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you."<sup>22</sup>Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father.<sup>24</sup>Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel.<sup>25</sup>Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.<sup>26</sup>And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.<sup>27</sup>When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim,<sup>28</sup>brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils,<sup>29</sup>honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
17.overview:
Ahithophel's plan is right, and the whole chapter depends on seeing that. Twelve thousand men — a strike force, not an army — moving tonight, while David is on foot somewhere short of the Jordan with women and children and a weeping crowd. Weary and discouraged, because Ahithophel has sat in that council for years and can read him. And then the surgical part: I will strike down only the king. He has grasped what Absalom has not — this is not a war between armies, it is a question about one man. It is also humane: one death instead of a battle, no Israelite killing another, the nation coming home like a bride. The elders agree and it is settled.

Then Absalom says let us also hear Hushai, which is a piece of nothing from a man who likes to be consulted. And Hushai's answer is a study: every fact he states is true and every conclusion he draws is wrong. David's men are mighty men and a bear robbed of her cubs — which is exactly why Ahithophel wanted to hit them tonight. Then the flattery: all Israel from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea, and you go to battle in person. That is the flaw he spotted in the better plan — in Ahithophel's version somebody else kills the king and hands Absalom a kingdom.

They vote for the worse plan unanimously, and they are not stupid; they have just heard a better speech. Ahithophel gave a plan and Hushai gave a vision. And then the writer stops the narrative for one sentence — the only time in the whole rebellion — to say that the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. That is nine words prayed barefoot on a hillside, answered.

What the answer looked like on the ground was a servant girl carrying a message, two young men down a well, and an unnamed woman who spread a cloth over the mouth of it and scattered grain on top so it would look like a drying floor — and then lied to armed men on her own doorstep. Ahithophel rode home, set his affairs in order, and hanged himself. And three men brought bedding and cheese to a defeated king at Mahanaim.
17.theology:
The plan that would have worked (vv. 1-3). Speed, surprise, one target, minimum bloodshed, and the army brought home intact. Kill David and there is no rebellion, because there is nothing to rebel against — the Gittites and the mighty men are not fighting for a cause, they are fighting for him. Ahithophel proposed an assassination to prevent a civil war, and the narrator himself calls it the good counsel.

Hushai's technique (vv. 8-10). Not a single false statement, and every inference wrong. He begins this time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good — conceding the man's whole reputation and disputing one occasion, because attacking him directly would be fatal. Then he finds Absalom's pressure point in ninety seconds: not tactics but reputation, that news of a reverse would empty his support overnight. A man who spent four years building a following one handshake at a time will hear nothing else after that.

Why the worse plan won (vv. 11-13). All Israel from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea (which is Abraham's promise, Gen. 22:17, applied to a rebel army), and above all you go to battle in person. That is the flaw Hushai found in the better plan: Ahithophel goes and Absalom stays home, and somebody else wins him a kingdom. Militarily it is a disaster — surprise surrendered, weeks instead of hours, a muster that cannot be hidden, everything staked on one pitched battle — and none of that is the question Absalom is answering. The last two verses are not a plan at all but poetry: dew on the ground, a city dragged into a valley with ropes. Ahithophel gave a plan; Hushai gave a vision. The elders were not stupid; they had just heard the better speech, which is what carries a room.

Verse 14, and the three things in it. First, God's own historian calls the plan he is describing God as overthrowing good — so Absalom did not choose badly against a defective alternative; he chose badly against a sound plan, competently argued, by the best mind in Israel. Second, the LORD had ordained: not permitted, not foresaw — ordained, and the outcome was settled before anyone spoke, while every person in the room did exactly what he thought best. Nobody was coerced: Ahithophel gave honest professional judgment, Hushai used his own courage and wit, Absalom exercised a vanity he had been cultivating for years, the elders preferred a better speech. Every human factor is fully accounted for and the writer still says God ordained the result. Scripture holds these together everywhere without explaining the mechanism — Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, of the same act (Gen. 50:20); and men did what God's hand and plan had predestined and were lawless men held responsible for it (Acts 2:23).

And third: this is 15:31 answered. Nine words prayed by a barefoot man with dirt on his head. Look at how the answer came — not by a voice, not a sign, and not by anything David could have seen: an old man's courage, a young man's vanity, a room of elders who liked one speech better, and a decision that took perhaps a minute. Anyone in that council would have seen politics; there is no moment in the sequence where God is visible. And David never learns it. He is told only to cross the river at once. He does not get verse 14; we do. That is the honest position of everyone who prays — the answer normally looks exactly like other people making their own decisions for their own reasons, and the sentence explaining what was really happening is not available at the time.

Hushai does not trust his own success (v. 16). He has just won the argument and bought weeks, and his message is by all means pass over tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind — which he could, because the better plan is still available. Only the river makes the delay safe.

What the ordaining looked like on the ground (vv. 17-20). A servant girl walks out of the city with the most dangerous information in Israel in her head, because nobody notices a maid going to the spring. A boy sees the runners anyway and reports it. And a woman at Bahurim — the village where Shimei threw stones the day before — covers a well with two men in it and scatters grain across the top so that what a soldier sees is an ordinary courtyard with grain drying. That detail was in no plan; she thought of it while it was happening. Then she lies to armed men on her own doorstep, calmly, with a plausible direction attached. If her voice shakes, two men die in a well, David is not warned, and Absalom takes Ahithophel's advice after all. She has no name and gets two verses, and nobody in Israel ever knew.

Ahithophel calculates one last time (v. 23). Not despair over a professional slight. He can see the end from where he stands: Absalom will muster, David will have time, there will be a pitched battle, and David will win it — and when he does there will be a reckoning, and the counsellor who left the king's table will be at the top of it. He is a dead man either way and prefers to arrange it himself. The verbs are what make it terrible: he saddled his donkey, rode a day to Giloh, set his house in order — settled his affairs and provided for his family — and then did it. No rage and no impulse; a man completing his last piece of competent work. His family buried him in his father's tomb.

The other man who died that way. Ahithophel is the only man in the Old Testament to hang himself. The next is the one who sat at the table of the Son of David, ate his bread, took silver, and went and hanged himself (Matt. 27:5). David wrote about Ahithophel — even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9) — and Jesus quoted that verse in the upper room about Judas (John 13:18). Betrayal by the trusted counsellor, over the Kidron, on the Mount of Olives, ending in a rope: written into this book a thousand years before the night it happened again.

Two grandsons of the same woman (v. 25). Amasa is Joab's cousin and both are David's nephews, and the two armies about to meet are commanded by them. Keep the name: David confirms Absalom's appointment in chapter 19 as a peace offering to the rebels, and Joab kills Amasa for it in chapter 20 with the same greeting and the same wound he used on Abner.

Three debts repaid (vv. 27-29). Shobi is a son of Nahash — Hanun's brother, from the house that shaved David's envoys, and from Rabbah, the city at whose wall Uriah was killed while David was on the roof. Machir of Lo-debar sheltered Mephibosheth for twenty years when it was not safe to; he is consistent, and looks after whoever has been put out. And read the inventory: beds, basins, earthenware, wheat, barley, flour, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep, cheese. No weapons and no money. Nobody wins a war with lentils. The writer even gives their reason in their own words, which he did not have to — not the king's cause is just but the people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness. An Ammonite, a provincial, and an old man from across the river, at the moment when the whole country from Dan to Beersheba is mustering behind the king's son. The book has done this from the beginning: Obed-edom, Uriah, Ittai, and now these. The people who show up are from the edges.
17.examples:
Then: The best political mind in Israel proposed the plan that would have ended the war that night with a single death, and the council agreed to it — and then a young man who liked being consulted asked to hear one more opinion, and an old man in a torn coat talked them out of it with a speech about the sand by the sea. And somewhere in a village, a woman put a cloth over a well and scattered grain on it.

Now: Two things. Verse 14 is the one to sit with, and it is not comfortable in either direction. It insists that God ordained the outcome of a meeting in which every person present freely did what he thought best, and it does not explain how — and any account of providence that drops either half is not this verse. What is practically useful is the second observation: David got his answer and never knew it. He prayed nine specific words, and the answer came dressed as a committee preferring a better speech, and he was never told. Most answered prayer is like that. If you are waiting to see God's hand before you believe he moved, you will usually be waiting for something that only shows up in the account written afterwards. And the second is the woman at Bahurim, who is what verse 14 looks like from ground level: no name, two verses, an idea she had on the spot, and a kingdom depending on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The LORD Had Ordained to Defeat the Good Counsel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahithophel proposes to take twelve thousand men and set out that night, strike David while he is weary and discouraged, panic his people, and kill the king alone — I will strike down only the king, and I will bring all the people back to you (vv. 1-3). It pleases Absalom and all the elders (v. 4). But Hushai is called in, and argues the opposite: your father is a man of war, enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs, and will not spend the night with the troops (vv. 7-10); therefore gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and go into battle in person (vv. 11-13). And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahithophel's plan is right and the text says so: the good counsel. Speed, surprise, one target, minimum bloodshed, and the army brought home intact. Hushai's is worse in every military respect and wins because it is flattering — all Israel, the sand by the sea, and Absalom himself at the head of it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the writer lifts the curtain for one sentence. This is the only place in the whole rebellion where he tells us what God was doing, and it is the answer to a prayer prayed barefoot on a hillside two chapters ago: O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness (15:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight. I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king, and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace." And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel. Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say." And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak." Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good." Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people. Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.' Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men. But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person. So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left. If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there." And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight."'

Now listen to this plan, because the whole chapter depends on understanding that it is a very good one.

Twelve thousand, which is a strike force and not an army — enough to overwhelm a column of refugees and small enough to move fast. And tonight, which is the whole of it. David crossed the Kidron this morning. He is somewhere between Jerusalem and the Jordan, on foot, with women and children and a weeping crowd, and he has not yet crossed the river.

'"I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king,"'

Weary and discouraged. He knows exactly what condition David is in, because he has sat in his council for years and can read him.

And then the surgical part: I will strike down only the king.

Ahithophel has grasped what Absalom has not, which is that this is not a war between two armies. It is a question about one man. Kill David and there is no rebellion, because there is nothing to rebel against; the six hundred Gittites and the mighty men are not fighting for a cause, they are fighting for him.

'"and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace."'

The plan is not only effective, it is humane, which is the last thing anybody expects.

One death instead of a battle. The army comes home intact and changes sides without a fight. No Israelite kills another Israelite. He even puts an image to it: the nation returning to Absalom like a bride coming home.

Ahithophel is proposing an assassination to prevent a civil war, and he is right on the military facts, and he is right on the timing, and it would have worked. The narrator is going to say so in verse 14 in as many words.

'And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel.'

Everybody agrees. It is settled.

'Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say."'

This is the sentence on which the kingdom turns, and it is a piece of nothing.

The decision has been made. Ahithophel has spoken, the elders are convinced, and the correct course is agreed. And Absalom, who has been in the room for about a day, says: let us also hear from the other one.

He is not suspicious of Ahithophel. He is not weighing alternatives. He is a man who likes to be consulted and likes to hear things and cannot quite bring himself to act on a decision that is finished.

Why he says it, the writer does not tell us. Verse 14 tells us who was behind it.

'And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak."'

'Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good."'

He has to say that fast and he has to say it with total confidence, and he does.

Note the two words he adds: this time. He does not attack Ahithophel, which would be fatal, since the man's reputation is the word of God. He concedes everything about the counsellor and disputes only this one occasion.

'Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people."'

Now watch the technique, because it repays study.

Every single thing he says is true, and every conclusion he draws from it is wrong.

David's men are mighty men — the writer will list them by name in chapter 23. David is expert in war, more than anybody alive. A bear robbed of her cubs is the most dangerous animal in that country, and it is an exact picture of what those six hundred men are like at this moment.

All of which is precisely why Ahithophel wanted to hit them tonight, before they have slept, crossed the river, or organised anything.

Hushai takes the same facts and turns them into a reason to wait.

'"Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.'"'

'"Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men."'

Here is the hook, and it is aimed straight at the thing Absalom cares about.

The argument is: if the first attack goes even slightly wrong, the news will spread that Absalom's men are being slaughtered, and your support will evaporate overnight.

That is a fear about reputation, not about tactics. And Absalom is a man who has spent four years at a gate building a reputation one handshake at a time. Hushai has found the pressure point in about ninety seconds.

'"But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person."'

Now the flattery, and it is enormous.

All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba. Every tribe, the whole country, the formula that means the entire nation.

As the sand by the sea for multitude. That is Abraham's promise (Gen. 22:17), applied to Absalom's army.

And that you go to battle in person.

There it is. Ahithophel's plan had one flaw from Absalom's point of view, and Hushai has spotted it: in Ahithophel's version, Ahithophel goes and Absalom stays home, and somebody else kills the king and hands him a kingdom. In Hushai's version, Absalom rides at the head of the largest army ever assembled in Israel and wins it himself.

Militarily it is a disaster. It surrenders surprise, gives David weeks instead of hours, requires a national muster that cannot be hidden, and commits the whole rebellion to a single pitched battle. Every one of those is a reason not to do it.

None of that is the question Absalom is actually answering.

'"So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left."'

'"If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there."'

And the last two verses are not a plan at all. They are poetry.

As the dew falls on the ground. We shall drag the city into the valley until not even a pebble is to be found. Nobody drags a city into a valley with ropes. It is a picture of overwhelming, total, effortless victory, and it is exactly what a proud man wants to hear about himself.

Ahithophel gave a plan. Hushai gave a vision.

'And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel."'

They vote for the worse plan unanimously.

Be clear that they are not stupid. These are the elders of Israel, and they have just heard a better speech, and a better speech is what carries a room. The man with the correct answer spoke in numbers and hours; the man with the wrong answer spoke about the sand by the sea and dew on the ground and the king himself at the head of the nation.

The better argument lost to the more flattering one, which is not a phenomenon confined to ancient councils.

'For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.'

Here the writer stops the narrative and tells us what has actually been happening, and it is the only time in the whole rebellion that he does it.

Read it slowly, because there are three things in it.

First: the good counsel of Ahithophel. God's own historian, in the same sentence in which he describes God overthrowing it, calls Ahithophel's plan good. It was the right plan. It would have worked. Nothing here suggests that Absalom chose badly because the alternative was defective; he chose badly against a sound plan, competently argued, by the best mind in Israel.

Second: the LORD had ordained to defeat it. Not permitted. Not foresaw. Ordained. The outcome of that council was determined before anybody spoke, and every person in the room was doing exactly what he thought best.

Nobody was coerced. Ahithophel gave his honest professional judgment. Hushai used his own intelligence and courage. Absalom exercised his vanity freely, as he had for years. The elders were persuaded by a better speech. Every human factor in that room is fully accounted for, and the writer still says God ordained the result.

Scripture holds those together everywhere and never explains the mechanism. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, and both are said of the same act (Gen. 50:20). Men did what God's hand and plan had predestined to take place at the cross, and they were lawless men who are held responsible for it (Acts 2:23).

Third, and this is where the chapter connects back: two chapters ago, a barefoot man going up the Mount of Olives with dirt on his head prayed nine words. O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness (15:31).

This verse is that prayer being answered, and the writer wants us to see it.

And look at how it was answered. Not by a voice, not by a sign, and not by any event David could have seen. It was answered through an old man's courage, a young man's vanity, a room full of elders who liked one speech better than another, and a decision that took perhaps a minute. If you had been in that council you would have seen politics. There is no moment in the whole sequence where God is visible.

David never learns this. He is told, later that night, only that he must cross the river at once. He does not get verse 14; we do.

Which is the honest situation of anybody who prays. The answer, if it comes, will normally look exactly like other people making their own decisions for their own reasons, and the sentence that explains what was really happening is not usually available at the time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — A Woman Spread a Covering Over the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hushai sends word to the priests: do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over (vv. 15-16). Jonathan and Ahimaaz are waiting at En-rogel; a servant girl carries the message out to them, but a boy sees them and tells Absalom (vv. 17-18). They hide in a well in a man's courtyard at Bahurim, and the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it (v. 19). She sends the pursuers on with a sentence (v. 20). The two climb out and run (v. 21), and by daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything now depends on ordinary people doing something dangerous. A servant girl carrying messages, two young men in a hole in the ground, and a woman with a handful of grain.
verseByVerse.examples: She is not named, and she gets one verse. What she does is put a cloth over a well with two men in it, scatter grain across the top so that it looks like a drying floor, and then lie to armed men on her own doorstep. If she is wrong or nervous, the king dies at the fords that night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled. Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'" Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city. But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it. And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it. When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem. After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you." Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled."'

He gets the message out immediately, and note that he reports both plans. David needs to know what was proposed as well as what was decided.

'"Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'"'

And note the caution in it.

Hushai's counsel won. He has every reason to think he has bought David several weeks. And he does not trust his own success for one night: by all means pass over, tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind.

He is right to. Ahithophel's plan was better and Absalom could still take it, and the only thing that makes the delay safe is the river between the two armies.

'Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city.'

The network from chapter 15 is now working exactly as designed, and the first link in it is a servant girl.

She is the one who walks out of the city with the most dangerous information in Israel in her head. Nobody notices a maid going to the spring, which is precisely why she is doing it.

'But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it.'

And then it goes wrong. A boy sees them and reports it.

Bahurim is the village where Shimei came out throwing stones the day before. They run into a courtyard in hostile country and climb down a well.

'And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it.'

One verse, and the kingdom is inside it.

Think about what she does in the time available. Two strangers drop into her husband's well with pursuit behind them. She covers the mouth of it, and then — and this is the part that shows what kind of person she is — she scatters grain across the covering, so that what any soldier sees when he walks into that yard is a perfectly ordinary courtyard with grain spread out to dry.

That detail was not part of any plan. She thought of it while it was happening.

'When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.'

She lies to armed men on her own doorstep, calmly, with a plausible direction attached.

If her voice shakes, or she hesitates, or one of them decides to look under the grain, then two young men die in a well, David is not warned, and Absalom takes Ahithophel's advice after all.

She has no name. She gets two verses. Nobody in Israel ever knew.

The book is full of this, and it should stop a reader. The great sentence of the chapter is verse 14 — the LORD had ordained — and here is what that ordaining looked like on the ground: a woman with a handful of grain, thinking fast, in a village.

'After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you."'

'Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.'

By dawn the river is behind them, and every person is across.

The writer counts. Not one was left. The women, the children, the six hundred Gittites with their little ones, the priests' households, all of it — a night crossing of the Jordan by a whole community, and nobody is left on the wrong bank.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — He Set His House in Order and Hanged Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father (v. 23). David comes to Mahanaim; Absalom crosses the Jordan with all Israel, having made Amasa commander in place of Joab (vv. 24-25). Israel and Absalom encamp in Gilead (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: He is not despairing at a setback. He is the best political mind in Israel and he has just watched the council choose the losing plan — so he knows precisely how this ends, for Absalom and for a man who has publicly betrayed David.
verseByVerse.examples: The orderliness is the terrible part: he rides home, arranges his affairs, and does it. Two chapters ago the writer noted that he ate at David's table and that his advice was reckoned as the word of God. He is the only man in the Old Testament to die this way, and the next one in Scripture betrayed the Son of David for silver.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father. Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel. Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father.'

One verse, and it is one of the coldest in Scripture.

Understand first that this is not a man in despair over a professional slight. Ahithophel is the finest political mind in Israel, and what he has just watched is a council choose the losing plan. He can see the whole thing to the end from where he is standing: Absalom will muster, David will have time to organise across the Jordan, there will be a pitched battle, and David will win it, because David is expert in war and always has been.

And when David wins, there will be a reckoning, and the name at the top of it will be the counsellor who left the king's own table for the son's.

So he calculates, exactly as he has calculated everything else. He is a dead man either way, and he prefers to arrange it himself.

Now look at the sequence of verbs, because the orderliness is what makes it terrible.

He saddled his donkey. He went home to his own city, which is Giloh, a day's ride. He set his house in order, which means he made his arrangements, settled his affairs, and provided for his family. And then he did it.

There is no rage in any of that and no impulse. It is a man completing his final piece of competent work.

He is buried in his father's tomb, which means his family did not treat him as disgraced.

Two chapters ago the writer told us that the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God (16:23). This is the same man. All that ability, and he is dead in a house at Giloh because a vain young man liked a better speech.

And there is one more thing here, and the writer has been building it since chapter 15.

Ahithophel is one of only a handful of suicides in the whole Bible, and he is the only man in the Old Testament who dies by hanging himself. The other is in the New Testament, and he is the man who sat at the table of the Son of David, ate his bread, took silver to betray him, and went and hanged himself (Matt. 27:5).

The correspondence is not decoration. David wrote about Ahithophel: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9) — and Jesus quoted that verse in the upper room, about Judas (John 13:18). The betrayal of David by his trusted counsellor, over the Kidron, on the Mount of Olives, ending in a rope, is written into this book a thousand years before the night it happened again.

'Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel with him.'

Mahanaim is across the Jordan in Gilead, and it is a name with a history. Jacob met the angels of God there and called the place Two Camps (Gen. 32:2), on the night before he faced Esau. And it was Ish-bosheth's capital during the civil war, which means it is a defensible town used to housing a government in exile.

'Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.'

The genealogy is given because it matters.

Amasa is Joab's cousin. Both of them are David's nephews. The two opposing armies about to fight each other are commanded by two grandsons of the same woman.

Keep the name. Absalom made Amasa commander in place of Joab, and David is going to confirm that appointment in chapter 19 as a peace offering to the rebels — and Joab is going to kill him for it in chapter 20, with the same greeting and the same wound he used on Abner.

'And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–29 — Three Men Brought Beds and Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mahanaim, three men come out to David with supplies: Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim (v. 27). They bring beds, basins, earthenware, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep and cheese — for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness" (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Look at who they are. Shobi is a son of Nahash, which makes him a brother of the Hanun who shaved David's envoys and started a war. Machir of Lo-debar is the man in whose house Mephibosheth was living when David sent for him (9:4). Every one of these debts was incurred years ago.
verseByVerse.examples: And the inventory is domestic rather than military — beds, bowls, cheese, honey. Nobody sends an army lentils and curds to win a war. They sent them because the people were hungry, and the writer says so.

verseByVerse.quote: When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim, brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim,'

Three men come out to meet a defeated king, and every one of them is a debt being repaid.

Look at the first. Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites.

Nahash is the Ammonite king whose death set off the whole business of chapter 10. His son Hanun shaved the beards off David's envoys and started a war that cost the lives of an allied army. And Rabbah is the Ammonite capital — the city Joab was besieging when David was on the roof, the city at whose wall Uriah was killed.

Shobi is Hanun's brother. He is a son of the house David tried to show kindness to and was insulted for, from the city where David committed his worst act, and he has come out with food.

The second is Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and that name was last seen in chapter 9. Lo-debar is where Mephibosheth was living, in Machir's house, for the twenty years nobody in Jerusalem thought about him. Machir sheltered the grandson of Saul when it was not safe to.

He is now feeding David.

The man who took in the last of the old dynasty when the new king might have wanted him dead is the same man who supplies the new king when his own son has driven him out. Whatever Machir is, he is consistent: he looks after whoever has been put out.

The third is Barzillai, a very old and very rich man from Gilead, and chapter 19 will give him one of the finest speeches in the book.

'brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils,'

'honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."'

Now read the list, because it is not a military supply column.

Beds. Basins. Earthenware. Wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep, cheese.

Nobody wins a war with lentils and cheese. There are no weapons on that list and no money. What these men have sent is what you send to people who have walked a long way and are sleeping outdoors: something to lie on, something to cook in, and enough food for a few thousand exhausted people.

And the writer gives their reason in their own words, which he did not have to do: the people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.

Not the king's cause is just. Not we support the legitimate government. The people are hungry.

One last thing about the three of them together. An Ammonite from the enemy capital, a Gileadite from the far side of the Jordan, and the man who housed Saul's crippled grandson in a village nobody had heard of.

Israel has just thrown David out. The whole country from Dan to Beersheba is mustering behind his son, and Ahithophel and two hundred men of Jerusalem went over, and his nephew is commanding the rebel army. And what arrives at Mahanaim is a foreigner, a provincial, and an old man from across the river, with bedding.

The book has been doing this from the beginning. Obed-edom the Gittite took the ark when Israel was afraid of it. Uriah the Hittite would not sleep in his own bed while the ark was in a field. Ittai the Gittite went into exile with a king he had known a week. And here, at the lowest point of the reign, the people who show up are again from the edges.

18.title: The Death of Absalom
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.<sup>2</sup>And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you."<sup>3</sup>But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city."<sup>4</sup>The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands.<sup>5</sup>And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom.<sup>6</sup>So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.<sup>7</sup>And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men.<sup>8</sup>The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.<sup>9</sup>And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on.<sup>10</sup>And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."<sup>11</sup>Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt."<sup>12</sup>But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.'<sup>13</sup>On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof."<sup>14</sup>Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak.<sup>15</sup>And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.<sup>16</sup>Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them.<sup>17</sup>And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled every one to his own home.<sup>18</sup>Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's monument to this day.<sup>19</sup>Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and carry news to the king that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies."<sup>20</sup>And Joab said to him, "You are not to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you shall carry no news, because the king's son is dead."<sup>21</sup>Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab, and ran.<sup>22</sup>Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?"<sup>23</sup>"Come what may," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite.<sup>24</sup>Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone.<sup>25</sup>The watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." And he drew nearer and nearer.<sup>26</sup>The watchman saw another man running. And the watchman called to the gate and said, "See, another man running alone!" The king said, "He also brings news."<sup>27</sup>The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news."<sup>28</sup>Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well." And he bowed before the king with his face to the earth and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king."<sup>29</sup>And the king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was."<sup>30</sup>And the king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still.<sup>31</sup>And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! For the LORD has delivered you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you."<sup>32</sup>The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man."<sup>33</sup>And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
18.overview:
The professional is back. Two chapters ago he walked barefoot out of Jerusalem in tears; now the refugees who crossed the Jordan in the dark are an army in three divisions — and a third of it is commanded by the Philistine who arrived the week before last. His men refuse to let him fight, and their argument is cold and correct: the war is about one man, so he must not be on the field. Set that against 11:1, where kings went out to battle and he stayed home.

Then the order, and everything runs into it. He names all three commanders, gives it out loud at the gate while the army marches past, and the writer stops to say all the people heard. That is not carelessness — he has known Joab for forty years and watched him kill Abner at a gate, so he makes the order impossible to deny. And it is also a serious failure: he calls a man in his thirties who murdered his brother and took his father's throne the young man, and sends an army out to win a battle while asking it not to hurt the enemy. There is no way to obey both halves.

The forest devours more than the sword — broken ground, a national levy fighting professionals on ground the professionals chose, and twenty thousand dead where Ahithophel had offered one. Absalom is caught by the head in an oak. A nameless soldier refuses a thousand pieces of silver, quotes the king's order back at Joab with the names in it, and tells him to his face that he would have stood aloof — and Joab says he has no time for the conversation and does it himself.

Then two runners, and a king sitting between two gates with one question. Ahimaaz wanted to be the one who arrived; Joab twice tried to stop him for his own sake; he got there first and could not say it. And a father went up the stairs saying my son five times in one verse.
18.theology:
The order, and why it was public (v. 5). Three commanders named, given aloud at the gate with the whole army filing past, and the writer makes sure we notice: all the people heard. David knows exactly what Joab does with an inconvenient man, having watched him do it to Abner at the gate of Hebron, so he makes the order impossible to misremember or quietly not hear. It works, in a way — an ordinary infantryman can quote it back to the commander-in-chief with the list of names.

And it is also indefensible. The young man Absalom is a man in his thirties who murdered his brother, stole a kingdom, drove his father out of the capital and lay with his concubines on a roof before the nation. The men marching past are being asked to risk their lives against an enemy they have been publicly told not to hurt, and somebody has to win the battle. Every soldier on that road understands the arithmetic even if David will not. And for my sake does not claim it is right; it asks a favour.

The forest devoured more than the sword (v. 8). Ravines, scrub and rock east of the Jordan, and a national levy of farmers and townsmen called up in a hurry to fight professionals on the professionals' ground. Once such a line breaks, the terrain does the killing. The verb has an appetite in it — the same picture Abner used across a valley years before: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? (2:26). The bitter end is a wood full of dead Israelites, twenty thousand of them, where Ahithophel had offered one death.

What the text says about the oak (v. 9). His head caught fast — not his hair. What the writer did was stop the narrative four chapters earlier to weigh the hair, record that it was cut only when it grew too heavy to carry, and then leave it there without comment (14:25-26). He plants and does not point. Every reader makes the connection and the text still does not assert it. Suspended between heaven and earth, belonging to neither, held by nothing he chose — and the mule, the royal mount that Solomon will be crowned on (1 Kings 1:33), walks out from under him.

The best speech in the chapter has no name attached (vv. 12-13). Joab offers ten pieces of silver; the man says not for a thousand — which is not haggling but a statement that no sum makes this a category of thing he would do. Then the order quoted back with the names in it. And then the devastating half: there is nothing hidden from the king, and when the reckoning came, you yourself would have stood aloof. He has taken his commander's measure exactly and says so to his face, and he is right, because Joab has spent a career giving orders and letting other men carry the risk.

I will not waste time like this with you (v. 14). That is the entire answer, and it is not an argument. He does not dispute the order, deny it, or claim he did not hear it. Three javelins into a man hanging helpless — and then ten armour-bearers on a body that is already dead, which spreads the act across eleven men so that no one of them can be held responsible and Joab is one voice among many. The soldier said he would stand aloof; Joab arranges matters so that there is nobody to stand aloof from.

The case for Joab, and what is left of it. Absalom alive is a permanent rallying point, there would be another rising within five years, the kingdom is safer with him dead, and David is a father who cannot see it. All true, and Joab is not wrong about the politics. And he had a direct order from his king, given publicly, which he heard, and he killed the king's son. Third time: Abner in a city of refuge in peacetime, Absalom here, Amasa in two chapters with the same greeting and the same wound as Abner. Each time a real political argument, and each time Joab decides his judgment outranks the king's. David never punishes him — he cannot, and says so at 3:39, and is still saying it on his deathbed (1 Kings 2:5-6). And the other half of the man belongs in the record too: the moment the objective is dead he sounds the recall, and thousands who would have been hunted through that forest go home.

Two monuments in consecutive verses (vv. 17-18). A pit and a heap of stones is not a burial, and Israel knew what it meant: they raised one over Achan in the Valley of Achor (Josh. 7:26) and over the king of Ai (Josh. 8:29). It is the marker of a man who died under judgment, and his father a day's ride away was not asked. And then the pillar he had built for himself in the King's Valley while he was alive, called after his own name. The reason is the sad part: I have no son to keep my name in remembrance — and 14:27 said he had three sons, unnamed and never mentioned again. They must have died. Whatever else he was, he had buried his children. And the pillar is still the whole man: the chariot and fifty runners, the hair, the kisses at the gate, the tent on the roof in the sight of all Israel, and at the end a stone with his name on it so that people would keep saying it. His sister's memorial was a daughter he named after her. His own was a rock.

Joab's one kindness (v. 20). The man who has just put three javelins into that son will not let Ahimaaz be the one to report it, and he is entirely clear-eyed: he has seen what happens to the man who brings David that news — the Amalekite came to Ziklag with Saul's crown expecting a reward and was executed. So he sends a Cushite instead, a foreigner and probably a slave, who bows and goes without being asked whether he wants to. And when Ahimaaz insists, Joab calls him my son and tells him the truth: you will have no reward for the news.

He got there first and could not say it (v. 29). A small, very human study in wanting to be the one who arrives. He had been in a well and on the road, it was his war too, and the thought of somebody else running up to that gate was more than he could bear — and he had not thought about what he would say. He knows exactly what happened; Joab told him plainly. And he says he saw a commotion and does not know what it was. Joab knew he could not do it, which is why he tried twice to stop him.

The one question, and the pun (v. 29). Twenty thousand dead, the rebellion over, the kingdom his again — and he does not ask about the battle, the casualties, or whether Ittai survived. Is it well with the young man Absalom? Ahimaaz had shouted shalom, all is well; David asks whether there is shalom for Absalom. Same word, and the answer is no. Note too the line before it: he recognises a man from a distance by the way he runs, and instantly concludes that a good man brings good news. He has been sitting between two gates all day looking for any reason to believe the answer will be the one he wants.

The lament, counted (v. 33). My son five times in one verse, and three more in 19:4 — eight in two verses. And he says it as he went, out loud on a staircase where the guards can hear, which is what Joab throws at him in the next chapter. This is not the lament for Saul and Jonathan, which was a made thing written down and taught to Judah. Grief speaks like this: it circles, it does not develop, it says the one true thing again. And notice the words — not the rebel, not the man who would have killed him yesterday if the battle had gone the other way. My son. Every reason to hate him is true and none of it is in the room.

Would I had died instead of you. The oldest wish of love, and in David's mouth useless — he must have known it while he said it. Had he died in that forest, Absalom would have been a rebel king with his brother's blood on him and nothing changed in his heart, and the exchange would have purchased nothing. A father can want to take his son's place; he cannot do it, and he cannot make it mean anything if he does. Which is where the verse opens onto something larger, and the value depends on not flattening the difference.

A thousand years later another Son of David, in the same city, went out to die for rebels who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom from its rightful King and wanted a throne that was not theirs. He did not wish it; he did it. And the difference is not only that it happened but that it worked: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10). David on that staircase is not a picture of the cross. He is a picture of the longing the cross answers — and the one thing he wanted most was impossible for him and was not impossible for God.
18.examples:
Then: A king stood at a gate and told three commanders, in front of his whole army, to deal gently with the man who had taken his throne — and when a soldier found that man hanging helpless in a tree and refused a thousand pieces of silver to touch him, the commander-in-chief said he had no time for the conversation, walked over, and killed him with three javelins.

Now: Three things. The nameless soldier is the model, and what makes him one is not courage in the abstract: he had a clear word from his king, quoted accurately, and he could see exactly what the man pressuring him was like. You yourself would have stood aloof is the line to remember next time somebody powerful asks you to do the thing they will not put their own name to. Second, Ahimaaz — who wanted to be the one who arrived, ran faster than the man with the real message, and then could not open his mouth. Wanting to carry the news is not the same as being willing to say it, and the difference only shows up at the gate. And third, the lament, which does not need improving. Grief circles and repeats and finds no better words, and Scripture records five my sons in one verse without tidying a single one of them away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Forest Devoured More People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David musters and divides the army in three under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, and proposes to go out himself (vv. 1-2). The men refuse: you are worth ten thousand of us (v. 3). He stands at the gate as they march out, and gives one order in everybody's hearing: deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom. And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom (vv. 4-5). The battle is fought in the forest of Ephraim; twenty thousand fall; and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: He gives the order publicly and to all three commanders at once, which means he knows perfectly well that one of them will kill his son if he can. He is trying to make it impossible.
verseByVerse.examples: And the terrain does most of the killing. Ravines, thickets and broken ground turn a national muster into a rout, which is precisely what Hushai's plan exposed them to and Ahithophel's would have avoided.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds. And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you." But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city." The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands. And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom. So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim. And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men.
