The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.'

The professional is back.

Two chapters ago he was walking barefoot out of Jerusalem in tears. He has now had the time that Hushai bought him, and he uses every hour of it: the refugees who crossed the Jordan in the dark have been organised into an army with a command structure.

'And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite.'

Three divisions, and the third of them is commanded by the Philistine who arrived the week before last.

Ittai said wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, and David has given him a third of the army. That is what David thought of the speech.

'And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you." But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city."'

He offers to fight and his men refuse to let him.

Their argument is cold and correct. This war is about one man, exactly as Ahithophel said. If half the army dies it changes nothing; if David dies it is over. He is the objective, so he must not be on the field.

Set that against 11:1 — at the time when kings go out to battle... but David remained at Jerusalem. He stayed home then and should have gone. He offers to go now and is told to stay. Everything since has come out of the first of those.

'The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands.'

'And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom.'

Here is the order, and everything in the chapter runs into it.

Look at how he gives it. He names all three commanders. He gives it out loud, at the gate, while the whole army is marching past — and the writer stops to make sure we understand that: all the people heard.

That is not carelessness. David knows Joab. He has known him for forty years, and he knows exactly what Joab will do with a rebel prince hanging in a tree, because he watched him do the same thing to Abner at the gate of Hebron. So he makes the order public, in front of thousands of witnesses, so that it cannot be denied or misremembered or quietly not heard.

He is trying to make it impossible.

And a word about the order itself, because it is also a serious failure and both things are true.

He calls him the young man Absalom, which is what he called him when he brought him back from Geshur. Absalom is a man in his thirties who has murdered his brother, stolen a kingdom, driven his father out of the capital, and lain with his father's concubines on a roof in front of the nation.

And the king is sending an army out to fight a battle and telling it to be gentle with him.

The men marching past that gate are about to risk their lives against an enemy their king has publicly asked them not to hurt. There is no way to obey both halves of that. Somebody has to win this battle, and winning it means Absalom does not survive it, and every soldier on that road understands the arithmetic even if David will not.

For my sake. He is not even claiming it is right. He is asking for a personal favour.

'So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.'

Against Israel. The writer will not soften what this is.

'And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men.'

Twenty thousand dead.

Now recall what Ahithophel offered: twelve thousand men, one night, one death, and the nation brought home like a bride. This is the alternative that was chosen instead of it.

'The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.'

There is the sentence, and it is one of the strangest in the book.

The forest devoured more people that day than the sword.

The country east of the Jordan is broken ground — ravines, gullies, thick scrub, rocks, and trees. It is the worst possible terrain for a large army that does not know it, and Absalom's national muster is exactly that: farmers and townsmen from Dan to Beersheba, called up in a hurry, fighting professionals on ground the professionals chose.

Once a line like that breaks, men run into a forest in panic, and the forest kills them. They fall into ravines, they are lost, they are hunted down in ones and twos. More died that way than in the fighting.

And the writer uses a verb with an appetite in it. The forest devoured them. It is the same picture Abner used when he called across a valley years ago — shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? (2:26).

The bitter end is a wood full of dead Israelites.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — The King's Command Concerning You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom rides into the branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on (v. 9). A soldier reports it and Joab asks why he did not kill him on the spot (vv. 10-11). The man's answer is the finest speech in the chapter: even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not put out my hand against the king's son... And if I had dealt treacherously against his life, then you yourself would have stood aloof (vv. 12-13). Joab takes three javelins and thrusts them into Absalom's heart, and ten armour-bearers finish him (vv. 14-15). The trumpet sounds and the pursuit stops (v. 16). They throw the body into a pit in the forest and raise a great heap of stones (v. 17). And the writer notes the pillar Absalom had set up for himself in his lifetime, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance" (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The text says his head caught, not his hair. What the writer did was weigh the hair four chapters ago and record that it was cut only when it grew too heavy to carry, and then leave it there. He plants and does not point.
verseByVerse.examples: And two monuments close the section. Absalom built one for himself because he had no son left to remember him; the army built the other, a heap of stones over a pit, which is what Israel raised over Achan and over the king of Ai.

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on. And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak." Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt." But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.' On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof." Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak. And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him. Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them. And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled every one to his own home. Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's monument to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on.'

Say what the text says, and then say what the writer did with it.

The text says his head caught fast in the oak. It does not say his hair. What it says is that a man riding a mule at speed under low branches was caught by the head, and the animal kept going, and he was left hanging.

And what the writer did was this. Four chapters ago he stopped the narrative to describe Absalom's beauty, and then his hair — how he cut it once a year, only when it grew too heavy to carry, and weighed it, and the figure was known (14:25-26). He recorded it and moved on and made no point of it whatever.

Now a man is hanging by the head in a tree.

The writer does not join them up. He has never joined anything up in this book; he plants things and waits. Every reader makes the connection, and the connection is almost certainly intended, and the text still does not assert it.

Suspended between heaven and earth. That is the phrase, and it is exact in more than one way. He is between the two, belonging to neither, held by nothing he chose, and the animal he was riding has gone on without him.

The mule is worth a note too. It is the royal mount — Solomon will be put on David's own mule to be proclaimed king (1 Kings 1:33). Absalom is riding the animal of a king, and it walks out from under him.

'And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."'

'Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt."'

Joab's reaction is instant, and it tells you he had already decided.

He does not ask whether the man is sure, or where the tree is, or what the king's order was. He asks why the soldier did not kill him, and he names a price on the spot — ten shekels and a belt, which was a mark of honour.

'But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not put out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.'"'

Here is the best speech in the chapter, and it is made by a man with no name.

Take the first half. Joab offers ten pieces of silver; the man says he would not do it for a thousand. He is not haggling and he is not being pious. He is saying that the number is not the category — that there is no sum which turns this into a thing he would do.

And the reason he gives is the king's order, quoted back at Joab, with the names in it: the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai.

In our hearing. There it is. That is why David gave the order at the gate in front of the whole army. An ordinary soldier is now able to quote it, accurately, with the list of commanders, to the commander-in-chief.

'"On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof."'

And the second half is even better, and it is devastating.

He tells Joab exactly what would have happened. The king finds out everything — there is nothing hidden from the king — and when he did, and when there was a reckoning for the death of his son, Joab would have stood aloof.

He would have stepped back. He would have let the soldier hang for it alone. He would not have said a word about the ten pieces of silver.

The man has taken his commander's measure precisely and says so to his face, and he is right, because that is exactly what Joab is like. He has spent his career giving orders and letting other people carry the risk, and this soldier has watched him do it.

So here is what the writer has put in front of us. A nameless infantryman in a wood, offered money by the most powerful soldier in Israel, refuses on the ground that the king said so — and the commander-in-chief, hearing it, goes and does the thing himself.

'Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak.'

I will not waste time like this with you.

That is his entire answer to the argument, and it is not an argument. He does not dispute the order, deny it, or claim he did not hear it. He says he has no time for the conversation, and walks off to do it.

Three javelins into the heart of a man hanging helpless in a tree.

'And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.'

Then ten more.

He was already dead, or dying, with three javelins in his chest. Joab has his own armour-bearers finish the body — which spreads the act across eleven men, so that no single one of them can be held responsible and Joab himself is one voice among many.

The soldier in verse 13 said Joab would stand aloof. Ten verses later Joab arranges matters so that there is nobody to stand aloof from.

Now, the case for Joab has to be put, because it is not nothing. Absalom alive is a permanent rallying point; there would be another rebellion inside five years; the kingdom is safer with him dead; and David is a father who cannot see it. Every bit of that is true, and Joab is thinking about the kingdom, and he is not wrong about the politics.

And he had a direct order from his king, given publicly, which he heard, and he disobeyed it and killed the king's son.

This is the third time. Abner at the gate of Hebron, in peacetime, in a city of refuge. Absalom here. Amasa in two chapters, with the same greeting and the same wound as Abner. Each time there is a real political argument for it, and each time Joab is the one who decides that his judgment outranks the king's.

David never punishes him. He cannot: he needs him, and he says so at 3:39 — these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I — and he is still saying it on his deathbed forty years later, when he tells Solomon to deal with what he could not (1 Kings 2:5-6).

'Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them.'

And having killed him, Joab immediately stops the battle.

That is the other half of the man, and it should be recorded. The moment the objective is dead he sounds the recall, and thousands of Israelites who would have been hunted through that forest for the rest of the day go home. He did the same thing at Gibeon when Abner called across the valley.

'And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled every one to his own home.'

A pit in a wood and a pile of rocks.

That is not a burial; it is a disposal, and Israel knew exactly what it meant. Achan was stoned in the Valley of Achor and they raised over him a great heap of stones (Josh. 7:26). The king of Ai was hanged, and thrown at the gate, and a great heap of stones raised over him (Josh. 8:29). The heap is the marker of a man who died under judgment.

He is not carried back to Jerusalem. He is not put in a tomb. His father is a day's ride away and is not asked.

'Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's monument to this day.'

And the writer, having buried him under a heap of stones in a forest, tells us about the monument he built for himself.

The placing is deliberate and it is merciless. Two memorials, in consecutive verses: the one he raised, and the one the army raised.

Look at what is in it.

He took and set up for himself. He commissioned his own monument, in the King's Valley, near the capital, while he was alive.

He called the pillar after his own name. He named it Absalom.

And the reason: I have no son to keep my name in remembrance.

Which is a strange thing to read, because four chapters ago the writer told us he had three sons and a daughter (14:27). The sons are not named there, and they are not mentioned again, and the plain sense of this verse is that they died. Three children buried, and one daughter left, and a man building a stone tower with his own name on it because there will be nobody after him.

Pause there before passing any verdict on him. Whatever else he was, he had lost his children.

And the pillar is still the whole man. He spent his life on being seen — the chariot and the fifty runners, the hair, the kisses at the gate, the tent on the roof in the sight of all Israel. The last thing recorded about him is that he put up a stone with his name on it so that people would keep saying it.

His sister's memorial was a daughter he named after her. His own was a rock.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–32 — Is It Well with the Young Man Absalom?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahimaaz asks to run with the news and Joab refuses: you are not to carry news today... because the king's son is dead (vv. 19-20). A Cushite is sent instead. Ahimaaz asks again, is told why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?, insists, and outruns him (vv. 21-23). David is sitting between the two gates, and the watchman calls the runners in one at a time (vv. 24-27). Ahimaaz arrives shouting all is well, and then, asked the only question David cares about, retreats into I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was (vv. 28-30). The Cushite comes and gives the news in the accepted formula: may the enemies of my lord the king... be like that young man (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The king asks one question and asks it twice, and it is not about the battle. Is it well with the young man Absalom? Twenty thousand men are dead in a forest and he wants to know about one of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Ahimaaz wanted to be the one who ran, and Joab — who is not a sentimental man — twice tried to stop him for his own sake. He arrived first with nothing to say, and when the question came he could not say it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and carry news to the king that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies." And Joab said to him, "You are not to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you shall carry no news, because the king's son is dead." Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab, and ran. Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?" "Come what may," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite. Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone. The watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." And he drew nearer and nearer. The watchman saw another man running. And the watchman called to the gate and said, "See, another man running alone!" The king said, "He also brings news." The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news." Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well." And he bowed before the king with his face to the earth and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king." And the king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was." And the king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still. And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! For the LORD has delivered you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you." The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and carry news to the king that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies."'

Ahimaaz wants to run.

This is the young man who spent a day in a well at Bahurim under a covering of grain, and he has earned the right to ask. Note how he phrases the message: the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies. That is a true sentence and it is a victory report, and it says nothing about a body in a pit.

'And Joab said to him, "You are not to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you shall carry no news, because the king's son is dead."'

And Joab — who has just put three javelins into that son — will not let this young man be the one to say so.

It is one of the few kind things Joab does in this book, and it is entirely clear-eyed. He knows what happens to the man who brings David that particular piece of news. He has seen it: the Amalekite who came to Ziklag with Saul's crown, expecting a reward, was executed on the spot.

The king's son is dead. Joab names it plainly to Ahimaaz, and it is the only time he says it.

'Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab, and ran.'

So he sends a foreigner instead. A Cushite is a man from south of Egypt, probably a slave or a mercenary, and he is expendable in a way the son of the high priest is not.

He bows and goes without a word. He was not asked whether he wanted to.

'Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?"'

He asks a second time, and Joab tries again to talk him out of it, and calls him my son while doing it.

You will have no reward for the news. Joab is being blunt with him: there is nothing in this for you. Nobody is going to thank you. Whatever it is you think you are running towards, it is not there.

'"Come what may," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite.'

And he goes anyway, and he is faster, and he takes the flat route by the Jordan valley — longer and quicker — and overtakes the man who left first.

It is a small and very human study, this. He wants to be the one who arrives. He has been in a well and on the road and he is young and fast and it has been his war too, and the thought of somebody else running up to the gate is more than he can bear.

He has not thought about what he will say when he gets there.

'Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone.'

The king is sitting in the gateway, between the inner and outer gates, where he cannot be seen from the field and cannot see anything himself. He has been there all day.

'The watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." And he drew nearer and nearer.'

He is reading the runner. A man alone is a messenger; men in numbers would be a rout.

He is doing what any commander does, and it is not what he is thinking about.

'The watchman saw another man running. And the watchman called to the gate and said, "See, another man running alone!" The king said, "He also brings news."'

'The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news."'

And that line is heartbreaking, because of what is behind it.

He recognises a man by the way he runs, from a distance, off a watchman's description. He knows Ahimaaz. And he immediately draws the conclusion he wants: a good man brings good news.

He is telling himself something. He has been sitting between two gates all day with one question in his head, and he is looking for any reason at all to believe the answer will be the one he wants.

'Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well." And he bowed before the king with his face to the earth and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king."'

He shouts it before he arrives: all is well. Peace. Shalom.

And then the formal report, and it is genuinely good theology — blessed be the LORD, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against you. He gives the credit to God and he does not say a word that is untrue.

'And the king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?"'

There is the only question David has.

Twenty thousand men are dead in a forest. The rebellion is over, the kingdom is his again, and the runner has just told him God delivered him from his enemies.

Is it well with the young man Absalom?

He does not ask about the battle. He does not ask about Joab, or the casualties, or whether Ittai survived, or how many of the twenty thousand were his own. He asks about one man, and he calls him what he has always called him.

And there is a terrible pun in the Hebrew that a reader in English will miss. Ahimaaz shouted shalom — all is well. David asks whether there is shalom for Absalom. The same word, and the answer is no.

'Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was."'

He cannot do it.

He ran the whole way to be the man who arrived, and Joab told him twice not to, and here is the reason. The king asked the one question, and this young man — who watched the whole thing, who knows exactly what happened, who was told plainly by Joab that the king's son is dead — says he saw a commotion and does not know what it was.

It is a lie, and it is entirely understandable, and anybody who has ever had to tell somebody something like that will recognise the moment precisely. He got there first and could not say it.

Joab knew he could not. That is why he tried to stop him.

'The king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still.'

Four words, and the young man is put to one side to wait, and there is nothing else said to him.

'And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! For the LORD has delivered you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you."'

The foreigner arrives second and opens the same way.

'The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man."'

He says it.

He does not say he is dead, because that is not how such news was delivered; he uses the accepted formula, which is a wish rather than a report. May all your enemies be like that young man.

It is meant kindly, in its way. It is also the plainest possible answer, and the phrase that young man gives David back his own words.

The Cushite thinks he is bringing good news. He has been on the road for hours and has no idea what he is walking into; he was sent by a commander who did not explain, to a king he does not know, and he says the correct thing in the correct form and expects to be thanked.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
verseByVerse.theology: My son, five times in one verse, and three more in the next chapter. It is not rhetoric. It is the way grief actually speaks — the same words over and over, because there is nowhere else to go with them.
verseByVerse.examples: Would I had died instead of you. It is the wish of every love that has ever outlived its object, and in David's mouth it is useless: he could not have died for Absalom and changed anything. A thousand years later a Son of David did die instead of rebels who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom away from him, and that death was not useless.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept.'

He goes up the stairs.

The chamber over the gate is a small room above the gateway, and it is the nearest thing to privacy in a fortified town. He walks away from the messenger without a word to him, climbs the stairs, and breaks.

'And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"'

As he went. He is saying it on the stairs, out loud, where the guards at the gate can hear every word of it. That detail matters, and Joab is going to throw it at him in the next chapter.

Now count.

My son — five times in one verse. Absalom — three times. And in the next chapter, still going: O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son! (19:4). Eight times in two verses he says my son.

That is not rhetoric and it is not composition. This is not the lament for Saul and Jonathan, which was a made thing, a poem written down and taught to the people of Judah. This is a man on a staircase saying the same two words over and over because there is nowhere else for them to go.

Grief speaks like this. It circles. It does not develop, or find better language, or move on to a second point. It says the one true thing again, and then again.

And notice what the words are.

Not the rebel. Not Absalom the son of Maacah, which is how the book introduced him. Not the man who murdered Amnon, or drove his father out of Jerusalem, or lay with his concubines on the roof in front of the nation, or would have killed him yesterday if the battle had gone the other way.

My son.

Every reason to hate him is true, and none of it is in the room. That is what a father is.

'"Would I had died instead of you."'

There is the sentence.

It is the oldest wish of love and everyone who has lost someone has said some version of it. Let it have been me. Take me and give him back.

And in David's mouth it is useless, and he must have known it even while he said it. He could not have died instead of Absalom. If he had died in that forest, Absalom would have been a rebel king with his brother's blood on him and nothing changed in his heart, and the exchange would have purchased nothing at all. A father can want to take his son's place; he cannot actually do it, and he cannot make it mean anything if he does.

Which is the point at which this verse opens onto something larger, and it should be said carefully, because the value of it depends on not flattening the difference.

A thousand years later another Son of David, in the same city, went out to die for rebels — people who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom away from its rightful King, who wanted a throne that was not theirs, who were his enemies by their own choice and in their own strength.

He did not wish it. He did it.

And the difference is not only that his death happened; it is that his death worked. David's substitution would have been a gesture that saved nobody. Christ's substitution actually accomplished the thing — while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10). The rebels came home.

So David on that staircase is not a picture of the cross. He is a picture of the longing that the cross answers: a father who wanted to die in his son's place and could not, crying out over a kingdom he had won and a boy he had lost.

The one thing he wanted most in the world was impossible for him. It was not impossible for God.

19.title: The Return of the King
19.text: <sup>1</sup>It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."<sup>2</sup>So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son."<sup>3</sup>And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle.<sup>4</sup>The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!"<sup>5</sup>Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines,<sup>6</sup>because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now."<sup>8</sup>Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his own home.<sup>9</sup>And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom.<sup>10</sup>But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"<sup>11</sup>And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king?<sup>12</sup>You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?'<sup>13</sup>And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'"<sup>14</sup>And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants."<sup>15</sup>So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring the king over the Jordan.<sup>16</sup>And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David.<sup>17</sup>And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king,<sup>18</sup>and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan,<sup>19</sup>and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart.<sup>20</sup>For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king."<sup>21</sup>Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"<sup>22</sup>But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?"<sup>23</sup>And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath.<sup>24</sup>And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety.<sup>25</sup>And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"<sup>26</sup>He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame.<sup>27</sup>He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you.<sup>28</sup>For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?"<sup>29</sup>And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."<sup>30</sup>And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."<sup>31</sup>Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan.<sup>32</sup>Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.<sup>33</sup>And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem."<sup>34</sup>But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?<sup>35</sup>I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?<sup>36</sup>Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?<sup>37</sup>Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."<sup>38</sup>And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you."<sup>39</sup>Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home.<sup>40</sup>The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.<sup>41</sup>Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"<sup>42</sup>All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?"<sup>43</sup>And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
19.overview:
The men who won the battle are creeping back through the gate the way a beaten army comes home, because the king they saved is upstairs weeping for the man they killed. Nobody has said a word to them; no word was needed. And Joab walks in and says the hardest thing anybody says to David in the whole book — every clause of it true, from the man who manufactured the grief he is ordering the king to stop. You love those who hate you and hate those who love you is unfair about David's heart and entirely fair about what his behaviour has communicated, and Joab says out loud the arithmetic every soldier in that army has already done.

And David gets up and does it. A king spoken to like that by a subordinate who disobeyed a public order and killed his son does not answer back — he walks down and sits in the gate where the army can see him. The grief has not stopped; it has simply been put behind a duty he owes to other people.

Then three men on the road. Shimei gets to the river first with a thousand Benjaminites and a proper confession he has already begun trading on, and David swears he will not die — an oath he remembers on his deathbed when he tells Solomon to kill him anyway. Mephibosheth arrives unwashed and untrimmed since the day the king left, which settles chapter 16 completely, and David splits the estate rather than admit he judged carelessly — and the man who was robbed says let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home.

And Barzillai, eighty years old, gives one of the finest speeches in the Old Testament about being old, asks for nothing but a grave beside his parents, and sends his son instead. Then Israel and Judah start an argument about who got to escort the king across a river, and the writer ends the chapter by noting only which side shouted louder.
19.theology:
Stealing into the city (v. 3). They fought a national levy in broken country and beat it, twenty thousand of the enemy are dead, and they saved the throne — and they come home in ones and twos, not meeting anyone's eye. The lament was said out loud on a staircase and the whole army heard it.

Joab is right, and Joab is the reason (vv. 5-6). He was told publicly, at the gate, in front of the army, to deal gently with Absalom, and he put three javelins into him. Now he stands in the room ordering the king to stop grieving. And the list he opens with is accurate — your sons and your daughters and your wives and your concubines — because Absalom had already taken ten of those women on a roof and was not going to spare the rest. You love those who hate you is unfair as a statement about David's heart and exact as a description of what his behaviour has told everyone outside the room, and Joab is careful to claim only the second. And then the knife: every man in that army had done the same arithmetic and none would ever have said it.

The ultimatum is insolence and it is true (v. 7). An army that believes its king despises it does not stay, and if those men walk out tonight David has won a battle and lost a kingdom in the same week. Joab is telling him the greatest disaster of his life is four hours away.

And the king gets up (v. 8). Spoken to like that by the man who murdered his son, he does not answer back, defend himself, or have him removed. Nothing here says the grief is over — it will not be over for the rest of his life. What has happened is that a duty owed to other people has been put in front of what he wants to do, which is what the office requires and what grief makes nearly impossible. The New Testament never asks anybody to stop grieving; it asks them not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:13). The grief stays. It does not get to run the household.

Amasa, and what it costs (v. 13). The man who commanded the rebel army in the forest of Ephraim is offered the royal command, permanently, under oath. It is a masterstroke — nothing reassures defeated rebels faster than seeing their own general promoted rather than hanged — and it is personal, because Joab killed his son against a direct order and then humiliated him in his own room, and this is the one thing David can do about it. It is also Amasa's death warrant. Joab does not lose positions; he removes the men who hold them.

Shimei, and the oath David did not keep (vv. 22-23). He hurried, and brought a thousand men of Saul's tribe, because no king executes a man standing in front of a thousand of his own tribesmen on the first day of a reconciliation. His confession is proper and unverifiable, and the sentence he attaches to it — the first of all the house of Joseph to come down — shows him already trading. And David's answer is magnificent: a reign that resumes with a hanging at the river has told the whole country what to expect, and a secure man does not need to make an example of anybody. He swears it. Then, forty years later, dying, he names this very day to Solomon and says do not hold him guiltless... bring his gray head down with blood (1 Kings 2:8-9). No reading of that makes it admirable. The defences offered — that Shimei's later conduct forfeited protection, that the oath bound David personally and not the crown — are not worthless, and they amount to keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for somebody else to break its substance. The book records both scenes and reconciles neither.

Mephibosheth does not have to say a word (v. 24). Unwashed, untrimmed, in the same clothes since the morning David walked out — mourning kept for weeks, alone, in a city under Absalom's control, visible to anybody who cared to look. And his explanation turns on the one fact everybody knew: he cannot walk. He asked Ziba to saddle a donkey, and Ziba took two of them, loaded with food, and went alone and got there first. The lameness that made him harmless in chapter 9 is what made him helpless here.

The ruling is a bad one (v. 29). The facts are not in doubt: Mephibosheth's account explains everything and Ziba's required a crippled pensioner with no faction and no army to be plausibly expecting a crown during a coup by David's own son. Here at last is the hearing, and the verdict splits the land between the liar and the man he lied about. Why speak any more of your affairs? — he does not want to hear it, because revisiting the judgment means admitting he made it carelessly. This is the second failure in this book of the sentence that summarised his whole reign (8:15); the first was Tamar.

Let him take it all (v. 30). The last thing Mephibosheth says in Scripture, from a man slandered, robbed, and half-vindicated by a king who will not look properly at the evidence. Nobody is obliged to believe he meant it — and look at the man saying it: he kept mourning for weeks when nobody was watching and there was no advantage in it, walked in with no accusation prepared, said his family deserved death and had been given a table instead, and then gave up what was left. He never asked for the land in chapter 9 either.

Barzillai's inventory (vv. 34-35). Its power is the honesty. Three questions, each naming something gone: judgment, taste, and music — and the last is the saddest, because David is a musician and the best thing about his table is the thing Barzillai can no longer enjoy. He does not pretend to be too humble for a court, or make a show of declining an honour, or claim he is more useful at home. He gives a bleak account of what age has taken and concludes the offer would be wasted on him. Most people would take the seat and pretend to enjoy the singing.

Why should your servant be an added burden? (v. 35). He earned that place — he fed the king's army when it was starving, at eighty, at the risk of everything he owned, and nobody in Israel would have questioned his right to it. And he can see that what he would actually be in Jerusalem is an old man who needs looking after, and he would rather not be that. What he asks for is a grave beside his parents. Then, having asked nothing for himself, he asks for somebody else: here is your servant Chimham. He cannot use the offer; the next generation can. Four centuries later, when Jerusalem has fallen and the last Judeans flee to Egypt, they stop at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem (Jer. 41:17) — the name outlasted the kingdom. And on his deathbed David's list of instructions includes one that is not about revenge: deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai... for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother (1 Kings 2:7). He never forgot the bedding.

Both sides have a real point (vv. 41-43). Judah is the king's own tribe. Israel is ten-elevenths of the nation and did raise the question first — verses 9-10 recorded the north arguing about it while Judah said nothing and David had to send the priests to prod them. Neither side is lying and neither is listening. And note the verb Israel chooses: Judah stole the king, the same word used of Absalom stealing their hearts (15:6).

What the writer chose to record (v. 43). Not who was right, not what the king decided — David says nothing at all in this exchange. Only that Judah shouted louder. And the next verse is a trumpet and we have no portion in David... every man to his tents, O Israel! (20:1). Sheba's revolt comes straight out of this quarrel and is over in a chapter. The quarrel is not: two generations later the ten tribes walk out of Rehoboam's assembly saying the same words — what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16) — and the kingdom never comes back together. A squabble at a river crossing about who got to escort the king over the water is the first visible crack in the thing that finally breaks Israel in half. Every large division starts somewhere this size.
19.examples:
Then: An eighty-year-old man who had fed a king's starving army at his own expense and at the risk of everything he owned was offered a permanent place at the royal table — and turned it down on the grounds that he could no longer taste food or enjoy music, asked only to be buried near his parents, and sent his son in his place.

Now: Three things. Joab is the study in receiving a true rebuke from somebody with no right to give it: the man had disobeyed a public order and killed the king's son, and he was still correct, and David got up and did what he said. Whether the person telling you is entitled to is a separate question from whether they are right, and most of us answer the first to avoid the second. Barzillai is the study in knowing what you can no longer use — not false modesty, an honest inventory, and then asking for the next generation instead of yourself. And the quarrel at the end is the warning. Nobody in it was lying. It was about precedence, and who was asked first, and whose relative he was, and it was louder on one side — and the sentence shouted in that argument is the sentence that split the kingdom permanently two generations later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — You Have Today Covered with Shame the Faces of All Your Servants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Word reaches Joab that the king is weeping for Absalom, and the victory was turned into mourning for all the people, who steal into the city as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle (vv. 1-3). Joab comes in and says it: you have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life... because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. You have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you (vv. 5-6). And the ultimatum: go out and speak kindly to them, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night (v. 7). So the king sits in the gate (v. 8). Then he works to bring Judah back, offering Amasa the command in place of Joab (vv. 9-15).
verseByVerse.theology: It is brutal, and every word of it is true, and it comes from the man who created the grief he is ordering the king to stop. Both stand. This is the pattern of Joab from 10:12 onward: he says the right thing and he is the reason it needs saying.
verseByVerse.examples: And David does it. A king submits to a general who disobeyed a public order and killed his son, gets up, and goes and sits where the army can see him — because the men who saved his kingdom are creeping home like deserters.

verseByVerse.quote: It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom." So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son." And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle. The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!" Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines, because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased. Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now." Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his own home. And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom. But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?" And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king? You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?' And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'" And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants." So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring the king over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom." So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son."'

The lament on the staircase was said out loud, and now the whole army knows.

'And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle.'

That is a terrible sentence, and it is exact.

These men won. They fought a national levy in broken country and beat it, and twenty thousand of the enemy are dead, and they saved the throne. And they are coming back through the gate the way a beaten army comes home — quietly, in ones and twos, not meeting anybody's eye, because the king they did it for is upstairs crying over the man they killed.

Nobody has said a word to them. That is the whole problem: no word was needed.

'The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!"'

He is still saying it. Five times in the last verse of chapter 18 and three more here — eight my sons across two verses.

'Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines,"'

Joab walks in and says the hardest thing anybody says to David in the whole book.

Before hearing it out, note who is speaking. This is the man who was told publicly, at the gate, in front of the whole army, to deal gently with Absalom, and who put three javelins into him and had ten armour-bearers finish the body.

Joab manufactured this grief. He is now standing in the room ordering the king to stop it.

And every word he says is true.

Look at the list he begins with: your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines. He is naming what would have happened if the battle had gone the other way, and he is right. Absalom had already taken ten of those concubines on a roof; he was not going to spare the rest of the household.

'"because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased."'

There is the sentence, and it goes straight through.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you.

It is unfair as a statement about David's heart, and it is entirely fair as a description of what his behaviour has communicated. That is a distinction worth keeping, because it is the whole of Joab's argument. He is not claiming to know what the king feels. He is telling him what everyone outside that room has been given to understand.

And then the knife: if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased.

Every man in that army has just worked out the same arithmetic and none of them would ever have said it. Joab says it.

'"Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now."'

And then an ultimatum, sworn in the name of God, delivered by a general to his king.

It is insolence, and it is also true. An army that believes its king despises it does not stay, and if those men walk out tonight, David has won a battle and lost a kingdom in the same week. Joab is telling him that the greatest disaster of his life is currently about four hours away.

'Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king.'

The king gets up and does it.

That is remarkable and it should not be passed over. He has been spoken to like that by a subordinate who has just murdered his son, and he does not answer back, does not defend himself, and does not have him removed. He gets up, walks down, and sits in the gate where every man coming in can see him.

It is not a change of feeling. Nothing in this verse says the grief is over; it will not be over for the rest of his life. What has happened is that he has put the duty he owes to other people in front of what he wants to do, which is what the office requires and what grief makes nearly impossible.

The New Testament does not ask anybody to stop grieving. It asks them not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:13). The grief stays; it does not get to run the household.

'Now Israel had fled every man to his own home. And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom."'

'"But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"'

The country is now embarrassed and arguing about who will say so first.

They anointed Absalom. He is dead in a pit under a heap of stones. And nobody wants to be the first man to propose fetching David, because everyone in that conversation backed the other side six weeks ago.

'And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house?'"'

'"You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?"'

He uses the priests again — the same two men who ran his intelligence during the flight.

And he uses the phrase the elders of Israel used to him at Hebron when they made him king over all twelve tribes: we are your bone and your flesh (5:1). He is quoting the country's own words about him back to his own tribe.

Judah is the awkward case. Absalom launched the revolt from Hebron, which is Judah's own town, and the tribe is now the most compromised in Israel and the most nervous.

'"And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'"'

Here is David finally moving against Joab, and it is a considerable moment.

Amasa commanded the rebel army. He is the man who led the force that killed twenty thousand Israelites in the forest of Ephraim, and David is offering him the command of the royal army, permanently, sworn with an oath.

Two things are going on at once. It is a political masterstroke: nothing would reassure the defeated rebels faster than seeing their own general promoted rather than executed. And it is personal. Joab killed his son against a direct order and then humiliated him in his own room, and David cannot punish him, and this is the one thing he can do.

He is also, though he does not know it, signing Amasa's death warrant. Joab does not lose positions; he removes the men who hold them, and the reader who remembers Abner at the gate of Hebron knows exactly how chapter 20 ends.

'And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants." So the king came back to the Jordan.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — Shall Anyone Be Put to Death in Israel This Day?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shimei comes down with a thousand Benjaminites and falls at the king's feet: let not my lord hold me guilty... for your servant knows that I have sinned (vv. 16-20). Abishai wants his head; David refuses: shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel? (vv. 21-22). Then Mephibosheth, who had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back safely (v. 24), explains that Ziba deceived him and slandered him (vv. 25-27). David's ruling is to divide the land between them, and Mephibosheth answers: oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The pardon is genuine in the moment and it does not hold. On his deathbed David tells Solomon to deal with Shimei, and names this very day (1 Kings 2:8-9). The book records both and reconciles neither.
verseByVerse.examples: And Mephibosheth's appearance settles the facts of chapter 16 completely — and David does not reverse his judgment. He splits the estate, which is half-justice from the king of 8:15, and the man who was wronged does not argue. He says the only thing that matters to him is that the king is home.

verseByVerse.quote: And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David. And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king, and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan, and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart. For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king." Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?" But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?" And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath. And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety. And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?" He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame. He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you. For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?" And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land." And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David.'

The man who threw stones is at the river first.

He hurried, and the writer says so, and the reason is arithmetic. He cursed the LORD's anointed in public in front of witnesses at a moment when he was sure David was finished, and David is not finished, and he has perhaps a day to get in front of him before somebody else raises the subject.

'And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of Saul's house, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king,'

He brings a thousand men of Saul's own tribe with him, which is not repentance; it is a delegation. A king does not execute a man standing in front of a thousand of his own tribesmen on the first day of a reconciliation.

And Ziba is there too, with his whole household, having done extremely well out of the last three weeks.

'and they crossed the ford to carry over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan,'

'and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart."'

'"For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king."'

He says the right words and he says them first, and both of those are the point.

Your servant knows that I have sinned is a proper confession, and there is no way to tell from the outside whether he means it. What can be observed is the sentence he attaches to it: the first of all the house of Joseph to come down.

He is already trading. Note the credit, he is saying. I got here before the northern tribes.

'Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"'

Abishai, for the third time in the book, offers to kill somebody.

Saul asleep at Hachilah. Shimei on the hillside. Shimei at the Jordan. He is a brave and useful man who has exactly one idea, and note that he is quoting the law at David this time: cursing the LORD's anointed was a capital matter, and Abishai is not simply being bloodthirsty. He has a case.

'But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?"'

The answer is magnificent, and it will not survive the book.

Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day?

The reasoning is that this is the day the kingdom came back. Executions do not belong in it. A reign that resumes with a hanging at the river is a reign that has told the whole country what to expect, and David will not start that way.

Do I not know that I am this day king over Israel? A secure man does not need to make an example of anybody. It is the same instinct that spared Saul twice.

'And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath.'

He swears it. That is the strongest form of undertaking available to him.

And now the honest difficulty, which should not be smoothed over, because a reader who knows the rest will raise it.

Forty years later, dying, David gives Solomon his final instructions, and Shimei is on the list: and there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera... he cursed me with a grievous curse on the day I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, "I will not put you to death with the sword." Now therefore do not hold him guiltless... bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol (1 Kings 2:8-9).

He remembers the oath. He remembers this exact day. And he tells his son to do what he promised not to do himself.

There is no reading of that which makes it admirable. Some have argued that Shimei's later conduct forfeited the protection, and that the oath bound David personally and not the crown, and that a king has a duty to justice as well as to his word. Those arguments exist and they are not worthless. They also amount to keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for its substance to be broken by somebody else.

The book records both scenes and does not reconcile them, which is what it does with David throughout. The mercy at the Jordan is real. The deathbed instruction is real. He was capable of both.

'And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back safely.'

Here comes the man Ziba lied about, and he does not have to say a word.

Look at him. He has not washed, not trimmed his beard, not changed his clothes, since the morning David walked out of Jerusalem. Those are the signs of mourning, and he has kept them for weeks, alone, in a city under Absalom's control, where every day of it was visible to anybody who cared to look.

The man Ziba described was sitting in Jerusalem waiting to be given his grandfather's kingdom. This man has been in mourning for the king since the day he left.

'And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"'

The king asks the question, and there is an edge on it.

'He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame."'

The answer is complete, and it turns on the one fact everybody knew.

He cannot walk. He asked Ziba to saddle a donkey so that he could follow the king, and Ziba took the donkeys — two of them, loaded with food — and went alone, and got there first, and told a story.

The lameness that made him harmless in chapter 9 is what made him helpless here. He could not follow on foot and he could not saddle an animal himself.

'"He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you."'

'"For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?"'

And that is the argument he makes, and it is not a demand for justice.

He says his whole family should have been executed as a matter of course when David took the throne, and instead he was given a seat at the king's table for twenty years. Against that, he says, what claim could he possibly press?

'And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."'

The king's ruling is a bad one, and it should be said plainly.

The facts are not in doubt. Mephibosheth's account explains everything and Ziba's does not. Ziba's story required a crippled pensioner with no faction and no army to be plausibly expecting the tribes of Israel to crown him during a coup by David's own son, and David gave him an estate for it in one sentence, without a hearing.

Here is the hearing, and the verdict is to split the land between the liar and the man he lied about.

Why speak any more of your affairs? He does not want to hear it. He is tired, and he has a kingdom to reassemble, and revisiting the judgment means admitting he made it carelessly in the first place.

This is the king of whom it was written that he administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15), and this is the second time in this book that the sentence has failed — first with Tamar, now here.

'And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."'

And there is the last thing Mephibosheth ever says in Scripture, and it is the best line in the chapter.

Let him take it all.

He has been slandered, robbed of his inheritance, and now half-vindicated by a king who will not look properly at the evidence. And his answer is that Ziba can have the whole estate, because the king is home.

Nobody is obliged to believe he meant it. But look at the man who says it. He kept mourning for weeks when nobody was watching and there was no advantage in it. He walked into that room without a single accusation prepared. He said his family deserved death and had been given a table instead. And when he was half-robbed by the man who had shown him that kindness, he gave up the other half.

He never asked for the land in the first place. He asked for nothing in chapter 9 either.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–40 — How Many Years Have I Still to Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Barzillai the Gileadite, eighty years old and very wealthy, comes down to see the king over the Jordan, and David invites him to Jerusalem (vv. 31-33). His answer: how many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? (vv. 34-35). Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother — and let Chimham go instead (vv. 37-38). The king kisses him and blesses him, and he goes home (vv. 39-40).
verseByVerse.theology: It is one of the finest old-age passages in Scripture, and its power is the honesty of the inventory. He does not say he is too humble for a court. He says his palate has gone, his judgment is going, and music no longer reaches him.
verseByVerse.examples: And he asks for nothing except to be buried where his parents are. Chimham goes in his place, and four hundred years later people are still sheltering at a place called the lodging-place of Chimham near Bethlehem (Jer. 41:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan. Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man. And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem." But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward? Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you." And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you." Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home. The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan.'

Barzillai is one of the three men who brought bedding and cheese to Mahanaim when David arrived with nothing (17:27-29).

'Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.'

Eighty years old and very rich, and he fed an army.

The writer puts the two facts together, and there is a third implied. This man backed the losing side of a civil war at his own expense, at an age when nobody would have blamed him for staying out of it. If Absalom had won, an eighty-year-old landowner in Gilead who had provisioned David's army would not have kept his estate or his life.

'And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem."'

David offers him a place at court, which is the highest thing he has to give and is exactly what he gave Mephibosheth.

'But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?"'

Now one of the finest speeches in the Old Testament, and it is entirely about being old.

The first line is the frame for everything else. How many years have I still to live? He is not being morbid; he is doing arithmetic. He is eighty, and he is asking what would be the point of uprooting himself now.

'"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"'

Here is the inventory, and its power is that he is honest about it.
