Three questions, and each names something that has gone.

Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Judgment. The ability to tell good from bad, in the ordinary sense of appreciating things properly.

Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? His palate has gone. A court is a place of feasts, and food is wasted on him.

Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? His hearing, or his appetite for music, or both. And this one is the saddest, because David is a musician, and what Barzillai is saying is that the best thing about the king's table is a thing he can no longer enjoy.

Notice what he does not do. He does not pretend to be too humble for a court, or make a show of declining an honour, or claim he is more useful at home. He gives a plain and rather bleak account of what age has taken from him and concludes that the offer would be wasted on him.

That is a rare kind of honesty and it is available to very few people. Most of us would take the seat and pretend to enjoy the singing.

'"Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?"'

There is the sentence a great many people cannot say.

He has earned the place. He fed the king's army when it was starving and he risked everything to do it, and nobody in Israel would have questioned his right to be at that table. And he can see that what he would actually be, in Jerusalem, is an old man who needs looking after.

He would rather not be that.

'"Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?"'

He will walk him across the river and no further. Even the escort is measured out.

'"Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."'

The one thing he asks for is a grave.

That I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. Not a title, not land, not a position for himself. He wants to be buried where his parents are buried, in the town he has lived in for eighty years.

And then, having asked nothing for himself, he asks for somebody else. Here is your servant Chimham — almost certainly his son. Take him instead.

That is what an old man's request looks like when he has understood his own position. He cannot use the offer; the next generation can.

'And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you. And all that you desire of me I will do for you."'

And it was not a small thing. Four hundred years later, when Jerusalem has fallen and the last Judeans are fleeing to Egypt, the writer of Jeremiah notes where they stopped on the way: they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem (Jer. 41:17).

The lodging-place of Chimham. It is still there, still called after him, four centuries later. David gave that family land near Bethlehem — his own town — and the name outlasted the kingdom.

'Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home.'

A kiss at a river, and an old man walks back up into Gilead to die at home.

It is the last we hear of him — except that on his deathbed, forty years later, when David is giving Solomon the list of people to deal with, he includes one instruction that is not about revenge: but deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother (1 Kings 2:7).

He never forgot the cheese and the bedding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — The Words of the Men of Judah Were Fiercer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The men of Israel come to the king complaining that Judah stole you away and brought the king over the Jordan without them (v. 41). Judah answers that the king is their close relative and that they have eaten nothing at his expense (v. 42). Israel replies: we have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king? But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: The rebellion is over and the argument that starts here is worse, because it is not about Absalom. It is ten tribes against one, over precedence, and both sides are partly right.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer ends the chapter on the temperature of the exchange rather than its resolution, because there is no resolution. The very next verse is a man blowing a trumpet and saying we have no portion in David — and those are the exact words the ten tribes use when the kingdom finally splits for good (1 Kings 12:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?" All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?" And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"'

The war is over and the argument begins immediately.

The complaint is about precedence: Judah escorted the king across the river and the other ten tribes were not invited. That is the entire subject.

And the word they use is stolen, which is the same verb the writer used of Absalom stealing the hearts of the men of Israel (15:6). They are accusing Judah of doing to the king what Absalom did to them.

'All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?"'

Judah's answer has two parts and the first is honest and unhelpful: the king is our close relative. He is a Judahite. Of course we brought him home.

The second part is defensive: we have not taken anything, we have had no favours, we ate nothing at his cost. Which is true and is not what was being asked.

'And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?"'

Israel's reply is arithmetic. Ten shares — ten tribes to your one. We are the larger part of the country.

And their last question is a fair one. Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king? They were: verses 9 and 10 recorded the northern tribes arguing about it while Judah said nothing, and David had to send the priests to prod Judah into moving.

So both sides have a real point. Judah is the king's tribe. Israel is ten-elevenths of the nation and raised the question first. Neither is lying, and neither is listening.

'But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.'

And the chapter ends there, on the temperature of the argument rather than its outcome, because there is no outcome.

Read what the writer has chosen to record. Not who was right. Not what the king decided — David says nothing at all in this exchange and is not reported as intervening. Just that Judah shouted louder.

That is the last sentence of the chapter, and the first sentence of the next one is a man from Benjamin blowing a trumpet and saying: we have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel! (20:1).

Sheba's rebellion comes directly out of this quarrel, and it is over in a chapter.

The quarrel is not.

Two generations later, when Solomon is dead and his son Rehoboam has answered the north with a threat about scorpions, the ten tribes walk out of the assembly saying this: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16).

The same words. The kingdom splits at that sentence and never comes back together.

So this small squabble at a river crossing, about who got to escort the king over the water, is the first visible crack in the thing that finally breaks Israel in half. It is about nothing. It is about who was asked first, and whose relative he is, and who felt slighted, and it is louder on one side than the other.

Every large division starts somewhere this size.

20.title: Sheba's Revolt and the Wise Woman of Abel
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!"<sup>2</sup>So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself."<sup>5</sup>So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him.<sup>6</sup>And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us."<sup>7</sup>And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>8</sup>When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out.<sup>9</sup>And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.<sup>10</sup>But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>11</sup>And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab."<sup>12</sup>And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him.<sup>13</sup>When he was taken out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>14</sup>And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him in.<sup>15</sup>And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down.<sup>16</sup>Then a wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'"<sup>17</sup>And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening."<sup>18</sup>Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter.<sup>19</sup>I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?"<sup>20</sup>Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy!<sup>21</sup>That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall."<sup>22</sup>Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.<sup>23</sup>Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites;<sup>24</sup>and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder;<sup>25</sup>and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests;<sup>26</sup>and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.
20.overview:
Sheba is nobody — no army, no standing, no case, and the word the writer uses of him is the one Nabal's servants used of Nabal. What he has is a trumpet and twelve words. No portion and no inheritance are land words, the vocabulary of who owns what; the son of Jesse is the sneer Saul used when he would not say David's name. And he did not create the grievance. The previous chapter ended with ten tribes being shouted down in an argument about who got to escort the king across a river, and this man found them standing there humiliated and handed them a slogan.

His revolt is over in twenty verses and it does not matter. The sentence survives him: two generations later the ten tribes walk out of Rehoboam's assembly saying the same words, and the kingdom never comes back together. This chapter is showing a fracture, not a rebellion.

Then the bill for chapter 16 falls due, and it is paid by ten women who did nothing. Shut in a house, provided for, and finished at perhaps twenty — because two men conducted a political argument through their bodies on a roof. And Joab meets Amasa at a stone in Gibeon and kills him exactly as he killed Abner: the affectionate greeting, the hand on the beard, one blow to the stomach, no second stroke. The army stops and stares at the body in the road until somebody drags it into a field and throws a cloak over it, and then the column moves again.

And a woman with no office and no employer calls the commander-in-chief of Israel to the wall and stops a siege with three sentences. She is the third woman in this history to prevent a massacre with an argument, and we never learn her name. Then the cabinet list — and the first name on it is Joab's.
20.theology:
The sentence that outlives the man (v. 1). Twelve words in Hebrew, and they are quoted back a century later by ten tribes leaving for good: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16). Not similar — the same. Sheba loses; the sentence wins. He found the grievance fully formed and put words to it, which is all such men ever do.

The ten concubines (v. 3). They enter the story in a sentence that reads like a housekeeping note (15:16), are taken publicly on a roof because a counsellor wanted a bridge burned (16:22), and are now shut in a house with a guard and an allowance. He cannot take them back; he does not put them away; he provides for them — and the result is living as if in widowhood for perhaps forty years. They may have been twenty. They chose none of it: not the position, not being left behind, and certainly not the roof. Uriah did not choose it either, and neither did Tamar, and neither did twenty thousand men in a forest. Sin does not confine its damage to those who commit it, and the heaviest cost is usually paid by those with the least say in any of it.

David still will not use Joab (v. 6). He gives the order to Abishai and goes round the man — which is thin, since Abishai has spent his life doing what Joab does, and the troops who march out are called Joab's men. He has no command and the army is still his. And David's assessment is right: Absalom wanted the throne, Sheba wants the country in two pieces.

Abner's murder, repeated exactly (vv. 9-10). The same man, the same wound in the same place, the same appearance of intimacy used to close the distance, and the same detail recorded both times — without striking a second blow (3:27). He does not need one. Taking a man by the beard with the right hand to kiss him requires the other man to stand still and put his face forward; it only works if you are trusted, it occupies the right hand, and it puts his stomach eighteen inches from your left. Amasa's mistake is Abner's: neither saw a weapon, because a man who calls you brother is not a man you watch.

And this is worse than Abner. Abner was the enemy commander and had killed Asahel; Joab had a motive with a name on it, however illegitimately he acted. Amasa is the commander of the royal army, appointed by David personally under oath three weeks earlier. This is a serving officer murdering the man the king set over him, in the road, in front of the troops, to get his job back — and verse 23 records that he got it.

The body in the road (vv. 12-13). Every man who comes up the highway stops dead, the column jams, and the pursuit halts because thousands of soldiers are standing in a road looking at the king's commander lying in his own blood. They know what they are looking at. Then somebody drags him into a field and throws a garment over him, and the army moves again. That is the writer's comment and he makes none of his own: the problem was never the death, it was that it could be seen. Cover it and the campaign proceeds and nobody has to decide anything. Forty years later, dying, David still cannot say it himself and asks Solomon to (1 Kings 2:5).

The difference between the two wise women (v. 16). The woman of Tekoa was found by Joab, dressed by Joab and given a speech to recite, and the writer says so twice. This one has no employer, no script, and no part to play. She looked over a wall at a siege ramp and summoned the commander-in-chief of Israel to come and talk to her.

Her argument, in three moves (vv. 18-19). First, information rather than a plea: Abel is the town people come to when they want a matter settled, and you are battering its wall without having asked anybody anything. Then standing: I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel — there are loyal Israelites inside. Then the name for what he is doing: a city and a mother in Israel is how a town with dependent villages was spoken of, so knocking it down is not taking a fortress but killing a mother and orphaning what is around her. And finally the theological argument that ends it — why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD? The land is not his to destroy; every town is part of an inheritance God distributed. The verb is Abner's from Gibeon (2:26). Joab backs down instantly and even repeats her word.

Three times, and always a woman with an argument. Abigail came down a mountain track and talked David out of slaughtering every male in Nabal's household, on a theological argument about bloodguilt (1 Sam. 25). The woman of Tekoa changed the succession of Israel with a story. This one stops the army of Israel from destroying a city, from a wall, in three sentences — and then does the hard part, going to the town in her wisdom with no office and no authority and persuading it. She asks nothing for herself: no terms for her household, no reward, no safe conduct. We never learn her name.

The first name on the list (v. 23). Three weeks after the king appointed Amasa under oath in place of Joab (19:13), and after Joab answered that with a sword in a road, the establishment register records that Joab commands the army of Israel. No censure, no inquiry, no charge. The murder of the king's own commander in front of the troops is followed twelve verses later by an administrative note giving the murderer the job. That is the verdict on the chapter and on forty years: David could not touch him, said so after Abner (3:39), and was still saying it as a dying man handing the problem to his son.

A new office, and what it becomes (v. 24). Adoram over the forced labour is not in the chapter 8 list; somewhere in the intervening years the kingdom has acquired conscripted labour and a minister to run it. Under Solomon it becomes vast, and when he dies the northern tribes ask Rehoboam for one thing — lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke (1 Kings 12:4). He refuses; and King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death (1 Kings 12:18). The same office and quite possibly the same man. So both halves of the final split are already in this chapter: the slogan in verse 1 and the grievance in verse 24.

The list is a mercy and an indictment (vv. 23-26). It deliberately mirrors the one at the end of chapter 8, which came after the conquests and said: here is the kingdom, ordered, at its height. This one comes after Bathsheba, Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, the flight, the forest and Sheba, and says the same thing in the same form. The offices are filled, the government works, the ordinary business of governing goes on — which is how God generally keeps the world running after a catastrophe. And the reign is restored with the two things that will destroy the kingdom already inside the administration and drawing a salary.
20.examples:
Then: A woman with no office, no name recorded, and no one who sent her leaned over a city wall while the army of Israel was battering it down, summoned the commander-in-chief by name, told him what the town was and what the land was, and stopped the siege — then went inside and persuaded the whole city to do the hard thing she had promised on their behalf.

Now: Three things. Sheba is the study in how a fracture actually happens: he had no case and no following and it did not matter, because the grievance was already there and all he supplied was a sentence for it. Watch who hands people words for what they are already feeling. The body in the road is the second — the army could not move until it was covered, and once it was covered nobody had to decide anything, which is exactly how institutions handle a thing they have no intention of dealing with. And the woman of Abel is the third and the best. She did not plead, did not offer anything, and did not ask for a single thing for herself. She told a violent man what category his action belonged in, and then she went and did the part that cost something.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — We Have No Portion in David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!" (v. 1). All the men of Israel go after him; Judah follows the king (v. 2). And David comes to his house in Jerusalem and puts the ten concubines in a house under guard, providing for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The last sentence of the previous chapter was that Judah shouted louder than Israel. This is the next thing that happens. One man with a trumpet finds ten tribes already angry and gives them a sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: And it is the sentence. Two generations later the ten tribes walk out of Rehoboam's assembly with these words in their mouths — what portion do we have in David? To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16) — and the kingdom never comes back together.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!" So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem. And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite.'

There happened to be there. The writer's phrasing is almost dismissive, and it is the point.

Sheba is nobody. He has no army, no standing, no faction and no case; the word used of him is the one Nabal's servants used of Nabal and Shimei used of David. What he has is a trumpet and a sentence, and he is standing in the middle of an argument that was already burning.

'And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!"'

Twelve words in Hebrew, and they will eventually break the kingdom.

Look at what they do. No portion and no inheritance are land words — the vocabulary of tribal allotment, of what belongs to whom. He is saying that the house of David is Judah's business and the north has no stake in it.

And the son of Jesse is a sneer with a history. It is what Saul called David when he would not use his name (1 Sam. 20:27; 22:7).

Every man to his tents is the formula for breaking up a national muster — go home, this is not our war.

Now read the last sentence of the previous chapter: but the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel (19:43). Ten tribes have just been shouted down in an argument about who got to escort the king across a river, and they are standing there humiliated, and a man with a trumpet gives them a slogan.

He did not create the grievance. He found it fully formed and put words to it, which is all such men ever do.

'So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem.'

The whole north walks out.

The rebellion is over in twenty verses and it does not matter. What matters is that the country divided along the exact line it will divide along permanently: ten tribes on one side, Judah on the other.

Two generations from now, Solomon will be dead, and his son Rehoboam will answer a northern delegation with a threat about scorpions, and the assembly will break up. And this is what they say as they go: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16).

The same words. Not similar — the same. Sheba's sentence is quoted back a century later by ten tribes leaving for good, and the kingdom never comes back together.

Which means this chapter is showing us a fracture, not a rebellion. Sheba loses; the sentence wins.

'And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.'

Here is the bill for chapter 16, and it is paid by ten women who did nothing.

Follow what happened to them. They appear first in a sentence that reads like a housekeeping note: David left them to keep the house when he fled (15:16). Then Ahithophel advised Absalom to take them publicly, and a tent was pitched on the roof, and it was done in the sight of all Israel (16:22) — on the roof, which is where the whole business began (11:2).

Now David comes home and has to decide what to do with them, and there is no good answer available.

He cannot take them back; the law and the custom of the time made that impossible after what had been done. He does not put them away or send them off. He provides for them — a house, a guard, food, for the rest of their lives.

And the writer records the result in one clause: shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.

They may have been twenty years old. They will not marry, will not have children, will not leave that house, and will be fed and housed and forgotten for perhaps forty years.

They chose none of it. They did not choose to be royal concubines, they did not choose to be left behind, and they certainly did not choose the roof. Two men conducted a political argument through their bodies and this is what it cost, and the cost is being paid entirely by them.

The book has been doing this steadily. Uriah did not choose it. Tamar did not choose it. Twenty thousand men in a forest did not choose it. Sin does not confine its damage to the people who commit it, and the ones who pay most are usually the ones with the least say in any of it.

David is provided for. Absalom is dead. These ten are alive, and shut in a house, and that is the last we hear of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–13 — Is It Well with You, My Brother?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David gives Amasa three days to call up Judah; Amasa takes longer (vv. 4-5). So the king sends Abishai after Sheba, and Joab's men go with him (vv. 6-7). At the great stone in Gibeon Amasa meets them, and Joab's sword drops out of its sheath as he steps forward (v. 8). And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died (vv. 9-10). Joab and Abishai go on after Sheba. A young man stands over the body calling the troops to follow Joab, and the whole army stops and stares at it in the road until someone drags it into a field and throws a garment over it (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every element of this is Abner's murder repeated. The affectionate greeting, the hand, the stomach, one blow, and the phrase the writer used then and uses again now — and Amasa's mistake is the same as Abner's, which is not seeing a weapon in the hand of a man calling him brother.
verseByVerse.examples: And the difference is that Amasa is the king's own appointed commander. David's single act of discipline against Joab was to give this man his job, and Joab has answered it in the road at Gibeon with a sword. The army halts and looks at the body because it does not know what has just happened to the chain of command.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself." So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him. And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us." And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri. When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out. And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri. And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab." And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him. When he was taken out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself." So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him.'

Amasa's first task in his new job, and he is late.

The writer does not say why. He was Absalom's general three weeks ago and may have found Judah unwilling to muster for him; he may simply have been slow. What matters is that the delay gives Joab a reason to be in the road at Gibeon.

'And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us."'

Note who he speaks to. Abishai, not Joab.

David is still refusing to give Joab a command, and he is going round him through his brother — which is a thin arrangement, since Abishai has spent his whole life doing what Joab does.

And his assessment is right: Sheba will do us more harm than Absalom. Absalom wanted the throne; Sheba wants the country in two pieces, and David can see it.

'And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.'

Joab's men. He does not have a command and the army is still his.

'When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out.'

The sword falls out of the sheath as he walks.

Commentators have argued about this verse for centuries and the Hebrew is awkward. It may mean that the sword genuinely worked loose and he picked it up, so that a man standing in front of him sees him bend down and stand up with a blade in his hand and thinks nothing of it. It may be that the whole arrangement was contrived so that the weapon would be in his left hand while his right hand was empty and reaching out.

Either way the effect is the same, and the writer tells us about it before the greeting, so that we watch the greeting knowing what is in the hand.

'And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.'

Is it well with you, my brother?

They are cousins. Both are David's nephews; their mothers were sisters. Brother is not even much of an exaggeration.

Taking a man by the beard with the right hand to kiss him is the most intimate greeting available between men in that culture. It requires him to stand still and put his face forward and let you touch him. It is a gesture that only works if you are trusted, and it occupies the right hand, and it puts the other man's stomach eighteen inches from your left.

'But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died.'

Now go back seventeen chapters and read it again.

And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died (3:27).

The same man. The same wound, in the same place. The same method: an appearance of intimacy used to close the distance, and then one blow.

And the same detail both times: without striking a second blow. He does not need one. He knows exactly where to put it and how hard, and the writer records his competence twice.

Amasa's mistake is Abner's mistake. Neither of them saw the weapon, and neither of them was looking for one, because a man who takes you by the beard and calls you brother is not a man you are watching.

Now consider what Joab has actually done here, because it is worse than Abner.

Abner was the enemy commander and there was a blood feud: Abner had killed Asahel. Joab had a motive with a name on it, however illegitimately he acted.

Amasa is the commander of the royal army, appointed by David personally, under oath, three weeks ago. Killing him is not a private vengeance; it is a serving officer murdering the man the king put over him, in the road, in front of the troops, in order to get his job back.

And he gets it. Verse 23 says so.

This is what happens when a king cannot discipline his general. David's one attempt to act against Joab was to give the command to somebody else, and Joab answered it with a sword at Gibeon, and by the end of the chapter he is back at the head of the list and nothing whatever has been said about it.

'Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.'

He steps over the body and carries on with the campaign.

'And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab."'

A soldier stands beside the corpse shouting a loyalty formula.

Read the order of the names: whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David. Joab first. That is either a slip or it is not, and either way it is an accurate description of who is running this army.

'And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him.'

Here is the writer's comment on the whole business, and he makes it without a word of his own.

The army will not walk past. Every man who comes up the road sees the king's commander lying in the middle of it in his own blood and stops dead, and the column jams, and the pursuit of Sheba halts because thousands of soldiers are standing in a road looking at a body.

They know what they are looking at. It is not a battle casualty. It is the man the king put in charge, killed by the man he replaced, on the way to a war.

So the young man drags him off the road into a field and puts a cloak over him, and the moment he is covered the army moves again.

That is the sentence to keep. The problem was never the death; the problem was that it could be seen. Get it out of the road and throw something over it and the column marches on and the campaign proceeds and nobody has to decide anything.

Nothing in this book is said about Amasa afterwards, until David is dying and tells Solomon: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war (1 Kings 2:5).

Forty years later, on his deathbed, he still cannot say it out loud himself. He asks his son to do it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — A City and a Mother in Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sheba is pursued to Abel of Beth-maacah in the far north, and Joab's men throw up a siege ramp and begin battering the wall (vv. 14-15). Then a wise woman called from the city, "Hear! Hear! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'" (v. 16). She reminds him what the town is: they used to say in former times, "Let them but ask counsel at Abel," and so they settled a matter. I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD? (vv. 18-19). Joab answers that he wants one man (vv. 20-21). She takes it to the city, and they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: She is hired by nobody and scripted by nobody. The woman of Tekoa came with Joab's words in her mouth; this one calls him to the wall on her own authority and argues with him, and she is the third woman in this history to stop a massacre with a speech.
verseByVerse.examples: And her argument is not a plea. She tells him what the place is — a town people came to for counsel — and then names the category he is about to put himself in: destroying a city and a mother in Israel, swallowing up the heritage of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him in. And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down. Then a wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'" And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening." Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter. I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?" Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy! That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall." Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him into the city.'

Sheba runs the length of the country and ends up in the far north, near the sources of the Jordan, about as far from Jerusalem as it is possible to get and still be in Israel.

And note what he has left: all the Bichrites, his own clan. The ten tribes who followed him out of the argument in chapter 19 are not with him. They went home.

'And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down.'

They build a siege ramp against an Israelite town and start knocking the wall in.

'Then a wise woman called from the city, "Hear! Hear! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'"'

A woman shouts down off the wall and summons the commander-in-chief of Israel to come and talk to her.

She is called a wise woman, which is the same phrase used of the woman of Tekoa, and the difference between them is the whole point.

The woman of Tekoa was found by Joab, dressed by Joab, and given a speech by Joab to recite; the writer says so twice. This one has no employer. Nobody sent her, nobody scripted her, and she is not performing anything. She has looked over a wall at a siege ramp and decided to negotiate.

'And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening."'

The exchange is short and businesslike, and he stops the assault to have it.

'Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter."'

She opens by telling him what the town is.

Abel had a reputation. It was a place people came to for a ruling — a town of counsel, where disputes were brought and settled, and there was evidently a proverb about it.

So her first move is not a plea for mercy. It is information: you are battering the wall of the place people come to when they want a matter resolved, and you did not think to ask anybody anything before you started.

'"I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?"'

Three sentences, and each one puts a name on what he is doing.

I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. She establishes standing. She is not a rebel and neither is the town; there are loyal Israelites inside those walls.

You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. The phrase a mother in Israel is how an important town with dependent villages was spoken of — a place that has daughters. Knock it down and you are not taking a fortress; you are killing a mother and orphaning everything around her.

Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD? And there is the theological argument, and it is the one that finishes it. The land is not Joab's to destroy. Every town in Israel is part of an inheritance God distributed, and a general who flattens one is not conducting an operation; he is consuming what belongs to God.

The verb is the same one Abner used at Gibeon — shall the sword devour forever? (2:26).

'Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy!"'

He backs down instantly, and even repeats her verb.

This is Joab, who killed Abner at a gate and Absalom in a tree and Amasa in a road last week. He does not argue with her, does not threaten her, and does not tell her to send out the elders. He answers the argument on its own terms.

'"That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall."'

He states his actual objective, which is one man, and she agrees to it before consulting anybody.

'Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.'

The woman went to all the people in her wisdom.

She has no office and no authority. She goes to the town, tells them the terms, and persuades them — and a whole city does what she says.

The result is brutal and it is arithmetic: one head over a wall instead of a town under it.

Now stand back, because she is the third of these in this history and the pattern deserves a name.

Abigail came down a mountain track with two hundred loaves and stopped David from slaughtering every male in Nabal's household — and she talked him out of it with a theological argument about bloodguilt (1 Sam. 25). The woman of Tekoa stood in front of the king and changed the succession of Israel with a story. This woman stops the army of Israel from destroying a city, with three sentences, from a wall.

Three times in this history a massacre is prevented, and every time it is prevented by a woman with an argument, and none of them holds any office at all.

And there is something else about this one. She never asks for anything for herself. She does not negotiate terms for her own household, or ask to be spared, or trade information for a reward. She argues about what the town is and what the land is, and then she goes and does the hard part.

We never learn her name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Now Joab Was in Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; Benaiah over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; Adoram over the forced labor; Jehoshaphat recorder; Sheva secretary; Zadok and Abiathar priests; and Ira the Jairite was David's priest (vv. 23-26).
verseByVerse.theology: The list mirrors the one at the end of chapter 8 and does the same work: the period of crisis is over, and here is the kingdom in ordered operation again.
verseByVerse.examples: And the first name on it is Joab. He murdered the king's appointed commander in a road three weeks ago and he is back at the head of the army, which is the entire verdict on the chapter and on David's forty-year inability to touch him. Note also the new post: Adoram over the forced labour — and forced labour is the grievance the ten tribes name when they secede, and Adoram is the man they stone to death (1 Kings 12:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder; and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests; and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites;'

There it is, in the first four words.

Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel.

Three weeks ago the king appointed Amasa to that post, personally, with an oath, and told him he would hold it from now on in place of Joab (19:13). Joab met Amasa in a road, called him brother, took him by the beard, and killed him.

And here is the establishment list, and the first name on it is Joab's, and nothing has been said about any of it.

Not a word of censure. No inquiry, no charge, no demotion. The murder of the king's own commander in front of the army is followed, twelve verses later, by an administrative note recording that the murderer has the job.

That is the verdict on the chapter and it is the verdict on forty years. David could not touch him. He said so at 3:39 after Abner — these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I — and he is still saying it as a dying man, handing the problem to a son who will finally do what he never could (1 Kings 2:5-6).

'and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;'

Here is a name that was not on the list in chapter 8.

Adoram is in charge of the forced labor, and that office is new. There was no such post when the earlier cabinet was recorded (8:16-18). Somewhere in the intervening years the kingdom has acquired a system of conscripted labour and a minister to run it.

Hold that name, because it is going to matter enormously.

Under Solomon the forced labour becomes vast, and when he dies the northern tribes come to Rehoboam with one request: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (1 Kings 12:4). He refuses, with the line about scorpions. And then this happens:

Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (1 Kings 12:18).

The same office and, if the years allow it, very possibly the same man. The tribes stone the labour minister and go home saying what portion do we have in David? — which is Sheba's sentence from verse 1 of this chapter.

So both halves of the final split are already in this one chapter. The slogan is in verse 1 and the grievance is in verse 24.

'and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests;'

'and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.'

The list closes the way the list in chapter 8 closed, and the parallel is deliberate.

That one came after the conquests, and it said: here is the kingdom, ordered, at its height. This one comes after Bathsheba, Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, the flight, the forest, and Sheba, and it says the same thing in the same form. The offices are filled. The government works. Somebody is the recorder and somebody is the secretary and somebody keeps the priesthood.

That is a real mercy and should be seen as one. A kingdom that has been through what this one has been through still has a cabinet, and the ordinary business of governing a country goes on — which is how God generally keeps the world running after a catastrophe.

The list is also an indictment, because of the first name on it and the fourth.

Joab at the top, unpunished. Adoram over the forced labour, unnoticed. The reign is restored, and the two things that will destroy the kingdom are already inside the administration, drawing a salary.

21.title: The Gibeonites' Vengeance; War with Philistines
21.text: <sup>3</sup>David said to the Gibeonites, 'What shall I do for you? And how shall I make atonement, that you may bless the heritage of the LORD?' <sup>7</sup>But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan son of Saul, because of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul. (ESV)
21.overview:
Chapter 21 belongs to the book's final appendix (chapters 21–24), which is structured as a symmetrical chiasm around the two great poems of chapters 22 and 23. It opens with a three-year famine whose cause is revealed through inquiry: Saul had violated the covenant with the Gibeonites (a protected people since Joshua's time), and blood guilt lies on the land. David makes atonement by handing over seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, who execute them. The chapter then records four episodes of war with Philistine giants — the descendants of Goliath's family — and ends with Elhanan killing one of them.

The chapter is difficult for modern readers on multiple levels: the execution of Saul's descendants seems to punish the innocent for the guilty; the Rizpah episode (the mother of two of the executed, who guards their bodies for months against the birds and animals) is one of the most haunting scenes in the book. Both difficulties deserve engagement rather than avoidance. They are part of the honest, morally complex world of the OT that the NT's fuller revelation of God will eventually bring to its resolution in Christ.

sections.title: The Famine and the Gibeonites
sections.commentary:
Three years of famine prompt David to seek the LORD's face. The answer: there is bloodguilt on the land for what Saul did to the Gibeonites — a people who had been protected by a covenant oath sworn in the name of the LORD since the days of Joshua (Josh. 9:15–21). Saul apparently killed many of them in a fit of nationalistic zeal, violating the ancient covenant. The land cannot yield its produce until the breach is addressed. The covenant with the Gibeonites is older than the monarchy; its violation cannot be undone by royal decree; atonement must be made.

David's consultation with the Gibeonites and their request — seven of Saul's sons, to be executed at Gibeah before the LORD — is troubling. The sons are not guilty of their father's sin; they are dying as representative substitutes for a violation they did not commit. But this is the logic of ancient covenant law: the bloodguilt of a household extended to the household, and only the shedding of blood could atone for it. The NT sees this pattern as a shadow of the great substitution — the innocent dying for the guilty — that reaches its perfect expression in Christ. The difference is that in the NT, the substitute is the innocent one who volunteers and whose death has infinite atoning capacity.

David's specific protection of Mephibosheth — exempt from the seven because of the covenant with Jonathan — is the chapter's grace note. In the midst of difficult covenantal necessity, the covenant of chapter 9 holds. The man David brought to his table will not be handed over to the Gibeonites. The covenant is not dissolved by crisis. Alistair Begg notes that Mephibosheth's exemption is the practical demonstration that the covenant of grace operates on its own logic, independent of the surrounding circumstances: the man after God's own heart will not break his covenant even when the surrounding situation might seem to justify it.

Rizpah's vigil over her sons' bodies — from harvest until rain fell, guarding the exposed corpses against birds and animals, day and night — is one of the most heartbreaking acts of maternal love in the entire Bible. When David hears of it, he is moved to bring her sons' bones and the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and give them proper burial. Rizpah's grief becomes the catalyst for the belated honor of the house of Saul. The mother who would not let the birds touch her dead sons moves the king to restore the dignity of the dead. In the economy of God, grief honestly expressed sometimes accomplishes what official channels could not.

sections.title: Four Battles with Philistine Giants
sections.commentary:
The four brief battle narratives that close the chapter all share the same pattern: a descendant of the giants (the Rephaim — a race of warriors of extraordinary size and skill associated with the territory the Philistines now occupied) threatens an Israelite, and is killed by one of David's warriors. The first battle comes closest to disaster: David himself is nearly killed, and Abishai rescues him. After this, David's men swear he will not go into battle again — the lamp of Israel must not be extinguished. The king is too valuable to risk in personal combat; the heroic individual warrior must give way to the protected figurehead.

The four warriors — Abishai, Sibbecai, Elhanan, Jonathan — are representatives of the mighty men whose full list appears in chapter 23. The chapter is building toward the great conclusion of the book by establishing the quality of the men around David: these are the faithful who have fought alongside him, whose heroism sustains the kingdom even when the king himself can no longer fight in the front lines. Elhanan's killing of Goliath's brother (the parallel passage in 1 Chron. 20:5 clarifies that this is the brother, not Goliath himself) closes the Goliath narrative that began in 1 Samuel 17: the family of the giant that David defeated is finally fully subdued by the army of Israel.

21.theology: Covenant Obligation Across Generations. The Gibeonite episode establishes the sobering principle that covenant obligations persist beyond the individuals who made them, and that violating ancient covenants produces consequences that must eventually be addressed. This is the OT's moral equivalent of what the NT calls the ripple effects of sin: Saul's violence against the Gibeonites produced a national famine that David only understood through inquiry, and addressing it required a costly act of covenantal restitution. The church that ignores historical injustices done in the name of God does not thereby escape their consequences; addressing them honestly, as David addressed the Gibeonite grievance, is the path toward restoration.
21.examples:
Then: Rizpah's vigil is the chapter's most enduring image: a mother's love that will not allow the dead to be dishonored, persisting through months of exposure, moving eventually the king himself to do what should have been done long before. Her grief accomplishes what official process had not. The God of Scripture consistently uses the grief of the marginalized to move the powerful toward the justice they owe.

Now: The chapter's most important pastoral word for the contemporary church is the examination of what ancient covenants have been violated and what genuine atonement — acknowledgment, restitution, restoration — those violations require. The question David asked the Gibeonites — what shall I do for you, and how shall I make atonement? — is the question faithful leadership must ask about its inheritance of historical wrong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-14 - The Gibeonites and the Famine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three years of famine. David inquires of the LORD and learns it is because Saul broke the ancient covenant with the Gibeonites. The Gibeonites request seven of Saul's male descendants; David spares Mephibosheth but hands over seven others who are hanged. Rizpah's vigil over the bodies moves David to gather and bury all of Saul's family's bones.
verseByVerse.theology: The episode raises difficult questions about divine justice and covenantal obligation. Saul broke a covenant Israel had made in Joshua's day; the famine is the divine response. David honors the Gibeonites' request for blood-justice. Kidner notes that the account is not presented as a model to be imitated but as a record of how ancient covenant obligations worked in the ancient world - and of how seriously God takes sworn oaths.
verseByVerse.examples: Rizpah's vigil is one of the most moving passages in the narrative. She sits beside the exposed bodies of the seven from the beginning of harvest until rain falls - six months - keeping birds and animals away. Her love is fierce and helpless. David hears of her vigil and it moves him to gather all of Saul and Jonathan's bones for proper burial. Rizpah's love accomplishes through faithfulness what no political argument could.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell upon them from the heavens. And she did not allow the birds of the air to come upon them by day, or the beasts of the field by night.
verseByVerse.commentary: Rizpah was Saul's concubine and the mother of two of the seven. Her vigil over the exposed bodies - sitting on a rock for six months in sackcloth, driving away birds and animals - is a statement of love against powerlessness. She cannot undo the judgment; she can refuse to let their bodies be dishonored further. When David hears of her faithfulness, he gathers the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and buries them together with the seven in the tomb of Kish. Rain falls. The land mourns and is comforted. God answered prayer for the land after that.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four accounts of battle with Philistine giants. David grows faint; his men make him swear not to go to battle anymore, lest you quench the lamp of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase the lamp of Israel applied to David is remarkable: the king's life is not his own; he is the source of light for all the people. MacArthur notes that this understanding of royal responsibility - the king's life sustaining the life of the nation - runs from David to its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who is the light of the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner observes that the four accounts of battles with Philistine giants include the brother of Goliath and men of great stature - confirming that the family or clan of giants remained a persistent threat. These brief records of faithful soldiers fighting obscure battles are a reminder that most of God's work in history is done by people whose names are barely remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David's men swore to him, You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The four brief battle accounts - David nearly killed by Ishbi-benob, the killing of Saph, the killing of Goliath's brother, the killing of a giant with twelve fingers and twelve toes - are connected by the recurring theme of faithfulness in obscure places. David's mighty men fight and win battles that no one will celebrate. The plea to David not to risk himself is both practical and poetic: lamp of Israel is a title that will be echoed in the Psalter and applied in its fullest sense to the one who said I am the light of the world.

22.title: David's Song of Deliverance
22.text: <sup>2</sup>'The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence. <sup>50</sup>For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.' (ESV)
22.overview:
Chapter 22 is David's great song of deliverance — virtually identical to Psalm 18 — placed here as the theological summary of his entire life. It is the longest single poem in the book, and it sweeps from the most intimate personal experience (the cords of death encompassed me) to the most cosmic declaration (the LORD lives, and blessed be my rock). The poem has five movements: crisis and cry (vv. 1–7), theophanic response (vv. 8–20), righteousness and reward (vv. 21–31), divine empowerment for battle (vv. 32–46), and closing doxology (vv. 47–51).

The poem is David's retrospective theology of his entire life: the valleys and the summits, the Saul years and the Absalom years, the victories and the failures — all of it is narrated through the lens of the God who saved him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul (v. 1). It is not a naive poem that pretends the difficulties were not real; the opening verses describe genuine terror: the cords of death, the torrents of destruction, the cords of Sheol (vv. 5–6). But the poem's movement is entirely from crisis to praise, from peril to exaltation, from the pit of verse 5 to the doxology of verse 50.

Paul quotes verse 50 in Romans 15:9 as evidence that the Gentile mission was always part of God's plan: David's declaration — I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations — becomes Paul's evidence that the inclusion of the Gentiles is the fulfillment of the Davidic covenant, not its contradiction.

sections.title: The Rock, the Fortress, the Deliverer
sections.commentary:
The poem's opening catalogue of metaphors for God — rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, stronghold, refuge, savior — is the most concentrated accumulation of divine-protection language in the OT. Each metaphor carries specific resonance: rock (tsur) suggests permanence and solidity, the reliable surface that does not shift underfoot; fortress (metsudah) suggests an elevated, strongly defended place; deliverer (mephalti) suggests someone who creates space, who extricated the trapped; shield (magen) suggests immediate physical protection; horn of salvation suggests the power of a charging animal turned to the defender's benefit. Together they constitute a theology of divine protection that encompasses every dimension of human vulnerability.

The prayer at the center of the opening section — I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies — establishes the poem's logic: the cry precedes the saving, and the saving precedes the praise. This is the grammar of all authentic worship: genuine need, genuine prayer, genuine rescue, genuine doxology. The poem traces exactly that sequence across fifty-one verses. David is not praising an abstract deity but the specific God who was his specific rock across the specific valleys of his specific life. R. C. Sproul writes that the poetry of the Psalms (and this poem especially) is the primary scriptural evidence that emotional, experiential engagement with God is not sub-rational but supra-rational — the form of language that the soul uses when theological content has become personal reality.

sections.title: The Theophanic Response
sections.commentary:
The description of God's response to David's cry is one of the most vivid theophanies in the OT: the earth trembles, the foundations of heaven shake, smoke goes from his nostrils, fire from his mouth, darkness under his feet, riding on a cherub and flying, making darkness his canopy, voice like thunder, lightning like arrows, the channels of the sea seen, the foundations of the world laid bare. This is not merely poetic decoration; it is theology — the God who hears and comes to rescue does not come as a benign grandfather but as the warrior-king whose approach shakes creation.

The purpose of this dramatic divine approach is, remarkably, personal: He reached down from on high and took hold of me; he drew me out of many waters... He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me (vv. 17–20). The cosmic warrior comes to the crisis of one person. The God who shakes the earth does so to draw one man out of many waters. This is the consistent mystery of OT prayer theology: the infinite God attends to the particular cry of the finite human with the same comprehensive engagement he brings to governing the cosmos. He is not too great to be personal; his greatness is the ground of his personalness. Tim Keller writes that verse 20 — he rescued me because he delighted in me — is the simplest and most astonishing summary of grace in the OT: not 'he rescued me because I deserved it' but 'because he delighted in me.' The rescue is rooted in the divine pleasure, the undeserved, free delight of God in his elect servant.

sections.title: Righteousness, Power, and Doxology
sections.commentary:
The righteousness section (vv. 21–25) has troubled many commentators: David claims righteousness, integrity, clean hands — was this not the man who committed adultery and murder? The resolution is in the section's context: David is speaking of his integrity in relation to Saul specifically (he did not raise his hand against the LORD's anointed), and more broadly of the general orientation of his life toward God rather than the claimed perfection of every act. The man after God's own heart is not the man who never sinned; it is the man who never abandoned the fundamental orientation of heart toward God, who repented genuinely when he fell, and who returned to the path of covenant faithfulness. This is the righteousness David claims — relational faithfulness, not moral perfection.

The empowerment section (vv. 32–46) traces the divine equipping of the warrior: strength like a deer's feet, trained hands for battle, a divine shield, the girding of the warrior — all of it God's work, enabling David to do what he could not have done in his own strength. The final doxology (vv. 47–51) returns to the opening: the LORD lives, my rock, my deliverer. The circle is complete. The poem that began with crisis ends with praise; the God who was invoked in terror is worshipped in triumph; the nations will hear — for this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations. The Davidic covenant's global horizon is declared: the God who saved one shepherd-king is the God who will be praised among all the Gentiles.

22.theology: The Song of the Delivered: A Theology of a Life. Chapter 22 is the OT's most comprehensive summary of what it means to live in covenant relationship with the living God — across an entire life, through its defeats and victories, through moral failure and genuine repentance, through betrayal and restoration. The poem does not pretend the life was clean; it testifies that the God who met him in the clean moments also rescued him from the consequences of the unclean ones. The theology of the psalm is the theology of grace: not that I was worthy, but that he delighted in me; not that I was strong, but that he girded me with strength; not that I was never in many waters, but that he drew me out.
22.examples:
Then: Paul's quotation of verse 50 in Romans 15:9 shows that the Davidic song of praise among the nations is the OT ground of the Gentile mission. The song that David sang as thanksgiving for personal deliverance is simultaneously the charter of universal proclamation: the God who saves one person in one crisis is the God who saves people from every nation through the one act of salvation in Christ.

Now: The poem invites the believer to write their own version: to identify the rocks and fortresses of their specific life, the specific crises from which the specific God drew them out. The Psalms are not merely documents to be read; they are templates to be inhabited, models showing the grammar of experiential faith that takes the specific texture of each person's life as the material for praise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sings this song when the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul. It is virtually identical to Psalm 18. He praises God as his rock, fortress, shield, and deliverer. He describes his cry in distress, God's theophanic rescue, his own integrity as the basis of God's blessing, and his God-empowered victories. It ends with praise to God who gives great salvation to his king.
verseByVerse.theology: The placement of this song near the end of 2 Samuel is deliberate: it is the theological summary of David's life. After all the complexity of adultery, murder, rebellion, grief, and civil war, the final word is praise. Sproul notes that David's claim to integrity in verses 21-25 - The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness - is not self-righteousness but covenant faithfulness: David, unlike Saul, returned to God in repentance and walked with God through suffering.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that the cosmological imagery of God's theophanic rescue - he bowed the heavens, darkness was under his feet, he rode on a cherub, coals of fire blazed - is the language of Exodus and Sinai. David's personal rescue is set in the context of the God who parts seas and moves mountains. His salvation is not small; it participates in the vast narrative of divine redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence. I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary: The accumulation of metaphors for God in the opening verses is breathtaking: rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, stronghold, refuge, savior. David is piling image upon image, each one born from actual experience: the caves where he hid from Saul, the battles where God fought for him, the moments of rescue that came without explanation except divine intervention. The song moves from personal crisis (the waves of death encompassed me) through theophany (the LORD roared from heaven) to victory and praise. It ends: The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation. This is the theology of the whole book distilled: God is the rock; the king is the servant; all the victories belong to the LORD.

23.title: David's Last Words and His Mighty Men
23.text: <sup>3</sup>'The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel has said to me: When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass sprout from the earth. <sup>5</sup>For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure.' (ESV)
23.overview:
Chapter 23 divides into two distinct sections: David's last words (vv. 1–7), a brief but majestic poem that functions as his theological testament, and the list of his mighty men (vv. 8–39), the roster of the warriors who fought beside him across his lifetime. Both sections are theologically significant: the last words summarize the covenant that has defined his reign; the list of mighty men honors the human instruments through whom God's purposes were accomplished.

David's last words are introduced with a striking formula: the oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel. The titles accumulate: son of Jesse (human origin), raised on high (divine elevation), anointed (covenant election), sweet psalmist (the primary gift of his life). And then the content: just rule in the fear of God is like the morning light, like the sun on a cloudless morning. This is David's vision of kingship at its best — not power for its own sake but the illuminating, life-giving presence of a just ruler who fears God. And the ground of his confidence: the everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure.

sections.title: David's Last Words: The Everlasting Covenant
sections.commentary:
The last words are a meditation on the covenant of chapter 7, seen from the end of a life. David does not rehearse all his victories or all his failures; he returns to the theological center of his kingship: the everlasting covenant God made with him, ordered in all things and secure. The phrase is one of the most compressed and beautiful descriptions of God's covenant in the entire OT. Ordered — it is arranged with care, every element in its proper place. Secure — it cannot be undone; it will not fail; it holds even when the covenant-holder fails. This is the covenant David stakes his hope on at the end: not his own performance but the arrangement of a God who makes covenants that hold.

The vision of just rule — the ruler who dawns like morning light, like the sun shining forth, like rain making grass sprout — is David's description of what the king is meant to be. It is simultaneously a description of his best moments and an aspiration that points beyond him: no human king, including David, has consistently been the morning light for his people. The king who is always the morning light, whose reign is always the sun on a cloudless morning, whose rule always makes the grass sprout — that king has not yet come when David writes these words. He is writing toward his own fulfillment, toward the Son who will fulfill every element of the covenant perfectly: just rule, fear of God, everlasting covenant, the morning light that never sets. Sinclair Ferguson writes that David's last words are less a farewell than a forward look: he is describing not what he has been but what the covenant promises, and trusting that the God whose covenant is ordered in all things and secure will bring it to pass in One greater than David.

sections.title: The Mighty Men: Honoring the Faithful
sections.commentary:
The list of David's mighty men is the OT's most extensive honor roll — thirty-seven names, with brief descriptions of specific acts of heroism for the most prominent. The Three, the first group, performed extraordinary individual acts: Josheb-basshebeth killed eight hundred in one encounter; Eleazar stood and struck the Philistines until his hand was weary and stuck to the sword, and the LORD brought a great victory; Shammah stood in a field of lentils when all the other men fled and killed the Philistines there, and the LORD saved by a great victory. The theology of the Three's exploits is consistent: the human act of courageous refusal to flee, and then the LORD's great victory. The courage creates the conditions; God provides the outcome.

The episode of the three who broke through the Philistine lines to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem (v. 16) is one of the most tender moments in the military catalogue. David had expressed a longing — not a command — for water from his hometown well. Three men broke through enemy lines to bring it to him. And David refused to drink it: Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives? He poured it out as a drink offering to the LORD. The act is extravagant, costly, misunderstood by anyone who thinks only in terms of utility.
